8951667468462afb8046ae873a155947851a52c6.summary: arXiv:2611.28426v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to assess employment candidates, yet consistent interview scoring does not establish whether automated recommendations are supported by sufficient evidence. This study introduces the Evidence Sufficiency and Decision Stability Assessment (ESDSA), which combines criterion-level evidence classification, deterministic quotation traceability and stability checks across linguistic variants assessed as substantively equivalent. We evaluated four approaches (scoring-only, evidence-aware, traceability-based and integrated ESDSA v2) using 540 synthetic interview responses from 60 evaluated scenario families across Software Engineering, Customer Support and Operations. In held-out testing (216 responses), integrated ESDSA achieved 85.19% actionable coverage and 3.80% disagreement among actionable recommendations against AI-assisted provisional references. Evidence-aware evaluation achieved 92.59% coverage and 4.50% disagreement; scoring-only evaluation achieved 71.30% coverage and 1.95% disagreement. The integrated stability gate deferred 11 additional previously actionable decisions, ten of which had agreed with provisional references. The findings demonstrate trade-offs between evidential constraints, decision consistency and abstention, rather than overall superiority of the integrated framework. ESDSA offers a reproducible methodology for examining when automated interview recommendations should be actionable or deferred. Synthetic responses and AI-assisted references do not establish real-world recruitment validity.
8951667468462afb8046ae873a155947851a52c6.title: When AI Should Not Decide: Evidence Sufficiency and Decision Stability in Automated Job Interviews

89ee3cb4461141edda6b34b085a726b102af4210.summary: arXiv:2611.30139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: General-purpose large language model (LLM) agents can develop complete solvers for combinatorial optimization problems. Their specialization, however, often relies on workflows engineered for individual problems, limiting the reuse of development expertise. We propose AutoSECO, an automated skill evolution method that learns reusable solver-development guidance from experience. The challenge is that external evaluation measures the completed solver, while the skill guides decisions during development. AutoSECO connects this feedback to guidance deficiencies by tracing performance shortfalls through solver code and recorded development decisions. Revisions are expressed as general instructions and retained only if a fresh solver developed under the revised skill achieves a lower mean evaluation gap. Evolved solely on the traveling salesperson problem (TSP), the skill guides fresh agents in developing solvers for capacitated vehicle routing, job-shop scheduling, and three-dimensional bin packing without further skill evolution. On TSP, the final mean benchmark gap is 0.52\%, compared with 0.98\% for the skill-evolution baseline SkillOpt. Across all four problems, the evolved skill achieves better aggregate results than no skill guidance, the initial skill, and SkillOpt. The same frozen skill also supports solver development under alternative model--harness configurations. These findings suggest that solver-development experience can be retained as reusable expertise for general-purpose LLM agents.
89ee3cb4461141edda6b34b085a726b102af4210.title: AutoSECO: Automated Skill Evolution for Cross-Problem Combinatorial Optimization with General-Purpose LLM Agents

89f60c4ab2f858c0ce832600678b6a1ffb1a6da4.summary: arXiv:2611.32159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Minimizer schemes sample at least one $k$-mer from every window of $w$ consecutive $k$-mers via a total order $\pi$ on $\Sigma^k$. For DNA ($\sigma = 4$), state-of-the-art lookup schemes such as GreedyMini and OptMini optimize a binary order ($2^k$ ranks) and lift it to $\Sigma^k$ by ranking one bit-plane primarily and breaking $2^k$-way ties lexicographically on the other bit-plane. At $(w, k) = (12, 5)$, this projection locks sets of $32$ DNA $5$-mers into contiguous blocks and restricts the active universal hitting set (UHS) prefix to $448$ of $1024$ $5$-mers, giving exact expected DNA density $2246214544 / 2^{34} \approx 0.1307468945$ for OptMini (k5-w12-13.txt) and $2248978620 / 2^{34} \approx 0.1309077849$ for GreedyMini (w12_k5.gm). We bypass binary lifting and optimize directly over native $4$-ary permutations ($|\Sigma^k| = 1024$) from scratch via: (i) an exact de Bruijn endpoint transfer-matrix dynamic program over $B(4, 4)$ ($256$ states), (ii) a weighted set-cover ratio initializer (SetCover4) producing a compact $U = 314$ UHS prefix, (iii) bitmask-sparse simulated annealing preserving the zero-cost $w$-walk-free tail invariant, and (iv) two-pass $O(N)$ exact best-insertion sweeps with large-neighborhood ruin-and-recreate search. The resulting explicit $4$-ary order achieves exact expected DNA density $2234289615 / 2^{34} \approx 0.130052772292$ (density factor $1.690686$), cutting charged windows by $11924929$ contexts ($-0.530890\%$ relative) below OrensteinLab/Minimizers and $14689005$ ($-0.653141\%$) below w12_k5.gm at $8200$-byte lookup storage ($1280$ bytes bit-packed). Warm-start relaxation stalls at $U = 379$ ($0.1301728789$), whereas native $4$-ary initialization breaks $32/32$ high-bit blocks across all $2+2$ nucleotide partitions.
89f60c4ab2f858c0ce832600678b6a1ffb1a6da4.title: Breaking the Binary-Lifting Barrier for DNA Minimizer Density: Exact Optimization of a Native 4-ary Order at (w, k) = (12, 5)

8a1c222c2e75ab21b45fbf04d23f5fc55ecbab48.summary: arXiv:2611.29290v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An intervention that improves one agent can break another, and adding a stronger harness on top need not repair the damage. Agent interventions such as skills, harnesses, and extra inference budget are nonetheless usually credited with one average gain, measured under one setup. We ask instead when each intervention helps and which failure it repairs. A matched factorial study over nine benchmarks, four models, four skill conditions, four harness levels, and three budgets, with nearly 0.9 million trajectories, changes one axis at a time. No configuration is best everywhere, interventions interact rather than add, and a harness can absorb a skill's gain, rescue a failure the skill causes, or leave the gain intact. The failure left by the current system points to the fix: missing knowledge to a stronger model, execution errors to a richer harness. Yet feedback is not recovery: a matched recovery repairs mainly failures that leave a visible error signal. Skills that evolve from the agent's own experience hit a bottleneck: they rarely beat a short human-written skill, can learn dataset shortcuts, break when moved to another model, and cannot supply missing facts, which outside information does. A benchmark-level switch to the model favored by a 20-task labeled pilot achieves both higher performance and lower cost than always using the stronger model. Agent interventions should be judged by which failure they repair and under which configuration.
8a1c222c2e75ab21b45fbf04d23f5fc55ecbab48.title: Which Failure Does an Intervention Repair? When Agent Interventions Help, and Where Self-Evolving Skills Stall

8a62ea05f675eb6ddfd1b499e750e87c3d7bc103.summary: Release: datasette-charts 0.1a0 I've been thinking about this problem for over a year now, but on Sunday I finally fired up Claude Fable 5.2 to build an initial prototype. The prototype went so well that this is now a full plugin. You can try it out in Datasette Lite here . It looks like this: The new charts plugin works against any table or arbitrary SQL query in Datasette. It defines several different chart types (using vendored D3 , Observable Plot , and topojson-client ), each with a set of heuristics for identifying when they might be a good match for a specific set of rows. Those suggestion thumbnails at the top are actual visualizations driven by the data, and selecting one pulls up the full chart along with tools for modifying it. You can also manually construct a chart from scratch. As with other Datasette visualization plugins, the current state of your chart is persisted in a #fragment in the URL - so you can bookmark charts or share them with others. The most important feature is that the charts take all rows into account . Previous charting plugins like datasette-vega would only show charts for the current page of results, generally up to 100 rows. The new plugin compiles each chart to a SQL query that aggregates across the entire result set (potentially millions of rows) using GROUP BY, time bucketing, and window functions. Each query returns a result capped at 5,000 rows, suitable for display on the chart. The plugin uses sampling to help suggest charts for larger tables without evaluating the full result set. I'm really happy with this initial release of the plugin. It's still very much an alpha, but it's the closest I've got to the dream of Datasette helping visualize data with as little required direction from the user as possible. 8a62ea05f675eb6ddfd1b499e750e87c3d7bc103.title: datasette-charts 0.1a0

8a866e68afd32a18f4cf16e3acabd8b8c1cf3e7a.summary: arXiv:2611.28849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When visual context makes an ordinary request unsafe to answer as asked, a blanket refusal may leave the user's need unresolved. Choosing how to help requires distinguishing an established hazard from a condition that still needs verification, a distinction that binary safety labels leave unspecified. We formulate this decision through four actions: allow, warn, review, and refuse. To ground these decisions in verifiable evidence, we build a corpus of 20,126 training audits and the JudiBench benchmark, connecting each action to diagnostic judgments, source evidence, and controlled context changes. Our guard, JudiAct, separately states what the source establishes, what condition governs the help, and how the rules apply. It then checks these three brief review items against the original inputs to predict diagnostic labels and a handling action. Supervised training learns individual judgments while comparing label assignments across related cases. A second stage swaps one review item at a time, using the resulting audit feedback to refine review generation. On JudiBench, JudiAct improves request and answer Macro-F1 by more than 28 percentage points over its 4B backbone. Across nine public benchmarks, it outperforms state-of-the-art guards on the mean delivered-answer score in both pre-generation and post-generation settings, cutting MM-SafetyBench attack success from 40.78% to 25.30%.
8a866e68afd32a18f4cf16e3acabd8b8c1cf3e7a.title: Guarding with Judgment: Learning to Intervene for Multimodal Safety

8b001cc651ce93867a56934e89a7fe3bce66ddd6.summary: arXiv:2601.08777v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) to serve users with heterogeneous and potentially conflicting preferences is a central challenge for personalized and trustworthy AI. We formalize an ideal notion of universal alignment through test-time scaling: for each prompt, the model produces $k\ge 1$ candidate responses and a user selects their preferred one. We introduce $(k,f(k))$-robust alignment, which requires the $k$-output model to have win rate $f(k)$ against any other single-output model, and asymptotic universal alignment (U-alignment), which requires $f(k)\to 1$ as $k\to\infty$. Our main result characterizes the optimal convergence rate: there exists a family of single-output policies whose $k$-sample product policies achieve U-alignment at rate $f(k)=\frac{k}{k+1}$, and no method can achieve a faster rate in general. We show that popular post-training methods, including Nash learning from human feedback (NLHF), can fundamentally underutilize the benefits of test-time scaling. Even though NLHF is optimal for $k=1$, sampling from the resulting (often deterministic) policy cannot guarantee win rates above $\tfrac{1}{2}$ except for an arbitrarily small slack. This stems from a lack of output diversity: existing alignment methods can collapse to a single majority-preferred response, making additional samples redundant. In contrast, our approach preserves output diversity and achieves the optimal test-time scaling rate. In particular, we propose a family of symmetric multi-player alignment games and prove that any symmetric Nash equilibrium policy of the $(k+1)$-player alignment game achieves the optimal $(k,\frac{k}{k+1})$-robust alignment. Finally, we provide theoretical convergence guarantees for self-play learning dynamics in these games and extend the framework to opponents that also generate multiple responses.
8b001cc651ce93867a56934e89a7fe3bce66ddd6.title: Asymptotic Universal Alignment: A New Alignment Framework via Test-Time Scaling

8b0f406a3f87479e56338f768bf53371daa99ff7.summary: arXiv:2611.32882v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) workloads has significantly increased data center (DC) power demand. Frequent operational and configurational changes, such as load surges caused by dynamic workload allocation, can induce electromagnetic transients (EMTs) whose accurate prediction is critical for reliable DC operation and maintenance. Although high-fidelity EMT solvers are widely adopted for transient analysis, their computational cost limits large-scale and multi-scenario studies. Digital twins address this computational bottleneck by emulating the behavior of a physical system and enabling fast prediction in place of expensive high-fidelity simulation. However,data-driven digital twins are non-adaptive and fail to generalize once the DC configuration changes. To address this limitation, this paper proposes an adaptive EMT-level digital twin for DCs based on in-context learning (ICL) with large language models (LLMs). We formulate the EMT prediction task as a system identification problem under parametric uncertainty and develop a GPT-2-based framework that adapts to unseen DC configurations at inference time from a small set of EMT trajectory samples, without model retraining. The proposed framework is validated on three representative EMT scenarios and benchmarked against three baseline non-adaptive twins. Results demonstrate superior prediction accuracy, improved adaptability to unseen operating conditions, and substantial computational speedups compared to high-fidelity EMT simulation.
8b0f406a3f87479e56338f768bf53371daa99ff7.title: Adaptive Electromagnetic Transient-level Digital Twins for Data Centers via In-Context Learning with LLMs

8b3afedc919fa6a00a38c1387ca21afe261624bb.summary: arXiv:2611.32946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The use of AI agents among the general public has been increasing exponentially throughout 2026, though it is often hard for users to determine which configuration is most effective for their personal use. To help provide clarity here we introduce ShellBench, 100 day-to-day tasks based on more than 10 million user requests, each set in a realistic workspace with messy files and competing data sources, and graded for both correctness and safety. We evaluate 12 models across 5 agent harnesses at 3 reasoning levels for a total of 53,100 rollouts, 20% of which are on tasks designated for public release. We find that model choice impacts performance more than harness choice, but the three leading models differ by only 1.1 percentage points. GPT-6.1 Sol passed 61.4% of attempts at about one-sixth of GPT-6 Astra's estimated token cost per attempt, while GPT-6 Astra led at 62.5%. We also found that harness choice had little effect on either performance or safety with all harnesses scoring between 42.9 (Claude Code) and 45.2 (OpenClaw) for pass@1.
8b3afedc919fa6a00a38c1387ca21afe261624bb.title: ShellBench: What Matters More for AI Agents, Models, or Harness for Everyday Tasks

8b7133a7b1b789f048e60a380750bc0f6ed12b4f.summary: arXiv:2611.31571v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autoformalization translates a natural-language statement into a formula that captures its intent, which depends on the statement's context: the background that disambiguates it. LLMs make autoformalization practical, but their probabilistic output carries no formal guarantees. We propose techniques for safe autoformalization that certify one-sided logical adequacy: a formula sufficient for the intent is safe to enforce, and a formula necessary for it is safe to rely on. We use LLMs to generate candidate formulas and order them by logical strength in an Entailment Graph (EG), an ordering a solver decides. Each edge carries a residual and a co-residual, the two adjoints of the entailment order, all fixed by the candidate pool alone. In a context, two searches return the sufficient frontier, the weakest candidates that entail the statement, and the necessary frontier, the strongest candidates the statement entails; each step is one local check against an edge's residual or co-residual. The frontiers bracket the statement and yield the ambiguity residue, which holds exactly of the situations the candidates certify neither as satisfying nor as violating it; the statement is ambiguous precisely when the residue is satisfiable. For natural-language statements and contexts, an LLM entailment oracle decides the checks; it is sound if it accepts only checks that hold, and complete if it accepts every check that holds. We prove that a sound oracle makes the search safe regardless of pool quality, and that a complete one makes the frontiers tight. On security-critical AWS properties, EGs are safe in all 20 cases of an expert-adjudicated study, where majority vote over equivalence clusters and Universal Self-Consistency are unsafe in 25% and 10%. An ablation with the same oracle but no graph is unsafe in 25% and rejects every candidate in another 30%. We machine-checked our proofs in Lean.
8b7133a7b1b789f048e60a380750bc0f6ed12b4f.title: Safe Autoformalization: Sufficiency and Necessity with Entailment Graphs

8bc1a07fd62abe586edf886885a703ca1007c966.summary: arXiv:2611.32114v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) depicts coronary anatomy and cardiac fat, but segmentation alone does not ensure anatomically consistent measurements. We propose an automated framework that combines deep learning with anatomical reasoning for quantitative cardiac phenotyping. Its anatomical measurement module uses graph geometry, branch identity, and surrounding structures to define vessel-specific pericoronary adipose tissue (PCAT) sampling and a surrogate epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) compartment. The latter also generates training targets without requiring expert pericardium contours. A companion module quantifies coronary calcium on non-contrast CT. Component-wise benchmarking was conducted on five public datasets: ImageCAS, ImageCAS-X, COCA, Visual Lab, and MultiD4CAD. On ImageCAS-X Test-160, lumen segmentation with validation-selected post-processing achieved a Dice score of 0.9133 and a clDice score of 0.940, exceeding the corresponding published CAS-Net point estimates. In the four-split ImageCAS evaluation, the four-member ensemble outperformed the single ResEnc-L model. Analysis of 800 paired scans showed that PCAT attenuation measurements differed between whole-vessel and lumen references. External EAT evaluation showed strong volume correlation and good spatial overlap. Explicit anatomical rules make the resulting measurements interpretable and inspectable. In practice, the framework provides a standardized pipeline for processing cardiac CT cohorts and quantifying coronary calcium, PCAT, and EAT for population-level analysis and comparison across studies. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/HarryTRAN207/CardiacCT-Research
8bc1a07fd62abe586edf886885a703ca1007c966.title: An Automated Framework Integrating Deep Learning and Anatomical Reasoning for Cardiac Phenotyping From CCTA

8be86a0b0af72b483a25ca2ac0f89a85bfbae0a7.summary: arXiv:2611.31686v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM-generated counseling dialogues are increasingly used for training and evaluating mental-health systems, yet existing evaluations focus largely on response quality and final outcomes rather than how support unfolds over time. We conduct a trajectory-centered evaluation of process fidelity across ten human, reconstructed, and synthetic counseling datasets. Our results show that synthetic dialogues often reach plausible endpoints but differ from human support in recovery dynamics and turn-by-turn responsiveness. While generation design can shift global properties such as recovery timing and trajectory structure, contingent patient--counselor responsiveness remains consistently lower in fidelity across models and generation paradigms. Our experiments on controlled synthetic datasets show that targeted generation interventions can narrow the gap with real data on several trajectory-level measures, but do not fully recover interactional fidelity, with turn-level responsiveness remaining limited. We release three controlled synthetic datasets comprising 2,050 dialogues, together with annotations and the evaluation framework.
8be86a0b0af72b483a25ca2ac0f89a85bfbae0a7.title: Right Destination, Wrong Journey: Synthetic Counseling Dialogues Miss Human Interactional Dynamics

8c21885a65f4f49bf2179b17c3e132d114f1180e.summary: arXiv:2609.33295v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An agent can complete a task while exhibiting undesirable behavior during execution. Developers need tests for the specific behaviors encountered in deployment, beyond fixed benchmark suites. We present TraceDance, an agent system that constructs targeted benchmarks from deployment traces for user-specified undesirable behaviors. For efficient construction, Anchor-and-Confirm combines programmable retrieval with candidate-level confirmation by a Flash large language model (LLM), while the Anchor Synthesis Loop generates and revises specifications for custom behaviors. The benchmarks use decision-point continuation to evaluate an LLM's next turn at a recorded decision point with a behavior-specific rubric, without a reference answer or environment replay. Experiments in coding and general tool use draw on 252,557 sessions and produce 107 benchmarks with 4,125 instances, fulfilling 95.3% of build-target requests. Both human annotators confirm the requested behavior in 84% of sampled instances, and the automated grader's agreement with human pass/fail judgments is comparable to that between the annotators. Nine frontier LLMs achieve a mean pass rate of only 26.7%, showing that they still struggle to respond appropriately at the evaluated decision points. Analysis across behavior-specific benchmarks further reveals weaknesses in how current LLMs behave as agents. By turning deployment problems into targeted benchmarks, TraceDance could serve as a key component of the recursive self-improvement (RSI) loop.
8c21885a65f4f49bf2179b17c3e132d114f1180e.title: TraceDance: An Automated System for Building Agent Behavior Benchmarks from Real-World Agent Deployment Traces

8c4d2c72f271043d51f9c3735d444a4afe0fd972.summary: arXiv:2610.09108v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Policy learning drives many of the most consequential and heavily-invested applications of reinforcement learning today. Yet the core optimization problem it rests on (maximizing expected return) is notoriously non-convex, even under a direct policy parameterization, and the field has largely responded by avoiding it: optimizing convex surrogate approximations of the return under trust-region constraints (NPG, TRPO, PPO, AWR). We show that this seemingly unstructured problem is not actually structureless. In log-density-ratio coordinates $y := \log[\pi/\pi_n]$, the exact per-iteration objective, computable via per-decision importance sampling (PDIS), is a difference-of-convex-constrained difference-of-convex (DC-constrained DC) program. This structure lets us move beyond surrogate approximations: it recovers CPI, NPG, TRPO, and AWR as special cases along interpretable axes, and it opens a multi-step axis $k$ that couples consecutive decisions. We solve the per-iteration program with sequential convex programming (SCP), the standard solver for difference-of-convex problems, and establish inner-loop descent and limit-point stationarity for the theoretical algorithm, together with a conditional outer-loop performance bound. Empirically, multi-step Convex-Concave RL (CCRL) wins on diagnostic MDPs where credit must propagate across a horizon (its advantage growing with the dependency length), is competitive with a tuned PPO on classic control, and on a clinically motivated, stochastic, mid-horizon sepsis simulator converges markedly faster than tuned PPO to the same near-optimal survival, with an 11.3% higher area under the training curve. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/UMass-SCALAR-Lab/Convex-Concave-RL
8c4d2c72f271043d51f9c3735d444a4afe0fd972.title: Convex-Concave Reinforcement Learning

8d07686f4dae0025276705c90a457c13c6becb86.summary: arXiv:2609.22086v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deployed software agents face a continuous stream of user requests while their foundation-model weights remain frozen between releases. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) via external memory offers a practical path to continual adaptation, yet prior methods largely assume programmatic verifiers, cheap retries, or a single global prompt. Creative software breaks these assumptions, as open-ended visual briefs lack ground truth, VLM judges are noisy, and multi-step tool executions are costly and confounded by external assets. We present Designer-RSI, which evolves a modular skill bank from unlabeled design trajectories for an agent spanning over 230 raster, vector, and layout tools. Designer-RSI couples widening (acquiring new skills for recurring capability gaps) with deepening (revising failing skills by contrasting successful and failed runs), and screens updates through a Pareto-style matched replay gate that requires strict gains on sampled briefs without local regressions. Across held-out product briefs, eight external benchmarks, and two backbones, traffic-driven evolution outperforms static documentation skills, lifts execution success up to 99.8%, improves requirement fulfillment, and reaches up to a 67.6% blind win rate over the base agent. Ablations further show that skill acquisition and revision are strongly synergistic: neither suffices alone, and reliable gains require evolving coverage and execution quality together.
8d07686f4dae0025276705c90a457c13c6becb86.title: Designer-RSI: Evolving Procedural Memory from User Traffic for Graphic Design Agent

8d87e8b0d6f1b25e6a5325f1880c813651b287b3.summary: arXiv:2611.29818v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A home robot that helps with chores needs to know where objects are, but people move objects according to routines that change and later change back. The robot's memory must adapt to the new routine without erasing experience that may become useful again. One approach is to have a language model maintain written summaries of the home from the robot's own observations, but existing evaluations of such memories use static worlds. We explore simulated households where a resident gets sick, recovers, and later gets sick again. We compare a rule that keeps every room an object has been seen in, language-model memories that store only written summaries, and language-model memories that can also read the raw history of sightings. The rule outperforms every summary-only memory, and giving language models the sighting history closes the gap. Surprisingly, writing summaries on top of the history adds nothing we can measure. When the illness returns, methods that keep the history search better than they did the first time, while summary-only methods show no consistent improvement. Deleting the first illness from memory removes all of the rule's gain and part of theirs. The summaries recorded where objects went during the illness but rarely distinguished sick-day patterns from normal routines. Our findings suggest that common approaches to summarizing robot memories struggle to remember facts about a routine that might return, highlighting the need for future benchmarks to evaluate this aspect of long-term robot deployment.
8d87e8b0d6f1b25e6a5325f1880c813651b287b3.title: How Should a Home Robot Update Its Memories When Human Routines Change?

8d96d2ea7063a3a7a0fb41bbc05c0ac26243c819.summary: arXiv:2611.32031v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real-world applications of modern AI systems require generalization to both unseen environments and novel human users. The field of zero-shot coordination (ZSC) has focused primarily on deploying AI to cooperate with novel partners in otherwise familiar environments. Popular population-based methods achieve this by partnering the agent with a diversity of simulated human users during training in a fixed environment, but does not consider the more realistic scenario where both the users and the environment are unseen during training. Recently, training across environments has been explored in training a single self-play agent, which shows better generalization on both novel human users and unseen environments. In this work, we ask whether jointly modeling partner diversity and environment diversity yields stronger coordination with novel partners in novel environments. We introduce Cross Environment Co-Play (CECP), a two-stage framework that first trains a population of self-play agents across a distribution of procedurally generated environments, and then trains a cooperator policy against this partner population. To further couple social and environmental reasoning, we add a next-state prediction module that encourages representations to encode both partner behavior and task structure. We evaluate CECP on both a neuroscience-inspired cooperative foraging task, and the popular ZSC benchmark Overcooked, under held-out partner and held-out environment conditions. CECP achieves the strongest performance among the compared baselines and attains state-of-the-art results under our evaluation protocol for human-AI collaboration. We analyze the model's latent representation encoded by the next-state prediction module, showing it can not only improve the performance of the cooperative AI, but also provide more interpretable latents, demonstrated by the inference of partner skill levels.
8d96d2ea7063a3a7a0fb41bbc05c0ac26243c819.title: Unifying Partner and Environment Diversity to Improve Human-AI Coordination

8dd2e13c55a7d6c08ce176e264039e297d280e52.summary: arXiv:2611.31974v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Games, especially modern AAA games, challenge language models to perceive complex scenes, control actions, and make decisions over long horizons. Existing game benchmarks primarily test language models as computer-use agents that query a language model throughout play, incurring repeated inference cost and, in real-time games, acting while the environment continues to evolve. We ask whether coding agents can learn from game interaction to develop standalone game-playing programs that run without language model inference. We thus introduce Coding4Games, a benchmark for evaluating whether coding agents can develop standalone programs that play modern games through visual observations and standard game inputs. Coding4Games has three defining features: 1) Diverse Modern Games, covering 15 games with diverse visual, strategic, and control demands; 2) Development-Test Separation, in which a coding agent uses a sandbox and the standard player interface to iteratively develop a program, after which the selected program is frozen and independently tested without language-model inference; and 3) Outcome and Process Evaluation, which measures not only game performance and reliability but also how agents use feedback, revise programs, and resolve problems during development. Across 15 games, the best program per game outscores the strongest GUI baseline on 13 and ties it on one. The human player outscores all agents on 10 games. We additionally examine the effects of development budgets. Coding4Games evaluates whether coding agents can turn their understanding of complex interactive environments into programs that work reliably on their own.
8dd2e13c55a7d6c08ce176e264039e297d280e52.title: Coding4Games: Can Modern Coding Agents Play Modern Video Games?

8de233372fae5463ee442952f501eab2aef7b9fc.summary: arXiv:2611.32055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) strengthens model capabilities through feedback from humans and environments. However, emerging evidence suggests that reward optimization can produce outputs whose errors are harder for humans to detect. To address this issue, we construct ITHV (the Image-Text Hallucination Verifiability Dataset), comprising 2,728 visually grounded instances that distinguish between obvious hallucinations, which humans readily detect, and elusive hallucinations, which humans struggle to identify. We then propose DAPO-V, an extension of DAPO that maximizes correctness subject to a budget on verifiability-aware risk. Specifically, DAPO-V combines a verifiability-aware reward with adaptive dual control, where larger penalties are assigned to incorrect responses on questions with lower human verification accuracy. An adaptive multiplier further adjusts the penalty strength according to risk-budget violations. Across three MLLM base models, DAPO-V improves overall accuracy while substantially improving accuracy on elusive hallucination questions by 5.78--9.72 percentage points over accuracy-only DAPO. We further test DAPO-V with a blinded human study, which shows that hallucinations are more readily detected in DAPO-V than those of the base model.
8de233372fae5463ee442952f501eab2aef7b9fc.title: More Powerful, Less Verifiable? Mitigating Hard-to-Verify Hallucinations in MLLM's Reinforcement Learning

8dfa089798ffbdbf2e1f7b3746206abc83daf2fb.summary: arXiv:2611.31932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model unlearning aims to remove the influence of designated training data while preserving unrelated model capabilities. Existing likelihood-based methods commonly optimize against fixed forget sequences, providing only negative supervision on what the model should not generate and overlooking the states visited by the evolving unlearned policy. We introduce Contrastive On-Policy Self-Distillation (CPSD), a new unlearning framework that constructs an explicit knowledge-reduced target distribution and distills it along the model's own trajectories. Given a student rollout, a frozen reference model evaluates each token under a plain context and a privileged context containing the forget information. CPSD treats the resulting distributional shift as a knowledge-associated direction and reverses it to obtain a counterfactual unlearning target. The student is then trained to match this target at every rollout position while retaining its utility on unrelated data. We further introduce a privacy-enhanced variant that combines distributional unlearning with lightweight sequence-level suppression. Experiments under OpenUnlearning show that CPSD improves the forgetting-utility trade-off over NPO across TOFU forget-set sizes and Llama models ranging from 1B to 8B parameters. On MUSE-News, the privacy-enhanced variant improves all reported knowledge, memorization, privacy, and utility metrics over NPO.
8dfa089798ffbdbf2e1f7b3746206abc83daf2fb.title: Contrastive On-Policy Self-Distillation for LLM Unlearning

8e35f8c8542e2d35b699310d61f3defa7df0d391.summary: arXiv:2611.28732v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables foundation models to perform unseen tasks from context without parameter updates. In robotic manipulation, a human video provides the context that specifies how a task should be performed. However, scaling human-video ICL on world-action models (WAMs) faces two challenges: task-level human-robot pairs are not temporally aligned with robot actions, and standard action losses allow policies to rely on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts rather than tracking the context. We present Entangle, an in-context world-action model that maps a single human video and current robot observations to future visual states and executable actions. To scale temporally aligned training data, we convert recorded robot videos into matched human contexts via video-to-video generation, supplemented by real paired recordings. For model training, we combine variable-length video windows with an intra-task contrastive objective that distinguishes the paired action trajectory from other executions of the same task, preventing task-identity shortcuts. Without task-specific fine-tuning, Entangle improves steadily as aligned training data scales, reaching an average score of 83.5/100 across six unseen tasks on an Astribot S1 robot, and achieves a 69.5% average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, outperforming Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points. Under Context-OOD, although trained only on scene-aligned pairs, Entangle transfers context-specified behaviors across rearranged layouts and substituted tools.
8e35f8c8542e2d35b699310d61f3defa7df0d391.title: Entangle: Scaling Human-Video In-Context World-Action Models across Unseen Tasks and Contexts

8e6f7bbdab8c200aa7ceb790de6fdfdd7cf3cf9f.summary: arXiv:2606.24231v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multimodal driving planning faces a long-standing tension between two paradigms: scoring-based methods benefit from dense reward supervision but are confined to a fixed action vocabulary, while anchor-based methods generate proposals dynamically yet suffer from sparse supervision constrained to a single ground-truth trajectory. In this work, we propose FlowR2A, which resolves this tension by reframing simulation-based rewards from discriminative targets into generative conditions. By learning the reward-conditioned action distribution from dense trajectory-reward pairs with a flow-matching decoder, FlowR2A unifies the dense supervision of scoring-based methods with the proposal generation of anchor-based methods in a single generative model, forcing the model to internalize the correlation between an action and its outcomes in safety, progress, comfort, and rule compliance. To balance hard safety constraints against soft progress objectives, we introduce fine-grained per-timestep reward conditioning and reward noise augmentation. The generative formulation naturally supports controllable test-time sampling via reward guidance and anchored sampling, producing high-quality proposals. FlowR2A achieves state-of-the-art results on the NAVSIM v1 and v2 benchmarks, with multimodal proposals of substantially higher quality than prior methods.
8e6f7bbdab8c200aa7ceb790de6fdfdd7cf3cf9f.title: FlowR2A: Learning Reward-to-Action Distribution for Multimodal Driving Planning

8e88be4de707423b1905320e593cfcbe5a5c9e79.summary: arXiv:2611.28972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) achieve strong performance on vision-language tasks but often remain vulnerable to distribution shifts due to their fixed parameters during inference. While Test-Time Training (TTT) offers a pathway for dynamic adaptation, existing approaches suffer from prohibitive computational overhead due to multiple sampling and the risk of error reinforcement from biased self-generated supervision. In light of this view, we propose RoTTT (Rotation-based Test-Time Training), a simple and efficient TTT approach that enables instance-specific refinement at inference time. For each test instance, RoTTT performs a small number of gradient updates by predicting the rotation angle of the input image. The known rotation angles naturally serve as a reliable self-supervised signal, enabling lightweight and stable adaptation without requiring additional annotations. Extensive experiments across multiple vision-language benchmarks demonstrate that RoTTT consistently improves performance across different MLLMs, providing a practical and efficient paradigm for on-the-fly MLLM adaptation.
8e88be4de707423b1905320e593cfcbe5a5c9e79.title: Learning from Another Angle: Rotation-Based Test-Time Training for Multimodal Large Language Models

8e90207dc8af755b2f8e81c79c888bc6a1dcb0ea.summary: arXiv:2607.18454v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantifying the risk of rare failures in language models, such as those triggered by adversarial distribution shifts or very large-scale deployments, requires estimating probabilities far too small for random sampling. While recent work has formalized low-probability estimation, existing pipelines remain fragile in the rarest regimes: standard evaluation losses can become unstable or poorly matched to asymmetric safety costs, and estimators can suffer zero-estimate collapse or systematic bias. In this work, we introduce the Shifted-Power Bregman (SPB) Loss, a proper scoring rule that remains finite for zero-estimates and offers tunable asymmetry between underestimation and overestimation penalties, making all estimators, including those whose estimates collapse to zero, comparable under an explicit cost profile. We also propose Gradient Activation Adaptive Multilevel Splitting (GA-AMLS), which adapts rare-event Monte Carlo methods to the continuous activation space of language models. Specifically, GA-AMLS uses a gradient-based MCMC kernel to navigate activation space, reducing zero-estimate failures of input-space search and replacing the independence assumptions of prior activation-space estimators with conditional sampling under an explicit, heavier-tailed activation prior. Experiments on small transformer models reveal distinct bias and cross-token dispersion profiles: GA-AMLS often outperforms the strongest baseline under symmetric evaluation, while methods with overestimation bias prevail under asymmetric penalties and have lower cross-token dispersion. Our findings highlight that estimator choice should be matched to deployment context. More broadly, our work establishes activation space as a tractable domain for rare-event estimation in language models, circumventing the brittleness of discrete input-space search.
8e90207dc8af755b2f8e81c79c888bc6a1dcb0ea.title: Estimating Rare Events in Language Models with Proper Evaluation

8edf310cbf9c0577d1442636c4cd5696451a55aa.title: Gauth Personal Study Agent

8f2b8a5267063890690be0524076415d19d9c4d1.summary: arXiv:2605.26667v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory systems to remain consistent across long-horizon interactions, but little empirical work has been done to understand the specific failure modes and design choices that these systems present. Existing benchmarks report aggregate question-answering accuracy and treat memory systems as black boxes, making it impossible to attribute an incorrect answer to a particular failure mode of the system. We introduce MemFail, a diagnostic benchmark that isolates the failure modes of modern LLM memory systems. We begin by formalizing memory systems as the composition of three canonical operations -- summarization, storage, and retrieval -- and identify the potential failure modes induced by each. Based on these hypothesized failure modes, we construct five datasets spanning four tasks, each adversarially designed to test a specific operation of a memory system. Using these datasets, we evaluate four state-of-the-art memory systems on MemFail and demonstrate how MemFail can be used to empirically understand the tradeoffs induced by differences in memory system architectures.
8f2b8a5267063890690be0524076415d19d9c4d1.title: MemFail: Stress-Testing Failure Modes of LLM Memory Systems

8f51180f74ef58bd6e8a02766173ba47bcfc69c5.summary: When agent ships code faster and faster, human review is no longer possible. Which brings 2 problems, at least for me: 1. I need to understand what my agent changes as quickly and easily as possible, cuz I don't wanna lose track of the current status of my product, or be the main bottleneck in shipping code. 2. I don't trust what my agent tells me. Many times, I've been suffered from agent telling me "all is well", then say "you are right, sorry, I missed..." after code failed on production. To mitigate those problems, I made Genesis, a skill for coding agent to generate a beautiful flow chart to understand all the business flows, flag all risk changes and untested code between commits. It worked very well on me, so I benchmarked it against vanilla Claude code and Codex: Vanilla → With Genesis 1. Test gaps caught: Claude Code 8% → 38% · Codex 4% → 23% 2. False alarms per review: Claude Code 2.1 → 0.7 · Codex 1.4 → 0.5 3. Real risks found per review: Claude Code 2.9 → 2.8 · Codex 2.4 → 2.4
8f51180f74ef58bd6e8a02766173ba47bcfc69c5.title: Show HN: Genesis Map – Visualize your agent's changes. See where they can break

8f68fcce44bbd5634c63451b87ece46b8dd2396b.summary: arXiv:2611.31460v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coding agents open many pull requests (PRs) that claim to make software faster. Most such claims also give a reason, such as "cache the result" or "read the file once". A stopwatch can show that code got faster, but not that it got faster for the stated reason. We present Below, a pipeline that checks these reasons at the kernel level. From 1,343 runtime-performance PRs in the AIDev dataset, Below extracts the mechanism each PR claims and maps it to the kernel and hardware signals that must change if the claim is true. A build agent that never sees the claim rebuilds the code before and after each PR. Below then measures both versions with plain timing runs, hardware counters and LTTng kernel traces. Most claims are not measured: 57.3% of the PRs offer only reasoning or no evidence, and only 31.4% state an effect size. Of 82 analyzed PRs, 32 ran faster, 28 showed no clear change and 22 ran slower. The expected signal of the claimed mechanism appeared in 34 PRs (20 in kernel-trace signals alone), and 42 PRs also changed their output. Kernel signals move about 1.7 times as often for a faster PR's claimed mechanism as for mechanisms it did not claim; the instruction count barely separates them (1.15 times).
8f68fcce44bbd5634c63451b87ece46b8dd2396b.title: Below the Stopwatch: Checking the Performance Claims of Coding Agents in the Kernel

8f794ae83f386ae6cdc44d2421207be7854824cc.summary: arXiv:2606.10089v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this work, we develop theoretical foundation for flow matching with neural-network-parameterized conditional velocity fields. We establish convergence guarantees for gradient descent in the over-parameterized 2-layered ReLU neural network regime. We derive generalization bounds for the conditional velocity-field matching objective. Building on these results, we provide Wasserstein-distance guarantees for the samples generated by the induced flow. Our analysis is based on generalization bound for multi-task representation learning with unbounded losses, which may be of independent interest beyond flow-based generative modeling. These theoretical results are validated through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world image benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/qishuoyin/FlowMatchNN.
8f794ae83f386ae6cdc44d2421207be7854824cc.title: A Theory on Flow Matching with Neural Networks

8f9c3726e861a00be405dc5979bf44f68eb32c4e.summary: tl;dr: We just open-sourced Wakeshift, which lets any MCP server serve interoperable events via MCP Events or harness-specific bridges. This allows MCP servers to push events to harnesses that don't support MCP Events today, including Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. Hi folks! The MCP Events spec was approved and merged five days ago, allowing MCP servers to emit events directly to agent subscribers. ( https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol... ) This allows MCP developers to push events directly to agents for long-running tasks (e.g. CI, crawls, starting agents) or external actions (e.g. emails, human approvals, alerts). However, the catch is that support for MCP Events is very light. Claude Code and Codex don't support it at all, and most of the implementations support the draft version rather than the merged spec. Many harnesses can work around this with plugins or hooks, but every MCP server has to build it for each harness. Wakeshift provides interoperable events to your MCP server. You call emit() and Wakeshift pushes the event to each subscribed agent in whatever format they accept: per the MCP Events final spec, an earlier draft, or through a hook / plugin where needed. If the harness requires a hook / plugin and it's not already installed, the agent will be notified and receive instructions on how to install it for the user. Additionally, the MCP Events spec defines three delivery mechanisms: webhook, push (via held HTTP request) and pull (via HTTP polling). The Wakeshift SDK serves push and poll from your MCP server, so agents that can't accept inbound HTTP webhooks (e.g. most agents running on laptops) can still get events within seconds. Subscriptions only start when an agent calls a tool that subscribes it, and users can list or stop them anytime. Some harnesses can only be woken by putting a message into the conversation, so Wakeshift wraps the content as an external event to reduce the risk of prompt injection. The repo linked has a quickstart guide to get this working locally in a few minutes. Or you can try our hosted webhook service to test it yourself without an installation. ( https://try.wakeshift.ai ) We'd love feedback, PRs for harnesses we don't cover, reports when it doesn't work. As you can imagine, there's a combinatorial explosion of servers, harnesses, models, OSs, etc. so we expect there to be some rough edges. Are there any MCP servers you're using that you think could benefit from having events today?
8f9c3726e861a00be405dc5979bf44f68eb32c4e.title: Show HN: Wakeshift – Open-Source MCP Events for Claude Code, Codex and More

8fa8f65aec030003b1cd0ff8c34b7a95f6f8a15f.summary: arXiv:2611.28348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) lacks a one-size-fits-all detector for heterogeneous data and anomaly types. Existing automation is limited by implicit objectives, potentially unreliable historical knowledge, or high computational costs. More fundamentally, it selects how to detect anomalies without explicitly defining what to detect. We propose SMAD, an LLM-based multi-agent framework that translates anomaly intent into executable, testable detection pipelines. Rather than selecting detectors against an implicit target, SMAD establishes a natural-language semantic contract grounded in measurable time-series properties, specifying target event patterns, expected score responses, and validation questions. This contract governs both detector construction and evaluation: LLM agents propose pipelines, while contract-matched synthetic interventions provide label-free evidence from the target series to assess semantic coverage and guide iterative self-refinement. A semantics-aware ensemble integrates validated candidates and attributes each alert to contributing detectors and supporting evidence. On univariate and multivariate TSAD benchmarks, SMAD improves detection performance over the strongest baseline by 11.5% and 9.6%, respectively, while outperforming general-purpose coding agents at 2-5x lower language-model token cost.
8fa8f65aec030003b1cd0ff8c34b7a95f6f8a15f.title: SMAD: A Semantics-Guided Multi-Agent Framework for Unsupervised Time-Series Anomaly Detection

9019971be0863197aaa745ac8623384e1ed8b7fa.summary: arXiv:2610.31495v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Complex objects such as engineering designs and proteins are often difficult to optimise because their design spaces exhibit high-dimensional structure and objective evaluations are expensive. Generative models provide continuous latent representations, but their latent spaces can have thousands to tens of thousands of dimensions, creating a regime where the latent dimension $D$ exceeds the evaluation budget. We introduce SABLE, a Bayesian optimisation method for high-dimensional latent spaces with an isotropic distribution and limited budget. SABLE uses a Bayesian affine surrogate for prediction and acquisition, treating higher-order structure as surrogate discrepancy. After $N$ observations, the slope update has dimension at most $N-1$, yielding a decomposition of each query into an in-span component optimised by expected improvement (EI) in at most $N$ dimensions and an off-span component governed by a scalar norm. We show that the off-span norm implicitly selected by affine EI can lead to underexploration, and SABLE instead prescribes it using an exploration schedule, without restricting search to a learned subspace. An efficient recompression scheme reduces information to $\mathcal O(M)$ pseudo-observations, bringing the overall time complexity per step to $\mathcal O(M^2D+M^3+D\log D)$ while keeping parameter inference, prediction, and acquisition decisions to tens of milliseconds. Across synthetic benchmarks and latent-space optimisation tasks, SABLE achieves high sample efficiency and reduces decision time by several orders of magnitude at large budgets.
9019971be0863197aaa745ac8623384e1ed8b7fa.title: SABLE: Scalable Affine Bayesian Latent-space Exploration

903c72733b2ca5e3b9cdee2b0076e181f12d692f.summary: arXiv:2611.29954v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Parallel-trainable recurrences such as Mamba, linear attention, and DeltaNet offer constant-cost streaming inference, but they suffer from two limitations: 1) they struggle to track discrete state, and 2) they read every parameter at every step, tying model capacity directly to CPU latency. We introduce Yggdrasil, a recurrent architecture that decouples capacity from per-step compute by looking up each layer's transition in a large, tree-routed bank of recurrent experts. Each router addresses its bank using the current token and the state of the layer below. We prove that this cross-layer context is necessary---a single token-indexed layer of non-expanding transitions with finitely many reachable states cannot perform conditional resets---while avoiding feedback from the layer's own past preserves parallel-scan training. Because each step traverses one tree path and reads a single expert per layer, active weights stay within a few hundred kilobytes in CPU L2 cache while the full bank resides in RAM. Among the parallel-trainable models we evaluate, Yggdrasil is the only one to solve all five state-tracking tasks. At matched active parameter counts, it achieves the lowest test bits on enwik8 (1.540 bpb) and the human genome hg38 (1.567 bpb), while stepping $3.0\times$ and $3.3\times$ faster on a single CPU core ($6.7\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ and $5.8\,\mu\mathrm{s}$) than the fastest streaming baseline, and delivering the highest GPU throughput of all models at batch 1024. On the Genomic Benchmarks, it is the strongest causal model at matched active parameters (86.0% mean accuracy).
903c72733b2ca5e3b9cdee2b0076e181f12d692f.title: Yggdrasil: Tree-Routed Recurrent Experts for State Tracking and Fast CPU Inference

90e4f71b2348fd530079b1bf3f90660eef343b2a.summary: arXiv:2611.31892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Block-causal video diffusion generates long videos block by block, conditioned on a persistent key-value (KV) cache. After each block is denoised, an extra noise-free ($t=0$) forward pass writes its clean KV into the cache; once distillation and speculative early exit make denoising cheap, this clean KV update dominates the runtime. Reusing stale KV shortens the update, but stale memory corrupts the conditioning of later blocks and inflates their denoising steps, so the saved compute reappears downstream. We present SAMR (Step-Aware Memory Reconstruction), a training-free method for frozen causal video DiTs that refreshes only part of the cache and reconstructs the rest without DiT forwards. Our key observation is that, once rotary position phases are removed, motion-aligned historical KV and the in-flight KV a token holds at its exit step are complementary estimates of its clean KV. SAMR debiases in-flight KV with offline-calibrated per-head affine maps in Pre-RoPE space, fuses the two estimates, and reserves true $t=0$ refreshes for tokens flagged by an attention-readout error proxy, all executed by tile-aligned, synchronization-free Triton kernels. On 48-second LongLive-1.3B videos, SAMR reduces DiT latency by 20.9% and principal FLOPs by 30.7% relative to dense KV updates, lowers downstream denoising steps, and improves final-quarter PSNR over token reuse by 1.61 dB (1.14 dB on held-out VidProM-16). The reconstruction also transfers to frozen Self-Forcing-DMD-1.3B: zero-shot, it reduces reuse-induced step inflation ($2.47 \to 2.30$ steps/token) and improves late PSNR by $+0.33$ dB, and a one-time training-free calibration recovers the diagnostic score that zero-shot transfer lowers ($89.62 \to 91.10$).
90e4f71b2348fd530079b1bf3f90660eef343b2a.title: Cheap Memory Costs Future Compute: Co-Designing Persistent KV and GPU Execution for Efficient Streaming Video Diffusion

913bc75b292a4941822129e75352cfcdc5743b83.summary: arXiv:2609.37196v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tool-using LLM agents can be redirected by attacker-controlled content into unauthorized actions. Existing tool-level guards may miss within-tool hijacking, where an attacker preserves the intended tool but changes a sensitive argument such as a recipient or destination. We present ToolFence, a provenance-aware dynamic authorization framework that combines model-based and rule-based judges to improve detection accuracy and efficiency. An LLM compiles the authenticated user request into typed, task-scoped capabilities specifying permitted tools, effects, argument sources, workflow stages, and budgets. A deterministic monitor based on Guarded Colored Petri Net (GCPN) checks each proposed call and its concrete argument values before execution. When a legitimate step requires a missing capability, an isolated LLM judge can review the action proposal and update the GCPN monitor. We evaluate ToolFence on AgentDojo, MCPTox, ASB, and AgentLAB on four different LLMs, covering environmental prompt injection, tool poisoning, memory poisoning, and long-horizon attacks. It achieves the lowest or tied-lowest attack success rate in 15 combinations. On AgentDojo with Qwen3-max, attack success falls from 21.2\% to 0\%, with a 2.0-percentage-point reduction in clean-task utility. A measured runtime subset incurs 1.63X overhead, versus 12.95X for CaMeL. Our code is released at https://github.com/PolyLiYJ/ToolFence_v2
913bc75b292a4941822129e75352cfcdc5743b83.title: ToolFence: Fine-Grained Authorization for Secure Tool-Using LLM Agents

9186f9efe7b3fd4ba3a547c12796f7603311b801.summary: arXiv:2611.29972v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Calendar arithmetic is non-linear. When 1:59 AM + 1 minute occurs during daylight saving spring-forward, the result is 3:00 AM, not 2:00 AM, as the hour is skipped. We introduce CivilTime-Bench, a benchmark for civil-time reasoning covering daylight saving transitions, non-hour offsets, date-line crossings, and ISO week boundaries. With 60,011 training and 10,500 evaluation examples under strict output-contract evaluation, we benchmark seven LLMs (six instruction-tuned models and Llama-3.1-8B base) and find: zero-shot exact match varies substantially across models, contract-aware prompting often improves format compliance but yields inconsistent accuracy gains, few-shot in-context learning provides model-dependent improvements, and fine-tuning achieves 74.6--86.6% EM on synthetic evaluation but only 36.6--45.2% on HumanTime-500 for models with valid results on both splits, highlighting substantial limitations in generalization. We release the benchmark and code.
9186f9efe7b3fd4ba3a547c12796f7603311b801.title: When 1+1 $\neq$ 2: Benchmarking Civil-Time Reasoning in Large Language Models

91bdf897b3a82c12e5ae02f14b8b0c5d427fe6a3.summary: arXiv:2609.16679v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Foundation models, alongside advances in learned game-world models, are reshaping AI across the game lifecycle. Beyond playing games, recent systems model players and game dynamics, support design and development, adapt player-facing experiences at runtime, and evaluate resulting artifacts. Yet these directions have evolved largely separately, obscuring which capabilities transfer across settings and which remain tied to particular games, engines, interfaces, or player populations. We organize the literature into six roles according to the immediate use of AI output: playing and acting; modeling players and games; designing games; building and maintaining games; generating and adapting at runtime; and testing and evaluating games. For each role, we examine what structure is supplied by the game or workflow, what AI learns or produces, which capabilities and artifacts transfer across settings and roles, and what evidence supports the claims. We identify cross-role connections: trajectories train world models, learned environments provide experience for agents, design specifications drive executable implementations, and play or testing feedback guides revision. Evaluation is most standardized for bounded game playing and selected learned environments, while persistent state in learned worlds, repeated software revision, validated player modeling, sustained runtime adaptation, and representative automated testing remain less established. The central challenge is to reuse or transfer outputs and capabilities across roles while re-establishing evidence for effectiveness in the game-specific contexts where they are used.
91bdf897b3a82c12e5ae02f14b8b0c5d427fe6a3.title: AI for Games in the Foundation Model Era

91ccc30646b3c1e35812c82735a20cb33fdd0a7f.summary: arXiv:2611.30516v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Demonstrations show how a task can be completed, but differences in embodiment, appearance, and execution speed make it difficult to identify the guidance relevant to the robot's current progress. We introduce JEPA-ICL, a vision-language-action framework that couples predictive planning with demonstration learning. The policy learns to plan by predicting ordered future states in JEPA feature space up to subtask completion, capturing what remains to be accomplished. These plans guide action generation and locate relevant stages in demonstrations, whose JEPA-supervised content features provide progress-aligned context. Learning from this context, in turn, updates the shared policy that produces the plans and actions. This coupling connects anticipating the robot's own execution with reusing demonstrated experience. On the Imitator Game, JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0% seen-task success under C15 pretraining, outperforming Zero-WAM by 12.0 percentage points. Without contextual demonstrations, JEPA-ICL outperforms the VLA-JEPA variant without human-video pretraining, improving success rates from 96.1% to 97.6% on LIBERO and from 62.9% to 73.2% on LIBERO-Plus. With demonstration-based training and contextual guidance at inference, LIBERO-Plus success further increases from 73.2% to 75.2%.
91ccc30646b3c1e35812c82735a20cb33fdd0a7f.title: JEPA-ICL: Progress-Aligned Latent Plans for In-Context Robotic Manipulation

91dc2886dd3fb39442674c9bc4ae290a825c48e5.summary: arXiv:2611.00102v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Creators publicly showcase generated content to advertise and sell their work, but these examples may also enable unauthorized reproduction and customization. We study whether an adversary can derive reusable inputs from a single public video for faithful reconstruction and controlled editing, without access to the original prompt or generator. We adapt captioning and prompt optimization approaches to video prompt stealing attacks (PSAs) and find that prompt recovery alone provides limited reconstruction fidelity. Even the original prompt produces different spatial and temporal realizations when the initial noise changes. Using an independent generator enlarges the reconstruction gap, as reusing the original prompt and seed can still produce substantially different videos. We propose V-PSA, which uses a recovered caption and DDIM inversion to construct a reference trajectory under an independent generator. Null-Text Inversion then optimizes per-step unconditional embeddings to reduce deviations from this trajectory during reconstruction. The resulting inputs also guide generation when the caption is modified, supporting edits that change selected content while preserving the target's layout and motion. We construct a benchmark containing 12,000 video-prompt pairs from three victim generators and four prompt sources. V-PSA achieves video-to-video similarity around 0.9 between target and reconstructed videos, substantially improving over prompt-only baselines with similarity score of 0.6, and supports multiple controlled variations that preserve the target's structure. Additional experiments show that augmenting prior image PSAs with inversion-derived inputs also improves reconstruction. Our results show that evaluations restricted to prompt recovery can underestimate an attacker's ability to reconstruct public generative outputs.
91dc2886dd3fb39442674c9bc4ae290a825c48e5.title: Demystifying Prompt Stealing Attacks against Synthetic Video

91e2d35d026a21e424d25c30f359a0937a8f75ec.summary: arXiv:2605.01945v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tandem mass spectrometry provides a high-throughput framework for identifying and quantifying proteins in complex biological samples. In computational proteomics, predicting peptide MS/MS spectra is a critical task, enabling downstream applications such as large-scale peptide identification and quantification. While deep learning architectures have substantially improved prediction accuracy, three evaluation challenges obscure the true progress of the field. First, inconsistent data preprocessing and incompatible model output spaces hinder fair model comparison. Second, flawed data splitting strategies can permit hidden sequence leakage and inflate reported performance. Third, existing evaluations typically lack systematic assessment of heterogeneous zero-shot domain shift and robustness to collision energy and precursor charge. To address these challenges, we propose PepSpecBench, a unified benchmark for peptide MS/MS spectrum prediction. The main leaderboard scores all six predictors on a shared b/y fragmention intensity subtask, so their outputs are directly comparable. PepSpecBench standardizes data preprocessing across complementary public datasets, enforces a strict backbone-disjoint splitting strategy to prevent exact backbone overlap across partitions, and evaluates diverse architectures within a shared fragment-ion representation space. It further introduces a heterogeneous zero-shot domainshift suite and metadata perturbation probes to assess robustness and whether models respond to fragmentation-relevant experimental conditions. Across six representative models, we uncover changes in model rankings across training sources and external test subsets, along with differences in their responses to collision-energy and precursor-charge perturbations. Code and data are available at https://github.com/zwYang2004/PepSpecBench.
91e2d35d026a21e424d25c30f359a0937a8f75ec.title: PepSpecBench: A Unified Evaluation Benchmark for Peptide Tandem Mass Spectrometry Prediction

91fc76669c66506ba312e7723516586ebd9f1235.summary: arXiv:2611.28137v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Interactive long-video generation lets users build a story through successive prompts and reuse earlier characters and settings under new instructions. Existing memory methods retain past content, yet they often fail at precise selective recall, returning the wrong appearance of a person, mixing different people, or keeping an unrequested background. Based on our analysis of memory form and retrieval, we introduce an object-aware key--value (KV) memory framework for a frozen autoregressive diffusion generator. It keeps the original KV of tracked object regions, selects background KV outside them by attention-scores, and links each memory with a readable record of its source scene and observed appearance. An LLM selects the requested records, and a memory integrator supplies their KV for generation under the current prompt. We also introduce a six-scene evaluation that tests selective attribute modification, time-specific appearance recall, and multi-object composition, in which each person's requested past appearance changes across requests. Experiments show that our framework more reliably preserves each person's identity while reproducing their requested past appearance than existing memory methods, under both explicit scene references and natural-language cues.
91fc76669c66506ba312e7723516586ebd9f1235.title: Choose What Returns: Object-Aware KV Memory for Selective Recall in Interactive Video Generation

92375464aa5eb8e7427836aee4d977d11eb32da1.summary: arXiv:2610.26098v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A game ships when a player can launch it, finish it, and return to a saved world, none of which a successful build guarantees, yet game-creation agents are mostly tested on one engine or on one-prompt browser games. We present CEGame-Bench, the first long-horizon benchmark for complete-game creation across five production engines: Defold, Godot, Roblox Studio, Unity, and Unreal Engine. Agents build each game from an empty project and a design document in runs averaging up to 295 steps and 65M tokens; the document doubles as a contract, and a hidden evaluator accepts a game only by real-input play. Under four scaffolds, agents earn most integration points but usually under half the gameplay points, and their games reach the ending in only 16% of runs, while references built by engineers with coding agents score near the maximum, which places this artifact-to-play gap in the agents. No two engines rank configurations alike (Kendall's tau 0.14-0.62), and the same game usually scores higher on Unity and Unreal Engine, which check more before play. We release Game Completion Boost, an agent skill for requirement-driven playtesting and repair that raises the execution-based score of three models by 14.1-24.3 points.
92375464aa5eb8e7427836aee4d977d11eb32da1.title: From Code to Playable Systems: CEGame-Bench for Long-Horizon Game Creation Agents

929ced5e0c97ca094e7e72a4b41ef37301e32fdd.title: Show HN: NocoDB – Open-Source Airtable Alternative

92bc91c67c205df92af22598a66c1cadfab16eaf.summary: arXiv:2611.32646v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Official statistics are critical datasets for a wide variety of actors, including policymakers and businesses. For providers of official statistics, improving accessibility, governance, and disclosure of their data is of key importance. This can be improved by providing question-answering systems based on text-to-SQL approaches. However, existing text-to-SQL benchmarks do not resemble this setting. Official statistics are published as open-domain catalogs of thousands of wide tables whose columns and values are codes, and whose meaning is recorded in separate metadata rather than in a relational schema. To address this gap, we introduce LOCuST, a text-to-SQL benchmark that pairs over two thousand English and Dutch tables from Statistics Netherlands with a semantic knowledge graph. The graph describes the tables, measures, and dimension codes through labels, definitions, hierarchies, and units, and is the external knowledge a system needs to find the right tables and ground a question in the right codes. The benchmark includes expert-annotated questions for different query and aggregation types, including raw value retrieval, summations, proportion calculations, and joins. Alongside standard evaluation measures, we introduce an observation F1 metric that measures how close a query is to the ground truth even when the answers are different. We evaluate a variety of state-of-the-art LLMs and find that they struggle to write SQL that answers the questions correctly.
92bc91c67c205df92af22598a66c1cadfab16eaf.title: A Text-to-SQL Benchmark for Official Statistics

92be29f148631f8f2c98069a4a76c61dc8aacf96.summary: arXiv:2611.29293v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Geometry-aware rotary positional encodings, such as RayRoPE, help attention reason about the 3D spatial relationships between tokens and the query camera. However, they implicitly assume a static scene, encoding each key at its observed position regardless of when it was captured. For dynamic scenes with temporally separated input views, this mismatch places the same moving object at a different position in each input frame, so it can be rendered at an inaccurate position. While temporal encodings inform attention when a token was observed, they do not resolve where its content should be at the query time. We introduce a simple and general approach that aligns positional encodings with dynamic scene geometry through Galilean transport. Before positional encoding, each key's 3D position is transported to the query time using its estimated velocity and the temporal offset. By modifying only key positions, our method integrates directly with existing encodings, including RayRoPE and URoPE, without altering their formulations. Velocities can be obtained from arbitrary sources. By default, we estimate them from token correspondences within the network. Integrated into LVSM, our method improves dynamic view synthesis on Syn4D, dynamic Objaverse, and real-world Stereo4D videos over baselines. Ablations show that encoding velocities as token features yields smaller gains, while attention visualizations reveal that our method attends to query-time locations of moving content, unlike RayRoPE. Beyond view synthesis, our method also reduces tracking errors on dynamic objects in a pretrained 3D point tracker and improves moving-vehicle generation in a video generator.
92be29f148631f8f2c98069a4a76c61dc8aacf96.title: GALILEO: Geometric RoPE with Galilean Key Transport for Dynamic Scenes

92c3a1c471fea4a565fabddd9bf707f8a045d1e2.summary: arXiv:2406.14745v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Information Extraction (IE) plays a pivotal role in transforming unstructured data into structured formats, such as Knowledge Graphs. One of the main tasks within IE is Relation Extraction (RE), which identifies relations between entities in text data. This process enriches the semantic understanding of documents, enabling more precise information retrieval and query answering. Recent works leveraging pre-trained language models have demonstrated significant performance improvements in RE. In the current era of Large Language Models (LLMs), fine-tuning these LLMs can mitigate the limitations of zero-shot RE methods, particularly in overcoming the domain adaptation challenges inherent in RE. This work explores not only the effectiveness of fine-tuned LLMs but also their integration into a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)-based RE approach to address domain adaptation challenges when general-purpose LLMs serve as generators within the RAG framework. Empirical evaluations on the TACRED, TACRED-Revisited (TACREV), and Re-TACRED datasets reveal substantial performance improvements with fine-tuned LLMs, such as Llama2-7B, Mistral-7B, and Flan-T5 Large and surpass previous methods on these datasets.
92c3a1c471fea4a565fabddd9bf707f8a045d1e2.title: Fine-Tuning Large Language Models for Relation Extraction within a Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework
