a66ac29987a223664337a6a9c1b51c139c4e9914.summary: arXiv:2605.14494v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Two-Stage Robust Optimization (2RO) with discrete uncertainty is challenging, often rendering exact solutions prohibitive. Scenario reduction alleviates this issue by selecting a small, representative subset of scenarios to enable tractable computation. However, existing methods are largely problem-agnostic, operating solely on the uncertainty set without consulting the feasible region or recourse structure. In this paper, we introduce PRISE, a problem-driven sequential lookahead heuristic that constructs reduced scenario sets by evaluating the marginal impact of each scenario. While PRISE yields high-quality scenario subsets, each selection step requires solving multiple subproblems, making it computationally expensive at scale. To address this, we propose NeurPRISE, a neural surrogate model built on a GNN-Transformer backbone that encodes the per-scenario structure via graph convolution and captures cross-scenario interactions through attention. NeurPRISE is trained via imitation learning with a gain-aware ranking objective, which distills marginal gain information from PRISE into a learned scoring function for scenario ranking and selection. Extensive results on three 2RO problems show that NeurPRISE consistently achieves competitive regret relative to comprehensive methods, maintains strong calability with varying numbers of scenarios, and delivers 17-200x speedup over PRISE. NeurPRISE also exhibits strong zero-shot generalization, effectively handling instances with larger problem scales (up to 5x), more scenarios (up to 4x), and distribution shifts.
a66ac29987a223664337a6a9c1b51c139c4e9914.title: Learning Scenario Reduction for Two-Stage Robust Optimization with Discrete Uncertainty

a67e63cf26a4472488b4184c814275aba494a149.summary: arXiv:2605.01643v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study AI alignment through the lens of law-and-economics models of deterrence and enforcement, which treats misconduct as a rational response to incentivizes, where actors weigh the expected gain from aligning against the expected loss from being caught. We argue that the same logic arises naturally in foundational language models: an agent trained by RLHF can be modeled as deriving intrinsic reward from producing a persuasive yet incorrect response, while an auditor can be viewed as balancing monitoring (which incurs some cost) against identifying solver misalignment. Therefore, alignment can be viewed as a mechanism design problem, where stronger penalties can deter solver misbehavior but also reduce auditing pressure. Under this framework, we can characterize misalignment as an adversarial post-training problem. While standard post-training optimizes against a stationary reward signal, our mechanism constantly adapts to mitigate reward hacking against a fixed monitor. We formalize this interaction as follows: a principal (e.g., a human) defines a value function over joint alignment outcomes, and a meta-optimizer adaptively chooses granular rewards for the solver and auditor to optimize the principal's value. In particular, we propose a bandit-based meta-optimizer for searching over a discrete set of reward profiles using noisy interaction feedback, and we show from experimental results on Qwen2.5-7B that this mechanism can reduce hallucinations on programming benchmarks by as much as 52\%.
a67e63cf26a4472488b4184c814275aba494a149.title: AI Alignment via Incentives and Correction

a6d41fc25b0885242f895d973dde1d2ad795ef09.summary: arXiv:2611.31286v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Nearly fifty years ago, DeMillo, Lipton, and Perlis argued that mathematical proofs are not static, isolated structures of formal logic, but the products of a vibrant, evolving social process of human critique, internalization, and shared intuition. In October 2026, OpenAI challenged this thesis by releasing a massive repository of 722 automated mathematical manuscripts, claiming full or partial solutions to 372 longstanding open problems. This paper examines the immediate crisis through the lens of the original DLP framework. We argue that the sudden, automated overproduction of dense, unreadable proofs represents an industrial pollution of the mathematical ecosystem. By examining the three fatal structural pillars of this automated approach (Specification, Regress, and Utility), we demonstrate that decoupling the act of mechanical solving from the human social process of understanding produces a sterile repository of dead logical artifacts. The resulting industrialization of unexamined manuscripts is self-fulfilling. Flooding the literature guarantees that the finite supply of human attention will lose the race to separate signal from noise. In this sense, posting a result is not the same act as submitting it to the community processes by which mathematics is vetted, digested, and incorporated into shared knowledge.
a6d41fc25b0885242f895d973dde1d2ad795ef09.title: The Industrialization of Noise: Why Automated Proof-Solving is the Same Old Dead End

a6d94ab944c993022eab7e57e49b338fedcfb835.summary: Today, Shreya Shankar and I are publishing evals skills , a set of skills for AI product evals 1 . Eval tools often get in the way. They nudge you toward generic off-the-shelf metrics and fully automated evals before you’ve looked at your data. These skills help you avoid common mistakes we’ve seen helping 50+ companies and teaching students in our AI Evals course . Why skills for evals There are many easily avoidable footguns in evals. These skills help you avoid them. evals-start is the entry point. It looks at your situation and routes you to the right skill. Most of the time it will send you to one of these two: eval-audit , if you already have an eval pipeline. It inspects your setup and recommends next steps. 2 error-discovery , if you have traces but haven’t analyzed them yet. It builds a customized annotation interface and helps you sample traces intelligently. Shreya does a live walkthrough of using this skill here . The skills Install the skills: npx skills add https://github.com/ai-evals-course/evals-skills Then give your agent this prompt: Run the evals-start skill from the evals plugin and follow the skill it picks. If it picks eval-audit, investigate each diagnostic area using a separate subagent in parallel, then synthesize the findings into a single report. If you’re experienced with evals, skip the router and pick the skill you need: Skill What it does evals-start Entry point. Routes to the skill that matches your situation eval-audit Audit an eval pipeline and surface problems with prioritized severity error-discovery Build a review app, select diverse samples, and organize your notes into failure modes generate-synthetic-data Create diverse synthetic test inputs using dimension-based tuple generation write-judge-prompt Design LLM-as-Judge evaluators for subjective quality criteria validate-evaluator Calibrate LLM judges against human labels using data splits, TPR/TNR, and bias correction evaluate-rag Evaluate retrieval and generation quality in RAG pipelines build-review-interface Build custom annotation interfaces for human trace review These skills are only a starting point. To make them better, tune them to be more specific to your data and domain. The repo is ai-evals-course/evals-skills . You can find me on X or email me through my newsletter . Footnotes Not foundation model benchmarks like MMLU or HELM that measure general LLM capabilities. Product evals measure whether your pipeline works on your task with your data. If you aren’t familiar with product-specific AI evals, check out my AI Evals FAQ .↩︎ The audit isn’t a complete solution, but it will catch common problems.↩︎
a6d94ab944c993022eab7e57e49b338fedcfb835.title: Evals Skills for Coding Agents

a71ece9bab8af7e4fd07262153cf8bfc1f3b1423.summary: arXiv:2605.29076v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLMs have advanced text classification, yet existing paradigms face a trade-off: supervised (label only) fine-tuning is scalable but offers limited reasoning on complex text and lacks broader model transparency, while discrete prompt optimization offers human-readable instructions but struggles with performance and scalability. We introduce eXTC (eXplainable Text Classifier), centered on a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP, or rulebook) learned in natural language, in three stages: (1) learning the SOP via a new Structured Prompt Optimization algorithm; (2) SOP-grounded reasoning distillation from a large teacher LLM into a compact LM; and (3) expanding reasoning capabilities beyond the SOP via reinforcement learning. This design enables eXTC to provide (i) fast inference via a compact LM, with (ii) inference-time local reasoning traces, alongside a global, modular explanation of its learned domain rules, while (iii) significantly outperforming existing paradigms across diverse benchmarks in both classification performance and explanation quality, with stage-by-stage gains.
a71ece9bab8af7e4fd07262153cf8bfc1f3b1423.title: Structured Prompt Optimization Advances Globally and Locally Interpretable Learning from Complex Text

a7b0b9c0119f82ffcd504db4fbc25e7523b1982d.summary: arXiv:2611.32195v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coding agents let plugins and remote services answer permission prompts, and Claude Code documents that such an answer cannot override the operator's deny rules. However, we show that this guarantee, checked one decision at a time, fails over a whole run, because an answer to one permission prompt can rewrite the policy that every later answer is checked against. For example, a remote service with no access to the operator's files approves an unrelated command and attaches an update that deletes the deny rule protecting the project's secrets. The agent then reads the secrets in that session and the next, even inside the vendor's strict sandbox. The root cause is that Claude Code checks only updates that add or replace allow rules. Relays that forward such deletions already exist, including the vendor's own Remote Control. In effect, the right to answer a prompt has become the right to administer the policy. Worse, the deletion leaves the same records as a local edit by the operator, so Claude Code cannot tell who wrote a rule. More generally, what a runtime records decides what it can safely delegate. A runtime that cannot tell who wrote a rule can accept only updates that keep every currently denied call denied, whereas, to protect every party's restrictions, a runtime that records who wrote each rule can let each party remove only the restrictions proven to be its own. We prove that these two bounds are tight. They correctly predict whether the operator's restrictions survive in all thirteen permission designs across ten agent systems, including predictions we wrote down before running Codex, Gemini CLI, opencode, and Goose. Enforcing the bounds at the shared update step blocks the attack. A survey of 2,227 fetched marketplace plugins finds only two that send policy updates.
a7b0b9c0119f82ffcd504db4fbc25e7523b1982d.title: When Answering Is Administering: Permission Replies That Rewrite Coding-Agent Policy

a7bf14fe26346b143374056c946764308ee58ede.summary: arXiv:2610.41231v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Coarse-to-fine 3D-native generation relies heavily on the first-stage sparse structure, which determines the global orientation and overall geometry for subsequent refinement. However, existing coarse generators suffer from two key limitations: their orientation is difficult to control due to ambiguous semantic canonicalization, and their structures are often inconsistent with input images due to weak 2D-3D grounding. We propose Coarse3D, a sparse-structure generation model that produces orientation-controllable and structurally faithful voxel geometry from arbitrary unposed images. Coarse3D introduces three designs: a first-frame anchored canonical space that aligns generation with the first input view while preserving object-centric normalization; a dual-tower DiT that couples generation with auxiliary feed-forward reconstruction to learn spatially grounded features; and spatial-prior guided attention that regularizes cross-attention with pixel-to-voxel correspondence. Coarse3D can directly replace the coarse stage of existing pipelines. Experiments show that it substantially improves sparse structure quality and consistently enhances final 3D generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
a7bf14fe26346b143374056c946764308ee58ede.title: Coarse3D: Controllable and Faithful Sparse Structure Generation for Image-to-3D

a8147e634edc9046ab2169490bd3804904df7356.summary: arXiv:2611.32755v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors (QCBs) cause large language models (LLMs) to exhibit malicious behavior after quantization while remaining benign at high precision. Existing defenses often rely on security-guided configuration selection or iterative optimization, but do not identify which quantization-induced changes should be repaired. We isolate module-local quantization effects from upstream drift by evaluating the high-precision and quantized versions of each module on identical states from the quantized inference trajectory, and formulate QCB defense as repairing the resulting same-state operator discrepancies. We propose ReQOR, a training-free defense that identifies the dominant directions of these discrepancies on benign calibration data and restores the full-precision computation along them in closed form, yielding a factorized residual adapter. ReQOR uses neither attack information nor gradient-based optimization and supports both full-span and low-rank repair. Experiments across four LLMs, three PGD-based QCB attacks, three malicious behaviors, and three quantization formats show substantial QCB mitigation while largely preserving benign utility. In additional experiments on a non-PGD outlier-injection attack, existing baselines largely fail, whereas ReQOR remains effective. Further analysis shows that dominant operator-discrepancy directions provide more effective and rank-efficient repair than rank-matched random, low-energy, or raw weight-error directions, while low-rank ReQOR reduces deployment memory overhead.
a8147e634edc9046ab2169490bd3804904df7356.title: ReQOR: Operator-Discrepancy Subspace Repair for Quantization-Conditioned Backdoors in Large Language Models

a81b65ca9b977ee906c25e28054643fa43d7b324.summary: arXiv:2606.00125v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Music recommendation systems typically treat songs as opaque tokens, relying on interaction histories that overlook semantic or acoustic content. Prior LLM-augmented, multimodal, and text-enhanced sequential recommenders partially combine semantic, acoustic, or engagement signals, and none jointly model all three within a unified LLM-based framework grounded in song content. In this work, we propose a multimodal framework for session-based music recommendation that enriches the LastFM-1K dataset with three complementary signals: (1) audio and lyric embeddings from pretrained music and text models, (2) LLM-generated semantic metadata using the MGPHot schema, and (3) listening completion ratios. We validate the generated metadata against human MGPHot annotations across all 58 attributes. We extend the E4SRec framework with multimodal features, ItemID encoder backbones including SASRec, BERT4Rec, and GRU4Rec, and LLM backbones including LLaMA-2-13B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and LLaMA-3-70B across zero-shot and fine-tuned settings. In addition, we evaluate four multimodal fusion strategies, benchmark five audio and five lyric encoders, and compare Spotify audio attributes with LLM-generated MGPHot metadata. Our experiments show that content-based features improve over ID-only baselines by up to 95% in Recall and 79% in NDCG, with the largest gains when the ItemID baseline is weakest. Fine-tuning substantially improves over zero-shot, after which the best audio or lyric setup outperforms the ID-only baseline for every backbone. Naive multimodal fusion does not always yield additive improvements, highlighting challenges in cross-modal integration, while structured LLM-generated metadata proves more useful than Spotify audio attributes. We release a large-scale multimodal benchmark for music recommendation research.
a81b65ca9b977ee906c25e28054643fa43d7b324.title: MusicRec: Audio, Lyrics, and Engagement Feature Enrichment for Music Recommendation

a9b77b75d835e8c8e11b7a469bd0b71b31b5de07.summary: arXiv:2512.03627v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite the remarkable advancements in multimodal large language models across various domains, AI agents still lack the ability to retain past information. Without reliable memory, agents struggle to leverage historical context, impairing long-horizon reasoning and coherent interactions in dynamic environments. In this paper, we introduce MemVerse, a model-agnostic, plug-and-play memory framework that combines fast parametric recall with hierarchical retrieval, enabling scalable and adaptive multimodal intelligence. MemVerse maintains short-term memory for recent context while transforming raw experiences into structured long-term memory graphs, empowering continuous learning and autonomous knowledge evolution. To meet real-time demands, we introduce a periodic distillation mechanism that compresses essential knowledge from the cognitive graph into the parametric model, providing fast and differentiable recall while preserving interpretability. Extensive experiments show that MemVerse boosts multimodal reasoning with superior efficiency, allowing agents to maintain coherence and adapt seamlessly throughout extended interactions. Our code is available at https://github.com/KnowledgeXLab/MemVerse.
a9b77b75d835e8c8e11b7a469bd0b71b31b5de07.title: MemVerse: Multimodal Memory for Lifelong Learning Agents

aa21b73bf279903468dfab77650b233ff07418d9.summary: arXiv:2611.29493v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Interpreting the predictions of complex black-box classifiers remains a central challenge in explainable artificial intelligence. While local explanations clarify individual predictions, there is a significant need for global probabilistic explanations that capture a model's overall behavior across the input distribution. Such an explanation is a small subset $K$ of features, whose relevance is measured by the expected probability, over a random input $\mathbf x$, that the classifier assigns the same label to $\mathbf x$ and to a random input agreeing with $\mathbf x$ on $K$. In this study, we investigate the task of identifying maximally relevant global explanations under a cardinality constraint, focusing on product distributions with full support on discrete feature spaces. We introduce a spectral explainer that leverages membership queries to the black-box classifier and employs Fourier-analytic, junta-learning methods to produce probably approximately correct (PAC) explanations. Our algorithm is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the explanation size limit, maximum feature cardinality, and desired accuracy. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the theoretical guarantees and show that the spectral explainer outperforms a greedy baseline as the explanation size increases.
aa21b73bf279903468dfab77650b233ff07418d9.title: Learning Global Probabilistic Explanations

aab2b620e4d421ea3c1b0984ce5e8fdce20c7fa6.summary: arXiv:2411.14062v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Existing benchmarks often rely on predefined questions or reference captions, limiting their flexibility for evaluating detailed descriptions on new image collections. We present MMGenBench, an automated benchmark framework for evaluating Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) from raw images without per-image questions or reference captions. The pipeline generates descriptions, reconstructs images with a frozen text-to-image model, and compares the original and reconstructed images using a frozen image encoder. It produces reusable per-image scores and inspectable reconstructions, supporting both model comparison and diagnosis of reconstructible visual information. We construct MMGenBench-Domain with 10,000 generated images and MMGenBench-Test with 1,284 images spanning 13 overlapping visual patterns. Evaluation of 68 LMMs reveals pattern-specific differences in reconstruction quality that overall scores can obscure. On 1,000 human-labeled caption pairs from six models, the default score achieves 90.00\% sample-level agreement. Factual perturbations and component analyses characterize the score's sensitivity under the evaluated pipeline, while a COCO study provides initial validation on natural photographs. MMGenBench complements existing benchmarks by linking automated comparisons to visual evidence of the information preserved in LMM descriptions. Project page: https://github.com/lerogo/MMGenBench.
aab2b620e4d421ea3c1b0984ce5e8fdce20c7fa6.title: MMGenBench: An Automated Pipeline for Evaluating LMMs from a Text-to-Image Generation Perspective

aabba291e5d4ec611e7f4eb49969e93eb625f9a8.summary: arXiv:2404.01332v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate human respondents in choice experiments, yet their answers depend on the exact tokens of a prompt rather than on the offered products alone. I show that invisible characters, blank lines, or minor wording changes shift or reverse simulated choice probabilities. This sensitivity, which I term token noise, creates an illusion of preference and exposes studies to prompt hacking. I introduce a Shapley value audit that divides a model's choice response among the pieces of its prompt and reads each share beside the effect of removing that piece. The edit game divides the effect of several wording and formatting changes beside an actual price change. The word game divides a prompt's response across its words or tokens and summarizes the credit earned by the product attributes as the attribute share. Across four open-weight models and three product categories, wording and formatting edits could rival a substantive price change, while product attributes consistently received a minority of the word-level credit, sometimes less than the answer instruction. Framing cues could take credit from the very price they emphasized and frequently vanished or reversed across equivalent wordings of the question. A persona (even a bare statement that the respondent is a consumer) also shifted choice probabilities and the attributes' credit. Declared with its "players," reference, scale, and uncertainty, my audit separates what a simulated respondent prefers from how the question was asked, the distinction a study must draw before it reads a simulated choice as a preference.
aabba291e5d4ec611e7f4eb49969e93eb625f9a8.title: Token Noise and the Illusion of Preference: A Shapley Value Framework for Auditing LLM-Simulated Choice Experiments

ab775922df761eba1d517e80e95646c20b3927af.summary: arXiv:2611.28902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Video generators can now render convincing short clips, yet complete audiovisual works require coordinating visuals, sound, and editing across multiple stages. Existing benchmarks focus on individual generators or video agents under narrower production settings, leaving end-to-end creation by general multimodal large language models (MLLMs) underexplored. We introduce StudioBench, a benchmark comprising 160 tasks across eight video genres and five task types, spanning diverse audiovisual production requirements. Models produce minutes of finished audiovisual content using 33 atomic generation, editing, and inspection tools, without shell access or workflow templates. We evaluate the delivered films, while analyzing reconstructed workflow graphs to characterize production behavior and diagnose failures. Across seven MLLMs, explicit requirements are nearly saturated, yet production quality varies substantially in picture clarity and composition, object structure, motion, and lip sync. All models spontaneously organize multi-stage production workflows without predefined templates. However, higher-quality models exhibit more selective production workflows, whereas additional tool calls alone show little association with quality. These findings identify the missing quality loop of effective inspection, selection, and revision as a key bottleneck in productive audiovisual creation.
ab775922df761eba1d517e80e95646c20b3927af.title: StudioBench: Benchmarking Agentic Multimodal Large Language Models for Productive Audiovisual Creation

abdeb59b50f690fc8d4ef046ba1b322b439bfb0d.summary: arXiv:2611.30149v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robot leading requires executing a route while continuously adapting to a designated follower. Existing robot-leading systems often mediate follower understanding and physical route execution through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces; directly learning this coupling through end-to-end trajectory prediction can instead entangle route execution with follower response. We introduce LeadVLA, a structured multimodal policy that preserves the route as an explicit Path reference while learning a Pace for route progress and a Residual for local follower- and scene-conditioned adaptation. To make this problem trainable and measurable, we develop LeadInfra, a configurable Unreal Engine-based closed-loop data-generation infrastructure from which we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus, and LeadBench, a standardized benchmark with 108 fully held-out closed-loop episodes. LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies on LeadBench while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness, and transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning. Project Page: https://louiszengCN.github.io/LeadVLA_PAGE/
abdeb59b50f690fc8d4ef046ba1b322b439bfb0d.title: LeadVLA: Learning Follower-Aware Route Execution for Robot Leading

abf0576daf6f3dda2cacef0484c4bc24a933d99e.summary: It seems to me the industry is at a divergence point, with strong forces pull in opposite directions. In the "developers are team leads / checkpoint verifiers" corner we have: - Microsoft, re "They build a software factory that builds the product. They don’t build the product" (Nadella) and "become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work" <https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/18/microsoft-ceo-satya-nadella-explains-why-he-asked-60k-employees-to-quit/> -- Microsoft has always championed "AI as a team member", even as a product. - Salesforce <https://www.salesforce.com/news/stories/how-engineering-became-agentic/> - Stripe <https://stripe.dev/blog/minions-stripes-one-shot-end-to-end-coding-agents> - Uber, Shopify, Spotify, Meta In the "developers use harnesses to improve personal velocity and quality corner we have: - Netflix <https://qconsf.com/presentation/nov2026/how-netflix-retrofitted-its-sdlc-ai-coding-agents> - Amazon <https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/company-news/amazon-software-engineer-role-guideline-ai> - ... Google, but it's hard to find more than anecdotal references These two approaches, in my view, are not compatible. Fully, or even just semi-automated feature factories keep the context, leaving the developer to validate artifacts and manage the flow, shifting responsibility to specs and building automated verifiers. It lets less technical people into the product development loop but keeps the code an AI-only territory. On the other hand, a harness keeps the developer in control, but sacrifices velocity and requires higher technical prowess, or at least understanding, of what's being generated. Which way is the industry going to go? Are AI-only maintained code bases going to collapse under their own weight? Are "technical" developers going to be sidelined for higher delivery velocity? Will we see two types of businesses - features and infra, each taking a polar position in this? Or even within the same business, different teams?
abf0576daf6f3dda2cacef0484c4bc24a933d99e.title: Ask HN: Harness vs. Feature Factories

abfcd83b98657f14e87e66c5746660d741db4b8e.summary: arXiv:2611.32660v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep search is a critical capability for agents tackling complex, open-ended tasks, where solving a problem requires iterative information gathering, query reformulation, and evidence-based verification rather than a single retrieval step. To address these requirements, we present Bathys 9B and 27B deep search agents built around a training framework that spans verifiable question synthesis, post-training, and online reinforcement learning (RL) under context compression. Our high-quality data construction ensures both search depth and reliability: each clue is reformulated as an indirect reference requiring independent retrieval, and retained evidence chains enable verification that the clues jointly determine a unique answer. Curated trajectories underpin a pipeline of supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO), and Compaction-Managed Group Sequence Policy Optimization (CM-GSPO): SFT provides a stable foundation for tool use over long horizons and query reformulation; KTO uses binary feedback on trajectories to improve the selection of answers grounded in evidence; CM-GSPO optimizes execution sub-trajectories with length-normalized likelihood ratios on the recorded rollout contexts and reweights sub-trajectory advantages to correct the extra weighting introduced by independently averaging sub-trajectory losses. Bathys 9B and 27B attain 66.51% and 80.49% on BrowseComp, respectively, under an evaluation protocol with trajectory self-verification and conditional retries.
abfcd83b98657f14e87e66c5746660d741db4b8e.title: Bathys: Advancing Deep Search Agents

ac17992db40c492c896e87deba47cbee493fe8ad.summary: arXiv:2610.14918v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evaluating an agent's ability to strictly satisfy diverse and procedurally complex requirements is essential to determining its practical reliability. Conducting such an evaluation demands agentic tasks that reconcile broad domain coverage with deep procedural complexity. Existing paradigms face a fundamental trade-off: expert-curated benchmarks achieve procedural depth but suffer from domain diversity bottlenecks, whereas crowdsourced benchmarks span diverse scenarios but lack execution rigor. To resolve this tension, we present SkillForgeBench, which leverages agent skills as unifying execution blueprints across three co-designed stages: (1) Resource Preparation uses domain-balanced skills to guide artifact retrieval, establishing broad workflow coverage; (2) Skill-driven Task Synthesis employs skills as procedural anchors to partition artifact roles, synthesize naturalistic task instructions, and package sandboxed scenarios for deep procedural execution; and (3) Holistic Evaluation Design translates skill-embedded requirements into fine-grained completion and process rubrics to enable strict requirement-level scoring. Comprising 842 sandboxed tasks across five major professional domains, SkillForgeBench reveals a steep capability hierarchy among eight mainstream agents, led by Opus 4.8 ($40.9\%$ strict completion). Requiring all constrains satisfaction uncovers severe capability bottlenecks across all model tiers that remain masked under individual rubric pass rates ($70.0\%$ to $85.7\%$ vs. $12.6\%$ to $40.9\%$). Crucially, under the external guidance from skills, top-tier agents obtain larger gains than low-tier agents (i.e., $\Delta 19.2\%$ for Opus 4.8 vs. $\Delta 5.8\%$ for Haiku 4.5). Finally, agents satisfy process rubrics far less frequently than completion rubrics (under $3\%$ for Haiku 4.5), proving that completion-only checks overestimate real-world agent reliability.
ac17992db40c492c896e87deba47cbee493fe8ad.title: SkillForgeBench: Evaluating Agent Reliability Grounded in Agent Skill Specifications

ac2b1db6b490103db6fe5bdae2ddc3e28d28aa2c.summary: arXiv:2611.30895v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Proactive assistants that guide people through physical tasks must decide, every few seconds, whether a step is complete and whether a mistake has occurred. We find that two benchmarks for this task largely reward knowing when rather than seeing what: a timer that never looks at the video, raising an alarm at 25 s and confirming each step at 30 s, reaches a mistake F1 of 0.373 on Ego-MC-Bench, above every published result (at most 0.27). We formalize this as the video-blind frontier, the best trade-off between completion accuracy and mistake F1 that policies reach from the elapsed time, the instruction and training statistics alone: every published per-step result on Ego-MC-Bench lies inside it, and so do all twelve zero-shot models we run on QICD. To move beyond it, we introduce Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT): fine-tune on the benchmark's own questions, and pair its positives with negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time, so that elapsed time cannot separate the two sides of a pair. Trained on 209 QICD videos in about 15 GPU-hours, a 2B model with ECT crosses the frontier on both benchmarks in all four seeds; transferred to Ego-MC-Bench without adaptation, it confirms 59% of mistake-free steps in time, against 30% for a published model with the same backbone trained on about 25k synthetic counterfactuals and real recordings. Its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains: at equal elapsed time it tells a finished step from an unfinished one in 90-92% of test pairs, where the instruction's typical duration reaches 65%, rescaling the time stamps between the frames leaves it essentially unchanged, and swapping in another recording, of the same recipe where one exists, cuts its completion accuracy by two thirds. The code and model weights will be publicly released.
ac2b1db6b490103db6fe5bdae2ddc3e28d28aa2c.title: Speak When You See It: Proactive Task Assistants Should Wait for Evidence, Not the Clock

ac2f786b30f6d45772c42167559dc1dfd027b2c7.summary: GPT-6 models design protein structures and sequences using reasoning and code. Lab tests found evidence of binding across five targets.
ac2f786b30f6d45772c42167559dc1dfd027b2c7.title: GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

ac6c0c136a283624eed0f2abc6193bcd35ee20d9.summary: arXiv:2611.08855v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Much of what people believe about the unseen, from germs to spirits, rests on testimony that cannot be checked. We ask how six language models weigh such testimony when it concerns the spiritual and when it concerns the natural, using two paradigms with human data and one new design. In all three, models treat the spiritual as a separate epistemic domain. It has its own credible sources. People credit an obscure New-Age statement more when a scientist says it, while models credit it more from a spiritual leader and switch to the scientist once the statement uses the vocabulary of physics. It has its own standard for an adequate answer. When a trusted expert calls the mechanism behind a belief a mystery, people lose confidence in religious and scientific beliefs, while models prompted as those same people lose it for science and keep it for religion. And credibility earned elsewhere does not readily carry into it. When a fictional forecaster builds a record on checkable river predictions, five models extend that record to hidden natural causes and almost none of it to spiritual ones, and every model trusts the forecaster less about natural causes once the forecaster credits a river spirit. For four of the five models this gap is not a floor effect. It remains when they answer as residents of a village where spirits are taken to exist and rate the spiritual claims well above the bottom of the scale. For the fifth the gap closes in that setting. One model extends the record to spiritual claims once the forecaster in that village credits a spirit, which suggests that transfer can depend on whether the record is seen as bearing on the claim.
ac6c0c136a283624eed0f2abc6193bcd35ee20d9.title: Whom to Trust About the Unseen: How Language Models Weigh Spiritual and Scientific Testimony

acf9975ead98d539c2fa724ce2c38dab34c4ca2e.summary: arXiv:2611.33119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate parallel programs, but their correctness and performance depend strongly on the instructions that guide generation. We present \textsc{MetaFORGE}, an execution-grounded meta-learning framework that iteratively optimizes persistent natural-language skill specifications for MPI C code generation. \textsc{MetaFORGE} combines correctness testing, compiler diagnostics, static-analysis findings, runtime measurements, and rank-level load-imbalance profiles into a scalar reward that drives textual-gradient refinement, while an external memory distills and retrieves reward-supported optimization knowledge across runs. Across six MPI tasks and three workload sizes, \textsc{MetaFORGE} improves static-analysis quality, runtime, and load balance relative to zero-shot generation and generally exceeds the evaluated \textsc{TextGrad} iterative baseline. A model-matched refinement ablation shows that the MetaFORGE advantage persists when its refinement model is reduced to \texttt{gpt-4o}. An expanded retrieval ablation across all 18 task--workload configurations shows consistent runtime benefit and broad static-analysis and load-balance benefit from retrieved context. Leakage-controlled held-out and zero-update experiments further provide evidence that optimization knowledge persists in both the transferred skill and external memory under the evaluated protocol.
acf9975ead98d539c2fa724ce2c38dab34c4ca2e.title: MetaFORGE: A Meta-Learning Framework for Harness Optimization in Automated Code Generation for Parallel Computing

acfde71f2e0d62337fa451eeb8c21accb8e36c12.summary: arXiv:2611.31762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We refactor existing Lean 4 proofs to reduce source length and checking cost while preserving theorem statements and compatibility across Lean versions. A locally served Qwen model uses the open-source Codex CLI to inspect source, retrieve declarations, and test proof replacements. The host keeps a replacement only if it improves the objective and Lean accepts it on every required version. A deterministic CPU pass then refines the verified proofs. On the 60 problems in Lean Refactor Arena, model search achieves a local mean combined score of 82.07, and cleanup raises it to 82.18. The final proofs pass all 127 required proof--version checks. Our system placed first in the open-source LLM track of Lean Refactor Arena at VeriCodeGen.
acfde71f2e0d62337fa451eeb8c21accb8e36c12.title: Verified Proof Refactoring with Codex and Qwen

ada7cab06142f9cd26c41c1586e78019111f3c7a.summary: arXiv:2611.32194v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Request-derived authorizers such as Progent protect LLM agents from prompt injection by deriving what an agent may do from the user's request. Their guarantee rests on attribution: the request is taken to be what the user said. Compaction breaks it. At every automatic compaction we observed, Claude Code and Codex placed a model-written summary of earlier turns as a user message, so the compactor's quotation of the user, documents and injected text reads as the user speaking. Because a policy frozen at the first request lets the agent finish few later tasks, we let Progent derive its policy for each request, and find that what it grants then follows what the compactor wrote. Even a payee the user stated is not safe: when an attacker's notice states another account as plain data and the user asks to pay the rent, the policy derived from a frontier compactor's summary admits the notice's account in 91% of cases, and the one derived from the user's own words in none. The cause is general: we prove that an authorizer that cannot see who wrote which bytes cannot treat a forged record differently from the legitimate one it imitates by more than the two are distinguishable, and that the bound is tight. Frontier compactors bear this out: they mark injected instructions, which have no legitimate twin, but rarely injected data, which does. What a compactor keeps, and how it marks it, is a security parameter. The fix follows from attribution: the authorizer credits only what the user said, authenticated on arrival and carried verbatim across the boundary, while the agent still reads the summary. We prove that it then receives exactly that text or nothing, so an attacker can block the policy but cannot shape it, and adaptive attacks on our implementation confirm it. In 40 attacked AgentDojo episodes re-run with the fix, no attacker action completes while the agent reads the summary.
ada7cab06142f9cd26c41c1586e78019111f3c7a.title: LLM Agent Authorization Across Context Compaction

adbcc01ca1cafe2291b588d9de0efadb355e4fd8.summary: How small can a language model be while still doing something useful? I wanted to find out, and had some spare time over the holidays. Z80-μLM is a character-level language model with 2-bit quantized weights ({-2,-1,0,+1}) that runs on a Z80 with 64KB RAM. The entire thing: inference, weights, chat UI, it all fits in a 40KB .COM file that you can run in a CP/M emulator and hopefully even real hardware! It won't write your emails, but it can be trained to play a stripped down version of 20 Questions, and is sometimes able to maintain the illusion of having simple but terse conversations with a distinct personality. -- The extreme constraints nerd-sniped me and forced interesting trade-offs: trigram hashing (typo-tolerant, loses word order), 16-bit integer math, and some careful massaging of the training data meant I could keep the examples 'interesting'. The key was quantization-aware training that accurately models the inference code limitations. The training loop runs both float and integer-quantized forward passes in parallel, scoring the model on how well its knowledge survives quantization. The weights are progressively pushed toward the 2-bit grid using straight-through estimators, with overflow penalties matching the Z80's 16-bit accumulator limits. By the end of training, the model has already adapted to its constraints, so no post-hoc quantization collapse. Eventually I ended up spending a few dollars on Claude API to generate 20 questions data (see examples/guess/GUESS.COM), I hope Anthropic won't send me a C&D for distilling their model against the ToS ;P But anyway, happy code-golf season everybody :)
adbcc01ca1cafe2291b588d9de0efadb355e4fd8.title: Show HN: Z80-μLM, a 'Conversational AI' That Fits in 40KB

adfa39a204d71fd81c61722749a0fac9191c099f.summary: arXiv:2605.26690v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Optimizing protein sequences under tight oracle budgets requires methods that can explore a vast combinatorial mutational search space. These methods must also remain robust in the presence of surrogate noise and propose mutations on positions where substitutions are predicted to have favorable effects. We introduce SILO (Self-improvement Imitation Learning Optimization), a trajectory-level approach for oracle-budgeted protein design. SILO combines a hierarchical edit policy with incremental stochastic beam search without replacement (SBS) to explore diverse candidate trajectories. A UCB-based proxy ensemble, complemented by a proxy-derived alanine-scan-inspired fitness score (AFS), guides candidate selection for in silico oracle evaluation. The policy is then updated by next-action cross-entropy imitation on the round's best oracle-labeled trajectories. Across eight in silico protein fitness landscapes and five strong baselines from prior work, SILO achieves competitive performance within the evaluated oracle budget, often demonstrating faster early-stage improvement than other reproduced baselines. Two-sided paired t-tests show positive mean differences in favor of SILO across all eight landscapes for both maximum fitness and top-100 mean fitness, with statistically significant improvements after Holm correction on two and four landscapes, respectively. Under low-labeled data and noisy-proxy conditions, SILO shows competitive, task-dependent performance. Ablations identify SBS as the primary driver of performance, while AFS guidance and iterative imitation provide complementary, task-dependent benefits within the oracle-budgeted optimization loop. Code is available at: https://github.com/grimmlab/SILO.git
adfa39a204d71fd81c61722749a0fac9191c099f.title: Oracle-Budgeted Protein Design with Stochastic Search and Iterative Imitation

adfed1aac49e42ab87aab9dd282a610e3bfb74b9.summary: arXiv:2601.21285v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurately capturing feature interactions is essential in recommender systems, and recent trends show that scaling up model capacity could be a key driver for next-level predictive performance. While prior work has explored various model architectures to capture multi-granularity feature interactions, relatively little attention has been paid to efficient feature handling and scaling model capacity without incurring excessive inference latency. In this paper, we address this challenge by presenting Zenith, a scalable and efficient ranking architecture that learns complex feature interactions with minimal runtime overhead. Zenith uses Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) as a common capacity-scaling mechanism across feature interaction and long-sequence encoding, while adapting its parameterization to each token regime. The Feature Interaction Unit applies tokenwise attention and SMoE to a small, fixed set of high-dimensional Prime Tokens. In contrast, the Sequence Encoding Unit processes thousands of temporal tokens with SMoE-based query, key, and value projections and an SMoE-based feed-forward network. For the livestreaming-specific delayed-feedback problem, Zenith's Target Modeling Unit efficiently connects timely but incomplete short-horizon supervision with complete long-horizon supervision. Its real-world effectiveness is demonstrated through deployment on TikTok Live, a leading online livestreaming platform that attracts billions of users globally. Our online A/B test achieves gains of 9.93% in Quality Watch Session / User and 8.11% in Quality Watch Duration / User.
adfed1aac49e42ab87aab9dd282a610e3bfb74b9.title: Zenith: Scaling up Ranking Models for Billion-scale Livestreaming Recommendation

ae3679f47ef36617ead722cb85dc4209566f4270.summary: arXiv:2605.04375v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: To unleash the full potential of AI for Science, we must untether the agents from a purely digital environment. The agent's ability to control and explore in real-world labs is essential because the physical lab remains foundational to scientific discovery. While some tasks can be performed on a computer (e.g., data analysis, running simulated experiments), Eureka moments could occur at any time while operating lab instruments (e.g., when a scientist notices unexpected clues, intuition may prompt a real-time course change). Although autonomous labs are on the rise, which expose programmable APIs to control scientific instruments via software, bridging the gap between increasingly powerful AI agents and automated lab equipment requires innovation that draws insights from computer systems. We propose a new paradigm called ``Experiment-as-Code (EaC) Labs,'' where a core concept is to encode experiments as declarative configurations that can be compiled down to device-level APIs. AI agents come up with hypotheses and experiments, written as an ensemble of declarative configurations. The systems layer performs program analysis, safety checks, resource assignment, and job orchestration. Finally, programmatic experimentation occurs via actuating the device APIs. This is a general stack that is science-, lab-, and instrument-independent, representing a novel synthesis across the physical, systems, and intelligence layers to unleash the next breakthrough in AI for Science.
ae3679f47ef36617ead722cb85dc4209566f4270.title: Experiment-as-Code Labs: A Declarative Stack for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery

ae811a1f5a4eb27895df1c02431d0633688847a0.summary: arXiv:2608.03921v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We reinterpret Transformer inference by developing a functionally equivalent mechanical-structural description of its functional architecture. Parameterized transformations of token representations are identified with simple neural networks organized through output-input and output-weight interconnections. This reconstruction makes explicit a constitutive feature of ordinary Transformer inference: outputs generated from the current input determine the weights, and hence the transformations, of other networks. We show that the resulting mechanical-structural organization is functionally equivalent to the standard matrix description and gives rise to Sequence-level Interactive Dynamic Parallel Processing (SIDPP). We then quantify the dynamic component of inference. For a fixed Transformer architecture, the number of dynamic parameters generated by a prompt grows linearly with prompt length, with a proportionality constant determined by the model architecture, whereas the number of static parameters remains constant. We call the resulting structural dependence of processing on the prompt strong prompt sensitivity. GPT-4.5's recent Turing test success provides a striking behavioral phenomenon for which this framework offers a viable explanatory route. Finally, we discuss implications for interpretability, control, predictability, and neuromorphic construction. We argue that known biological mechanisms support the in-principle neural constructibility of a form of SIDPP, and on this basis formulate Conjecture T as a conditional research hypothesis concerning cortical language processing.
ae811a1f5a4eb27895df1c02431d0633688847a0.title: The Transformer Revolution, Part 1: Dynamic Processing through Output-Weight Interconnections

ae8cd0aae3f0a9a9a034f61d8e4b5f848acfea76.summary: arXiv:2611.32238v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agent-orchestrated robot systems combine the general reasoning capability of multimodal agents with the precise physical control of learned visuomotor policies. Yet such systems often fail at the moment of handoff: a policy is reliable only from a limited set of start states, while the agent may invoke it outside this region. We call this region the policy's handoff boundary. Existing whole-task policies typically have handoff boundaries that are narrow and difficult for an agent to characterize, making reliable coordination challenging. We propose Boundary-Aware Policy Learning, which explicitly shapes and then expands the handoff boundary of a visuomotor policy. First, Boundary-Explicit Training fine-tunes the policy on contact segments with diverse start poses, yielding a wide and well-defined boundary that can be communicated to the agent through a simple handoff protocol. Second, Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement retrains the policy on curated successful system rollouts, extending the boundary toward earlier stages of each task and allowing the agent to hand over sooner with fewer language-model calls. Across RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo, our system outperforms the strongest baseline by over 26 percentage points, reaching 98.4% success in randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes, while further reducing its API cost and execution time by 41.3% and 37.5%, respectively. These results suggest that the key to robust agent-policy orchestration lies not only in improving either component individually, but also in explicitly shaping the boundary between them.
ae8cd0aae3f0a9a9a034f61d8e4b5f848acfea76.title: Boundary-Aware Policy Learning for Agent-Orchestrated Robot Manipulation

aeba07ed198dd93d8ad2820f5efacb3ebce161fe.summary: arXiv:2611.32687v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been widely adopted to enhance the multimodal reasoning of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, existing methods share a common limitation of Module-Level Credit Entanglement, in which the vision encoder, projector, and LLM modules are jointly optimized using the same advantage signals even when perceptual correctness and final-answer correctness differ. To address this limitation, we propose Module-Specific Policy Optimization (MSPO), a framework that separates perceptual and outcome-based learning signals across model modules. Specifically, MSPO uses responses to perception checklists comprising auxiliary questions about visual information to derive an advantage for training the vision encoder. From these responses, MSPO computes the Confidence-aware Perception Reward (CaPR), using a perception sign obtained by thresholding checklist accuracy to determine reward direction and posterior confidence from a Beta distribution over latent perception accuracy to scale reward magnitude. We then derive the vision advantage through group-relative normalization of CaPR and scale it using main-task success rates. This advantage guides updates to the vision encoder, while the projector and LLM retain outcome-based GRPO updates. Extensive experiments on seven mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that MSPO outperforms existing RL-tuned models on average at both the 3B and 7B scales.
aeba07ed198dd93d8ad2820f5efacb3ebce161fe.title: Are We Rewarding the Wrong Module? Module-Specific Policy Optimization for Multimodal Reinforcement Learning

aec907937d5cc279e98a23c9c6b59895a6b86dcc.summary: arXiv:2610.09127v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reconstructing an editable CAD model from a 3D shape remains a challenging engineering task. Existing methods can propose CAD operations, but no single source of proposals works equally well across different part geometries and stages of reconstruction. We introduce CADFather, an autonomous agentic system that coordinates complementary tools to recover parametric CAD programs from 3D meshes. A vision-language assistant inspects renders of the target and intermediate reconstructions, then decides which candidate CAD programs to extend, which tools to invoke, how many proposals to generate, and when to finish. Learned and algorithmic tools propose CAD operations, while numerical optimization refines the parameters of existing programs. Proposed or refined programs are executed and evaluated to provide feedback for subsequent decisions. The agent maintains alternative candidate programs for each target part and preserves the best valid result throughout reconstruction. CADFather uses pretrained generation and assistant models without additional training. We evaluate reconstruction quality and execution validity on the full DeepCAD, Fusion360, and MCB test sets, as well as on CADENA-Bench, CADBench, and BenchCAD. We additionally analyze computational cost and the trade-off between cost and reconstruction quality.
aec907937d5cc279e98a23c9c6b59895a6b86dcc.title: CADFather: Autonomous CAD Reconstruction through Coordinated Tool Use

aecdd526b3bf9ad5d77c500171c9620beddc43ca.summary: arXiv:2610.15267v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, but unconstrained autoregressive predictors may contract the latent distribution over long rollouts. We introduce Symplectic Hamiltonian JEPA (LeHami), which replaces the standard predictor with an action-conditioned Hamiltonian flow over a structured latent state (q, p) integrated using an exactly symplectic leapfrog step. This construction preserves phase-space volume at every rollout step and rules out uniform contraction, asymptotically stable fixed points, and merging of distinct latent states, independently of the learned parameters or action sequence. We obtain the momentum-like component from temporal derivatives of the learned position-like representation, providing an explicit second-order state for prediction and control. We measure rollout collapse on the data, with four ratios of the rollout to the truth, on five environments learned from pixels: conservative and actuated pendulums, a mass-spring, a two-body system and a cart pole. With the encoder and latent state held fixed, an MLP and a transformer predictor contract the rollout on every environment, while LeHami's rollouts do not merge. LeHami is the most accurate of the three at long horizons, in position on four of the five environments and in velocity on three, while at short horizons the free predictors are more accurate on two of the five. The learned flow also integrates at unseen sub-frame step sizes and, run backward with the recorded actions, recovers earlier frames as well as it predicts later ones. LeWM, with a richer three-frame encoder of its own, is more accurate on four of the five, which suggests incorporating a richer encoder within LeHami in future work. These results show how geometric structure can provide inference-time guarantees that are complementary to representation regularization in latent world models.
aecdd526b3bf9ad5d77c500171c9620beddc43ca.title: LeHami: Symplectic Latent Dynamics Toward Long-Horizon Rollouts in World Models

aef632472a5e3af7f91b4cd9c5d8e0ecee471353.title: Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases

af2cc4b8efc2d2ea8e6589c7bdfceb9704b69cd8.summary: arXiv:2611.28894v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neural collapse (NC) predicts that, late in training, last-layer class features concentrate at their means and the means form a simplex equiangular tight frame (ETF). We ask whether NC also leaves a signature in the functional connectome of each layer: the graph of Pearson correlations between hidden-unit activations, built per class and summarized by persistent graph homology. Using deep MLPs, we observe two topological phenomena that co-occur with the well-studied geometric NC in the final layers during the terminal phase. Contrary to NC1, the split-half variability of a class connectome increases (TNC1). The mean pairwise $H_0$ distance $\bar{D}$ between class connectomes also rises (TNC2), but unevenly across class pairs, unlike the equidistance of NC2. We find that 24-56% of last-layer units become dead for some classes yet stay active for others, which inflates $\bar{D}$. After correcting for these units, both signatures remain elevated. These results from MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 provide preliminary evidence that a topological mechanism may accompany the geometric signatures of NC.
af2cc4b8efc2d2ea8e6589c7bdfceb9704b69cd8.title: Topological Neural Collapse

af93a898ccc4eb9c397e64a1a1798729a8727c9d.summary: arXiv:2510.05197v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Assessing the capabilities and risks of frontier AI systems is a critical area of research; recent work has shown that repeated sampling can dramatically increase both. For instance, repeated sampling allows models to solve difficult math and coding problems, but it may also increase their risk of being jailbroken. Such results raise a crucial question: how can one accurately predict a model's behavior when scaled to a massive number of attempts, given a vastly smaller sampling budget? This question is directly relevant to model providers, who serve hundreds of millions of users daily, and to governmental regulators, who seek to prevent harms. To answer this question, we make three contributions. First, we find that standard methods for fitting these laws suffer from statistical shortcomings that hinder predictions, especially in data-limited scenarios. Second, we remedy these shortcomings by introducing a robust estimation framework, which uses a beta-binomial distribution to generate more accurate predictions from limited data. Third, we propose a dynamic sampling strategy that allocates a greater budget to harder problems. Combined, these innovations enable more reliable prediction of rare risks and capabilities at a fraction of the computational cost.
af93a898ccc4eb9c397e64a1a1798729a8727c9d.title: Efficient Prediction of pass@k Scaling in Large Language Models

afb34d273a5878993a0fff097e263393c3bbe00c.summary: arXiv:2611.29571v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transformer-based large models require huge computational and storage costs. Quantum computation is expected to address that due to its potential to speed up classical algorithms exponentially. Key challenges of implementing quantum large models include the linear, unitary nature of qubit evolutions contrast with the non-unitary matrices and nonlinear functions in classical Transformers, as well as the difficulty of implementing gradient back-propagation on quantum hardware. Here we propose a fully quantum large model containing all the Transformer layers, implementing the non-unitary transformations through SVD-decomposition-based quantum circuits, and approximated nonlinear activation functions through pre-trained parameterized quantum circuits. We also propose a quantum circuit training algorithm based on multi-agent Reinforcement Learning, which can train large-scale parameterized quantum circuits without back-propagation. The dependency between the inference time complexity and the model's hidden dimension has been reduced from polynomial to logarithmic, showing an exponential advantage. The inference executions on the quantum hardware verify our model's 300-1000 times speed-up, and the measurements on the sequence-to-sequence tasks shows its learning ability. The training algorithm achieves only 25% complexity of the best SOTA quantum circuit training algorithms, especially this ratio decreases fast as the parameter scale increases. Our work not only proposes a quantum large model that can significantly reduce the computational cost, but also promotes the quantum computation towards general computing.
afb34d273a5878993a0fff097e263393c3bbe00c.title: Non unitary and nonlinear quantum generative large model design and fast large-scale training without back propagation

b03e856411c0697d16197b2f4a0ae82209cac26d.summary: 🧠 两小时从 0 训出你的 64M 大模型。Train your own 64M LLM from scratch in 2 hours. License: Apache-2.0.
b03e856411c0697d16197b2f4a0ae82209cac26d.title: jingyaogong/minimind

b0445d85551146570ec6acf92956720517e9a968.summary: arXiv:2605.05951v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: World models enable model-based planning through learned latent dynamics, but imagined rollouts become unstable as the planning horizon grows or the dynamics distribution shifts: an unconstrained predictor feeds each predicted state back as input, so the latent distribution contracts until distinct states merge. We argue that this drift and contraction reflect two missing structures in planner-facing latents: a history-conditioned predictive state summarizing past observations and actions, and geometric organization that separates configuration, momentum, and task semantics. We propose HaM-World, a structured world model that decomposes the latent state into a canonical-like (q,p) subspace and a context subspace c, while using Mamba selective state-space memory as the history-conditioned input to the same latent dynamics. The (q,p) subspace evolves through an energy-derived Hamiltonian vector field plus learnable residual/control dynamics, while c captures semantic, dissipative, and non-conservative factors. The planner uses this single latent state for prediction, reward/value estimation, imagined rollouts, and CEM search. On six DeepMind Control Suite tasks, HaM-World ranks first on four and second on the other two, with the highest six-task Avg. AUC (91.9, +10.3% over TD-MPC2). Within the horizons the planner unrolls, it reduces imagined-rollout error to 45% of TD-MPC2's and wins 11/12 k in {3,5,7} MSE cells. Under 12 OOD perturbations spanning dynamics shifts, action delay, and observation masking it attains the highest return in every condition (+10.2% on Finger Spin, +13.6% on Reacher Easy). Ablations show that both selective memory and the Soft-Hamiltonian prior contribute to the gains. Mechanism diagnostics support the intended design, showing bounded action-free energy drift, structured energy variation under policy rollouts, and coherent control-induced energy transfer.
b0445d85551146570ec6acf92956720517e9a968.title: HaM-World: Soft-Hamiltonian World Models with Selective Memory for Planning

b0689cf87ab570a441c88635b910134907af4a34.summary: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo, an open-source runtime for Linux. It helps teams protect running systems while they roll out patches.
b0689cf87ab570a441c88635b910134907af4a34.title: OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo

b06f898e9161a827a4b08c386f066a1dddabac4d.summary: arXiv:2601.17829v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The construction of function calling agents has emerged as a promising avenue for extending model capabilities. A major challenge for this task is obtaining high quality diverse data for training. Prior work emphasizes diversity in functions, invocation patterns, and interaction turns, yet linguistic diversity of requests and coverage of arguments (e.g., \texttt{city\_name}, \texttt{stock\_ticker}) remain underexplored. We propose a method that generates synthetic datasets via optimizing general-purpose diversity metrics across both queries and arguments, without relying on hand-crafted rules or taxonomies, making it robust to different usecases. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our technique via both intrinsic and extrinsic testing, comparing it to SoTA data generation methods. We show a superiority over baselines in terms of diversity, while keeping comparable correctness. Additionally, when used as a training set, the model resulting from our dataset exhibits superior performance compared to analogous models based on the baseline data generation methods in out-of-distribution performance. In particular, we achieve an $7.4\%$ increase in accuracy on the BFCL benchmark compared to similar counterparts.
b06f898e9161a827a4b08c386f066a1dddabac4d.title: Linguistic and Argument Diversity in Synthetic Data for Function-Calling Agents

b0798d657cce2dd657d83080745d46aeb3e96135.summary: arXiv:2611.32517v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real-time traffic monitoring in smart cities demands ultra-low latency processing to support time-critical decisions such as incident detection and congestion management. While cloud-based solutions offer robust computation, their inherent latency limits their applicability for such tasks. This work proposes a localized edge AI framework that connects low-power IoT camera sensors to a client, or applies offloading of inference to an NVIDIA Jetson Nano (GPU). Networking is achieved via Wi-Fi, enabling image classification without relying on wide-area infrastructure such as 5G, or wired networks. We evaluate two processing strategies: local inference on camera nodes and GPU-accelerated offloading to the Jetson Nano.We show that local processing is only feasible for lightweight models and low frame rates, whereas offloading enables near-realtime performance even for more complex models. These results demonstrate the viability of cost-effective, Wi-Fi-based edge AI deployments for latency-critical urban monitoring.
b0798d657cce2dd657d83080745d46aeb3e96135.title: Wi-Fi Enabled Edge Intelligence Framework for Smart City Traffic Monitoring using Low-Power IoT Cameras

b0b8bb2231e934cd358d41167413e422211c91d3.summary: arXiv:2611.32119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Episodic-memory embodied question answering enables agents to answer questions based on previously recorded visual observations of the surrounding scenes. However, growing observation histories, varying observation quality across viewpoints, and limited computational resources make it challenging to construct and maintain compact visual memories while retrieving sufficient evidence for question answering. To address these challenges, we introduce CoverMem, which incorporates three key components: (1) a coverage-constrained memory construction method that selects a compact set of informative full frames satisfying object-quality and representative-scene coverage requirements; (2) a coverage-preserving incremental maintenance strategy that locally reselects only the affected frames to satisfy updated coverage requirements as observations arrive; and (3) a budgeted complementary frame selection method that balances question relevance, additional support for question requirements, and redundancy with selected frames within a fixed budget. Experimental results on three benchmarks covering diverse environments and question types demonstrate that CoverMem improves question-answering performance under limited visual budgets.
b0b8bb2231e934cd358d41167413e422211c91d3.title: CoverMem: Coverage-Constrained Visual Memory for Budgeted Embodied Question Answering

b109d095b1d42263fac1eff226270d8e899be2e6.summary: arXiv:2605.25786v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Efficiently solving Poisson equations on complex, irregular domains remains a fundamental challenge in scientific computing, as classical iterative solvers often suffer from prohibitive runtime due to ill-conditioned systems. While neural operators offer a fast alternative, they typically rely on large-scale labeled datasets or struggle with unstable training dynamics when using physics-informed residual losses. We propose \textsc{NPSolver}, a neural Poisson solver trained without solution labels via iterative physics supervision. Instead of relying on fully converged numerical solutions or raw PDE residuals, \textsc{NPSolver} utilizes a small number of preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) steps to refine its own predictions, providing a more stable and well-scaled training signal. Theoretical analysis confirms that this iterative supervision serves as a well-conditioned error proxy and that a stop-gradient design is essential for optimization stability. To better capture boundary-driven features under mixed boundary conditions, we further introduce the Boundary-Aware Transolver (\textsc{BA-Transolver}) architecture that explicitly separates interior and boundary tokenization. Extensive evaluations on 2D and 3D irregular geometries demonstrate that \textsc{NPSolver} outperforms both physics-informed and data-driven baselines. Furthermore, a downstream thermal control task highlights the model's capability for conducting efficient and reliable gradient-based boundary control. We will release our codes and data at https://github.com/intell-sci-comput/NPSolver.
b109d095b1d42263fac1eff226270d8e899be2e6.title: NPSolver: Neural Poisson Solver with Iterative Physics Supervision

b1a0380bffed5734e2314fc3b49009536f2c6389.summary: arXiv:2611.28104v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Source-free cross-domain few-shot learning (SF-CDFSL) adapts a pre-trained vision-language model such as CLIP to a distant target domain from a handful of labeled images, without access to source data. Recent methods improve the fine-tuning of CLIP with token-level interventions and apply them in the same way to every target domain. In this paper, we find that whether an intervention helps depends on how well frozen CLIP already recognizes the target domain: in 5-way 1-shot tasks, intervening improves accuracy by 0.72 points where frozen CLIP misclassifies most support images, but lowers it by 1.31 points where frozen CLIP already classifies them well, and the support set of a single episode suffices to tell the two cases apart; a bias-variance analysis explains both. Based on this finding, we propose Competence-Gated Adaptation (CoGA), which measures frozen CLIP's accuracy and margin on the labeled support set and decides, before training, whether to intervene on the visual tokens or to trust CLIP by fusing the adapted prediction with the frozen one. CoGA adds no trainable parameters and uses no query labels. On the four BSCD-FSL target domains, CoGA achieves the best average accuracy, 59.56% (1-shot) and 68.96% (5-shot), outperforms ATHA and TIR by at least 2.82 and 1.39 points on the same episodes, and consistently improves three further backbones, three parameter-efficient fine-tuning frameworks and five further target domains.
b1a0380bffed5734e2314fc3b49009536f2c6389.title: Intervene or Trust CLIP? Competence-Gated Adaptation for Source-Free Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning

b2208f46cc3a5d91e6ed411dd065d85ca78794be.summary: arXiv:2611.28963v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A world model should tell us not only what will happen, but what would happen under a different action. Learned Earth models now forecast remarkably well, yet forecast skill says little about what their state means or how it responds to a changed driver. We build LandWM, a world model of land-surface water in which rain is the action, learned from seven years of SMAP and CYGNSS observations: physical observation operators tie its latent state to soil water, and a mass-conserving balance governs how that state responds to rain. Over the U.S. Southern Great Plains, the model, never shown a soil-moisture value, tracks 28 in-situ probes as well as the operational SMAP Level-4 product, even from CYGNSS alone, and a storm added to the forcing of a station's cell wets its soil as natural storms wet the probes. Replace either piece and the forecasts stay, but the meaning goes: with neural operators, only a probe fitted to the stations finds the soil water; with a generic recurrent transition, rain on a single cell barely moves it. Yet when the same rain covers the whole region the two transitions swap roles, and the conserving one responds too weakly. Grounding makes a world model readable; its response to actions must be tested under more than one kind of intervention.
b2208f46cc3a5d91e6ed411dd065d85ca78794be.title: Learning Land-Surface Hydrology World Model from Satellite Observations

b2537428d0f1534040e2aced0a904058d5dde78a.summary: arXiv:2607.27073v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study online convex optimization on a compact convex domain of diameter $D$ in which the learner observes, at each round, one stochastic subgradient and no loss values. The observations are conditionally unbiased, and the noise has an unconditional $p$-th moment at most $\sigma^p$ for an unknown $p\in(1,2]$; for $p 1$, without knowing $G$, $\sigma$, $p$, or $P_T$: the constant of the first term is numerical, the constant of the second is $O(1+\log(p/(p-1)))$, and no logarithmic factor of $T$ appears. The analysis bounds the gradient energy separately on each restart block, which gives the exponent $(p-1)/p$ of $\Lambda_T$ in the noise term; a bound over the whole horizon gives the exponent $1/2$. Running the algorithm on epochs of doubling length removes the need to know $T$ at the cost of a factor $2+\sqrt2$. The appendices give a high-probability version and a synthetic study.
b2537428d0f1534040e2aced0a904058d5dde78a.title: Parameter-Free Dynamic Regret under Heavy-Tailed Noise

b3db5e935e12afb4156fdbb527f60223dc183fec.summary: arXiv:2611.28508v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding naturalistic brain activity requires going beyond the stimulus alone, as external inputs continuously interact with an individual's evolving brain state. A world model captures such dynamics in a latent state by inferring it from neural observations, predicting stimulus-driven evolution, and updating with new observations. However, existing brain world models fail to maintain a persistent latent state over time, and standard metrics of neural prediction accuracy cannot tell whether a model tracks an individual's brain state or relies solely on the stimulus. To directly test state inference, prediction, and updating, we introduce BrainStateBench, which evaluates a model's latent state through a frozen linear probe on whole-cortex, movie-driven fMRI. Its State task tests whether a model captures trial-to-trial variability in an individual's responses to repeated stimuli, while Forecast and Updating evaluate future activity predictions without and with new observations, respectively. To track individual brain state across time, we propose Spectator, a linear latent world model trained with a joint-embedding predictive objective. Spectator encodes short- and long-horizon observation histories into a two-timescale latent state and predicts state transitions linearly from the current state and stimulus. Stimulus-only encoders reach 0.320 in fMRI prediction correlation without observing the brain (0% on State), while prior deep brain world models reach 0.239 yet score at most 0.4% on State. In contrast, Spectator achieves 0.349 correlation alongside 5.5% on State, 16.0% on Forecast, and 20.3% on Updating, outperforming all baselines while forecasting over 20x faster than deep forecasting models.
b3db5e935e12afb4156fdbb527f60223dc183fec.title: State of Mind: Learning and Evaluating World Models of Naturalistic Brain Dynamics
