b3fc1a7f5176ff72d06243aa0768c24723bfcda1.summary: arXiv:2512.24635v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Automated Program Repair (APR) seeks to generate correct patches for buggy programs, but recent Large Language Model (LLM)-based repair systems remain sensitive to superficial code changes and often rely on coarse test outcomes during iterative repair. We propose DynaFix, an LLM-based APR framework that integrates execution-level dynamic information into a closed-loop repair workflow. The distinguishing feature of DynaFix lies not in using execution-level information per se, but in repeatedly updating and exploiting such information throughout the iterative repair process. In each repair round, DynaFix uses ByteTrace to collect variable states, branch paths, and call stacks, incorporates these runtime signals into structured prompts, validates generated patches through re-execution, and feeds the resulting updated traces into subsequent repair iterations. This process grounds patch generation in concrete execution behavior rather than static code alone. We evaluate DynaFix on Defects4J v2.0, the Real-World Benchmark, and a code perturbation benchmark, Defects4J-Trans. DynaFix repairs 236 single-function Defects4J bugs with GPT-4 and 186 with GPT-4o, including 23 bugs not fixed by existing baselines. On Defects4J-Trans, DynaFix achieves 15.6%-32.1% higher aggregate repair counts than ReinFix and shows higher repair retention under semantics-preserving transformations. It also reduces token consumption by 60%-70% compared with state-of-the-art LLM-based APR methods. These results show that repeatedly updating and exploiting execution-level information throughout iterative repair can substantially improve the effectiveness, robustness, and cost efficiency of LLM-based program repair.
b3fc1a7f5176ff72d06243aa0768c24723bfcda1.title: DynaFix: Iterative Automated Program Repair Driven by Execution-Level Dynamic Information

b3fd9f46a901fe4bc4df91cb9924c3f928c8d858.summary: arXiv:2610.23297v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Single-image refocusing changes the focal plane and depth of field of a photograph after capture. Users compare focal choices on one photograph, so content stability across edits matters alongside quality and speed. Recent generative methods rerun large diffusion models for every edit, even when they first restore an all-in-focus image, so content can change inconsistently between edits. Yet only this restoration is highly ill-posed and benefits from a generative prior, whereas rendering blur is largely determined by depth and the focal plane. We therefore propose FlashReFocus, which runs diffusion once per photograph and renders each edit with a lightweight network. A one-step diffusion deblurrer with a decoder refiner recovers fine detail efficiently while balancing fidelity and perceptual quality. The renderer uses an explicit defocus map for control and defocus-bias attention to promote information exchange between tokens with similar blur magnitudes. Because every edit reuses the same reconstruction, in-focus content stays consistent across edits, and editing the map enables tilt-shift and two-plane effects. We further collect 3CReal, a benchmark of 89 pairs from three camera-lens systems, to evaluate generalization to unseen optics. For zero-shot bokeh rendering on EBB! Val176 and 3CReal, FlashReFocus leads the evaluated methods in fidelity and perceptual quality. At 1536x1536, a complete refocus takes 2.45 s and each subsequent edit 0.46 s on one RTX PRO 6000.
b3fd9f46a901fe4bc4df91cb9924c3f928c8d858.title: FlashReFocus: Interactive Image Refocusing in Seconds

b444c386bca1f09d508d6dc2e6df904c3007185e.summary: arXiv:2512.15948v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Where do objective functions come from? How do we select what goals to pursue? Human intelligence is adept at synthesizing new objective functions on the fly. How does this work, and can we endow artificial systems with the same ability? This paper proposes an approach to answering these questions, starting with the concept of a subjective function, a higher-order objective function that is endogenous to the agent (i.e., defined with respect to the agent's features, rather than an external task). Expected prediction error is studied as a concrete example of a subjective function. This proposal has many connections to ideas in psychology, neuroscience, and machine learning.
b444c386bca1f09d508d6dc2e6df904c3007185e.title: Subjective functions

b4f06bf0be65c14f5b73d21c007d747d94bbcd38.summary: arXiv:2611.32464v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern games and applications increasingly employ artificial intelligence (AI), user modeling, and gamification to influence user behavior, sustain engagement, and monetize attention. Although these mechanisms can enhance motivation and enjoyment, they also raise concerns about manipulation, personal data usage, and transparency. To examine how players perceive these dynamics, we conducted a survey with 28 adult participants. Respondents expressed strong concerns about the collection and exploitation of personal information in games and gamified applications, while also reporting low awareness and a limited sense of control over how their data is used. They evaluated progression features such as leveling systems and leaderboards as motivating. In contrast, they rated retention-focused mechanics such as daily login rewards and random reward reveals as highly manipulative. Participants reported that these systems can create fear of missing out or resemble gambling. Participants also expressed support for regulatory measures that limit exploitative design and protect vulnerable users. These findings reveal a clear gap between increasingly powerful engagement strategies and user trust, illustrating the need for more responsible and transparent gamification practices.
b4f06bf0be65c14f5b73d21c007d747d94bbcd38.title: Gamification in the age of AI: surveying player perceptions of motivation, manipulation, and data protection

b4fb8c9d0efc9fe2d4d477d6f6af0fbd908f056b.summary: arXiv:2611.31541v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A coding agent may need to upload a report while its sandbox blocks network access. A host mediator can restore delivery, but an injected instruction may add a secret to the approved request. We study this interaction using files and HTTP receipts to measure effects independently of control logs. Two prospective frozen-input cohorts comprise 110 and 300 runs on previously explored authored tasks. Restrictive sandboxing produces no observed attack harm but reduces benign utility to 6/8 and 12/24. Mediation restores uploads and admits disclosure; complete-line matching retains full benign utility but misses two value-only disclosures in the expanded cohort. A separate 72-run boundary study identifies encoded disclosure, observer misses, and formatting checks that obscure benign refusals. An 80-run SafeAgents/OpenShell follow-up shows that containment stops the tested guard misses among valid observations, while mediation restores benign uploads and delivers both encoded-attestation attacks. Twelve judge-error rows remain unscored. A separate response-capture diagnostic reproduces their failures at the native token budget. A 12-run exact-publication-contract experiment blocks both attacks but also rejects both benign formatting variants; a 4-run normalized follow-up restores both benign uploads while still rejecting both attacks. These small, single-model studies identify delivery-path and measurement limits; they do not establish general attack resistance.
b4fb8c9d0efc9fe2d4d477d6f6af0fbd908f056b.title: Where Agent Defenses Fail: A Case Study of Policy Compositions and Measurement Limits

b5111dc2cef1cde98c00d7d41a8b1f5bf3908ea3.summary: arXiv:2611.27189v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: India's AI debate often swings between two insufficient options: replicating the compute-intensive, capital-heavy foundation-model programmes of the United States or China, or remaining a downstream adopter of foreign AI with localised interfaces and safeguards. Neither serves a country that must deliver AI to a very large, diverse population across uneven infrastructure and within constrained budgets. This white paper from the Centre for Responsible AI (CeRAI), IIT Madras, proposes a third path: Responsible Frugal AI, which applies principle-based frugal engineering alongside Responsible AI. Responsible Frugal AI is right-sized AI: it fixes the functional requirement first, asks whether AI is needed at all, and then chooses the smallest sufficient model, meeting the requirement with minimal resources while keeping a verified margin, robustness and responsible governance. The framework applies frugality across four dimensions (data, compute, model and operations) through seven levers spanning the AI lifecycle, each with practices and measures. It calls for public AI rails, vernacular-first design, measured resource use, human oversight for high-stakes decisions, and a cap on total resource consumption so that efficiency gains are not cancelled out by rising usage. We argue that India is resource-imbalanced rather than resource-poor, and that frugal principles offer the most viable route to population-scale deployment, fit naturally with India's digital public infrastructure, and make sovereignty operational by preserving India's capacity to specify, deploy, govern, inspect and adapt its AI systems. A seven-point adoption checklist and eleven policy statements translate the framework into practice, positioning AI in India as a responsible, frugal public-value system that maximises social value per rupee and per joule.
b5111dc2cef1cde98c00d7d41a8b1f5bf3908ea3.title: A Frugal AI Framework for India: Responsible and Right-sized AI

b51aab997211fd773a60b10006a9dd17c12b7158.summary: arXiv:2601.01792v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this report, we present HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni, the first any-to-any omnimodal model in the HyperCLOVA X family that supports text, audio, and vision as both inputs and outputs. By consolidating multimodal understanding and generation into a single model rather than separate modality-specific pipelines, HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni serves as an 8B-scale omni-pathfinding point toward practical any-to-any omni assistants. At a high level, the model unifies modalities through a shared next-token prediction interface over an interleaved multimodal sequence, while vision and audio encoders inject continuous embeddings for fine-grained understanding and grounding. Empirical evaluations demonstrate competitive performance against comparably sized models across diverse input-output combinations spanning text, audio, and vision, in both Korean and English. We anticipate that the open-weight release of HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni will support a wide range of research and deployment scenarios.
b51aab997211fd773a60b10006a9dd17c12b7158.title: HyperCLOVA X 8B Omni

b53c50f80542615b64082096ff7711aac3b30d9f.summary: arXiv:2605.12887v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Web-enabled LLM agents are changing how online information influences search outcomes. Existing Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) studies mainly focus on individual webpages. However, agentic web search is not a single-document setting: an agent may issue queries, crawl pages, follow links, reformulate searches, and synthesize evidence across multiple browsing steps. Influence therefore depends not only on page content, but also on how pages are organized, connected, and encountered along the agent's browsing trajectory. We study this shift through Ecosystem Generative Engine Optimization (EcoGEO), which treats GEO as an environment-level influence problem for web-enabled LLM agents. To instantiate this perspective, we propose TRACE, a Trajectory-Aware Coordinated Evidence Ecosystem. Given a recommendation query and a fictional target product, our method builds a controlled evidence environment that coordinates an agent-facing navigation entry page with heterogeneous support pages. These pages use shared terminology, internal links, and consistent product attributes to introduce, verify, and reinforce the target product. We evaluate our method on OPR-Bench, a benchmark for open-ended product recommendation. Experiments show that it consistently outperforms page-level GEO baselines in Recommendation. Trajectory-level metrics show improved initial target access and additional internal-link browsing, while follow-up-search effects vary across backbones and comparison methods. Together with the multi-page baseline and ablations, these findings support the role of evidence organization in shaping the agent's evidence-acquisition process. Overall, our findings support an ecosystem research paradigm for GEO, where web-enabled LLM agents are studied in relation to the broader evidence environments that guide search, browsing, and answer synthesis.
b53c50f80542615b64082096ff7711aac3b30d9f.title: EcoGEO: Trajectory-Aware Evidence Ecosystems for Web-Enabled LLM Search Agents

b5614bccdb7000a90f04357bdd9531943fa43018.summary: arXiv:2611.31256v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by using a lightweight draft model to propose tokens for verification by a target model. Draft training commonly optimizes token-level distribution alignment, but this does not directly optimize the length of the accepted prefix: once a draft token is rejected, all subsequent draft tokens are discarded. We propose FreDraft, an on-policy training method that directly maximizes the expected accepted length of drafts sampled from the current draft model. This objective accounts for first-rejection truncation and induces prefix-aware credit assignment, weighting each token by its contribution to the acceptance of the current and subsequent tokens. To optimize the objective efficiently, we analytically marginalize token-level acceptance rate, using the target model's vocabulary distribution to reduce gradient variance. We further redistribute part of this distribution-level gradient into an explicit penalty for sampled tokens whose probabilities are overestimated by the draft model, while preserving the expected gradient. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and target models show that FreDraft improves accepted length and decoding speedup over strong baselines, achieving faster on-policy training convergence.
b5614bccdb7000a90f04357bdd9531943fa43018.title: Directly Maximizing On-policy Expected Accepted Length for Speculative Decoding

b571fe4abd0264ce2f6d8a15daf1f0acc0a75d32.summary: arXiv:2604.01083v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Partial audio deepfakes, where synthesized segments are spliced into genuine recordings, are particularly deceptive because most of the audio remains authentic. Existing detectors are supervised: they require frame-level annotations, overfit to specific synthesis pipelines, and must be retrained as new generative models emerge. We argue that this supervision is unnecessary. We hypothesize that speech foundation models implicitly encode a forensic signal: genuine speech forms smooth, slowly varying embedding trajectories, while splice boundaries introduce abrupt disruptions in frame-level transitions. Building on this, we propose TRACE (Training-free Representation-based Audio Countermeasure via Embedding dynamics), a training-free framework that detects partial audio deepfakes by analyzing the first-order dynamics of frozen speech foundation model representations without any training, labeled data, or architectural modification. We evaluate TRACE on four benchmarks that span two languages using six speech foundation models. In PartialSpoof, TRACE achieves 8.08% EER, competitive with fine-tuned supervised baselines. In LlamaPartialSpoof, the most challenging benchmark featuring LLM-driven commercial synthesis, TRACE surpasses a supervised baseline outright (24.12% vs. 24.49% EER) without any target-domain data. These results show that temporal dynamics in speech foundation models provide an effective, generalize signal for training-free audio forensics.
b571fe4abd0264ce2f6d8a15daf1f0acc0a75d32.title: TRACE: Training-Free Partial Audio Deepfake Detection via Embedding Trajectory Analysis of Speech Foundation Models

b57a06f41f2f63eabba9e390266039e7d486dad1.title: Show HN: Apfel – The free AI already on your Mac

b58fa41079ffe391f6b1cac32600c57e273e8b49.summary: arXiv:2611.29968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Runtime model selection trades detection quality against energy and latency. However, comparing a selector only with a more costly static detector conflates detector choice with the benefit of adaptation. We present a framework for analysis and physical measurement that combines a pairwise reward criterion, matched static controls, paired blocks, a fixed load-prevalence factorial design, and reporting of actions outside training support. On one Raspberry Pi 4B with four frozen TON-IoT detectors, tabular Q-learning and a deep Q-network (DQN) both select LightLR throughout. A retrospective audit using validation data only rules out preference reversals for MedRF versus LightLR and HeavyMLP versus LightLR. However, TinyDT has a higher reward than LightLR in seven of the 2,500 windows, so the audit does not establish global LightLR optimality. We also evaluate a causal DeadlineGuard rule under a fixed factorial design with three arrival rates (50, 100, and 4,000 rows/s) and three attack prevalences (0.10, 0.50, and 0.90). Compared with Static-MedRF, DeadlineGuard saves 43.7 J per 500-s run (2.98%; 95% paired CI 41.4--46.0 J) and eliminates all 512 deadline misses among 5,000 windows, at a cost of 1.373 percentage points in F1. Outside training support, Tabular-Q's deterministic tie-breaking rule selects TinyDT, resulting in a false-positive rate of 67.76%. These single-board results motivate joint audits of reward attainability, realized actions, attribution against matched static controls, service feasibility, and default actions outside training support.
b58fa41079ffe391f6b1cac32600c57e273e8b49.title: When Learned IDS Model Selection Collapses to a Static Choice: A Measurement Study at the Edge

b61cb7f4a5958f02d476b4cc7fabcc6c692fdaf0.summary: arXiv:2605.22883v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI agents plan, call tools and retry failed attempts, so they decide at run time how many model calls a goal takes. Energy is commonly reported per call or per token, which cannot show the energy needed to deliver a successful goal. We introduce energy per submitted, completed and successful goal (EpG, EpCG, EpSG), which charge every attempt to its goal and distinguish completion from correctness. We also introduce the Orchestration Overhead Index (OOI), the ratio of agentic to linear EpSG, where the linear workflow is a single model call, with a rule that states when the agent's higher success rate compensates for its extra energy. We evaluate the metrics on 11,621 goals with 8 models on three hardware platforms (Intel x86, NVIDIA GB10 and Apple M4), using a measurement method that declares the window, the idle correction and the hardware boundary. Across 45 comparisons over 23 goal types, OOI ranged from 0.04x to 51.21x: the agent cost more per successful goal wherever a single call already succeeded often, and less on a calculation goal, where it handed the computation to a calculator that the single call usually got wrong. Ranking models by EpSG instead of EpG changed the chosen model in 6 of 14 rankings, because EpG can favor a model that spends little energy on each goal but often answers incorrectly. Each failed attempt added about the energy of one complete attempt, while energy per call stayed almost unchanged, so reporting per call hides what retries cost. Engineers can therefore use EpSG and OOI to choose the workflow and model that meet their success, energy and latency requirements, and the measured energy of a failed attempt to set retry budgets.
b61cb7f4a5958f02d476b4cc7fabcc6c692fdaf0.title: Energy per Successful Goal: Goal-Level Energy Accounting for Agentic AI Systems

b62bbc081878ab96f67ac98b5b8a7fe7d9b43eaa.summary: arXiv:2611.29127v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) weights every supervised token equally, so on knowledge-dense corpora the loss budget follows token count rather than importance: on a legal QA benchmark, citation strings absorb 81% of the supervised loss weight budget while the answers being taught absorb 5%. We present Group-Balanced SFT (GB-SFT), which equalizes the loss budget across the semantic roles of tokens within a target sequence. With one tunable dial and one structural switch, GB-SFT contains standard SFT, class- and span-level balancing as corners whose geometry we characterize exactly. On benchmarks in law, medicine, code, and mathematics, we show across model families that: (i) GB- SFT injects new knowledge better than uniform SFT, pointwise token weighting, memory editing, and matched-budget data mixing; (ii) it matches the injection of masking out everything but the knowledge payload while retaining the citation recall that masking destroys (0.98 vs. 0.38); and (iii) role-aware grouping carries the gain: label-free partitions recover at most a third of it, an LLM tagger nearly all where the groups are lexically distinctive; and and (iv) the budget governs what fine-tuning breaks as well as what it learns, acting as a monotone lever on the safety-guardrail erosion SFT causes, at matched task accuracy. We release two new contamination-controlled knowledge-injection benchmarks with validated ground truth.
b62bbc081878ab96f67ac98b5b8a7fe7d9b43eaa.title: Group-Balanced Supervised Fine-Tuning for Knowledge-Intensive Domains

b6342a36fc09b0c80bda1cc0192a9028008838b4.summary: OrchStep: Vendor-neutral pipelines turning AI session into replayable workflow
b6342a36fc09b0c80bda1cc0192a9028008838b4.title: OrchStep: Vendor-neutral pipelines turning AI session into replayable workflow

b6566f69339fa8a24be6f3b01e4b0e95eb75e8bd.summary: arXiv:2611.29162v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many defects violate project rules that the code itself does not reveal, such as layering constraints or required tests. We study whether LLM coding agents repair such violations better when an external checker reports them, with their location and a repair goal. Three models, a small, medium and large model, driven by an AI agent, worked on 25 pull requests with 31 planted defects in ten open-source projects, plus 5 correct controls, five times alone and five times with findings from CodeAssure (CA), a commercial checker. We also compare with GitHub Copilot code review, and compare CodeAssure's detection with nine free static-analysis tools run out of the box, including Semgrep and SonarQube Community. Counting a run as repaired only when the repaired code also compiles and keeps its feature, CA findings raised the repair rate from 26% to 69% for the smallest model, from 46% to 90% for the medium model and from 45% to 93% for the largest model (pull-request-level p < 0.001), and from 39% to 84% over all runs. Every Java, TypeScript and Python repair compiled. We found that agents often cleared a defect by deleting a newly added file. Metrics based on whether the defect is gone count feature deletion as a success. The largest model alone did so in 44 of 125 runs. CA includes a check for deleted files that largely prevents this. In an ablation with the check turned off, removals rose from 9 to 65 out of 375 runs and the repair rate fell to 54% (small), 70% (medium) and 85% (large model). The CA workflow also outperformed Copilot code review (p < 0.001). Together, the free tools detected 8 of the 31 defects, and CA detected all 31. With CA, the medium model repaired 90% of runs, against 45% for the largest model alone, at about one fifth of the mean cost per run ($0.17 against $0.91).
b6566f69339fa8a24be6f3b01e4b0e95eb75e8bd.title: Fixed or Deleted? External Feedback Lets Cheaper AI Coding Agents Repair Rule Violations

b6570dfd40dc6b100b7bb2832493c95c456e133f.summary: arXiv:2611.30233v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures have emerged as a promising approach for scaling deep learning models while maintaining computational efficiency. However, existing MoE adaptations for Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models suffer from significant computational overhead during sequential training and degradation of zero-shot capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose CLIP-FMoE, a novel approach that integrates MoE architecture into CLIP fine-tuning. Our method uses Isolated Constrained Contrastive Learning, a pipeline that trains specialized experts on cluster-based data partitions to accelerate expert specialization. Additionally, we introduce a Fusion Gate mechanism to mitigate catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves consistent improvements on downstream tasks while preserving zero-shot capabilities. Furthermore, our method demonstrates robust performance across varying context lengths, making it particularly suitable for diverse real-world applications.
b6570dfd40dc6b100b7bb2832493c95c456e133f.title: CLIP-FMoE: Scalable CLIP via Fused Mixture-of-Experts with Enforced Specialization

b660306808c9bb3cb4f3740d3d8b415126adba04.summary: arXiv:2611.31228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prompting language models to verbalize stepwise numerical confidence during generation is an increasingly popular approach for triggering backtracking and error correction in agentic reasoning. This strategy presupposes two capabilities: (1) in-situ monitoring fidelity (does confidence drop when an error occurs?) and (2) downstream steering control (does an uncertainty token causally steer the model to repair its error?). We evaluated four open-weights models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4, 14.7B) across 15,200 math benchmark attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors within each model's capability frontier. Applying 27,568 counterfactual continuations across these failure points, we demonstrate a consistent decoupling between monitoring and control. On monitoring, all four models fail to detect their own errors. Verbalized confidence does not distinguish mistake steps from sound reasoning, yielding near-chance within-position AUROCs between 0.500 and 0.561. Even at a model's first reasoning error, trajectory confidence remains saturated at 95.1% to 99.9%, with noticeable drops ($\ge 10$ points) appearing on fewer than 9% of errors in Llama and under 1.6% in the other three models. In contrast, models respond readily to external uncertainty: injecting a low-confidence tag (10%) at the error step significantly increases downstream correction across all models (+3.7 to +22.5 points over format-matched 95% certainty; all $p \le 0.0022$), reaching up to 38.5% under active rethinking instructions. However, injecting doubt onto already-correct steps causes models to discard valid reasoning, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points. Inference-time self-correction is thus bottlenecked by in-situ error detection rather than downstream repair capacity: models readily steer toward recovery when prompted with doubt, yet fail to self-monitor during generation.
b660306808c9bb3cb4f3740d3d8b415126adba04.title: Language Models Steer on Injected Uncertainty Tokens, but Fail to Self-Monitor In Situ

b684b12cc6a85fe49dfb6e528d19feefb9931cb4.summary: arXiv:2611.28685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate forecasts of traffic flow, occupancy, and speed are essential for congestion management and travel planning. These variables exhibit distinct spatiotemporal patterns, and their coupled dynamics characterize the evolution of traffic conditions, such as the onset and dissipation of congestion. Existing methods often either neglect this coupling or struggle to capture the distinct dynamics of all three variables within a unified model. In this paper, we propose DeCo, a decoupled traffic state modeling framework with cross-variable coordination for forecasting flow, occupancy, and speed. Specifically, DeCo first trains a dedicated forecaster for each variable to specialize in its unique spatiotemporal dynamics. It then estimates a residual correction for each forecast by jointly leveraging the predicted trajectories and recent observations of all three variables, thereby exploiting cross-variable coupling and mitigating systematic prediction errors. We extend the flow-only PeMS03 and PeMS07 benchmarks to all three variables on their original sensors and release the aligned data. Experiments on PeMS03, PeMS04, PeMS07, and PeMS08 show that DeCo achieves the lowest mean absolute error for every variable on every dataset, up to 4.9% below RAGC, the strongest baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/lixus7/DeCo.
b684b12cc6a85fe49dfb6e528d19feefb9931cb4.title: DeCo: Decoupled Traffic State Modeling with Cross-Variable Coordination

b6acf5f1712e21558d1979a12cfae8df0b944080.summary: arXiv:2610.18141v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Omnimodal large language models (OLLMs) are susceptible to cross-modal hallucinations under audio-visual interference. We find that, for a substantial fraction of incorrect joint predictions, the question-relevant unimodal branch can still recover the correct answer, suggesting that task-relevant evidence can remain recoverable from the relevant modality even when it is not reflected in the joint prediction. We refer to this recoverable failure pattern as \emph{modality misrouting}. We propose CaRe (Conflict-aware Residual Intervention), a training-free inference-time method for identifying and correcting modality misrouting. CaRe uses a text-only modality probe to identify a candidate modality-specific counterfactual branch, and flags potential misrouting when its prediction conflicts with the original joint prediction. For such cases, CaRe computes a residual direction from the discrepancy between the counterfactual and fused representations and uses it to steer the original multimodal state toward the relevant modality evidence, while retaining both modalities in the original audio-visual inference path. The intervention strength is adapted based on the confidence of the counterfactual branch. Experiments on CMM and AVHBench across two OLLMs show that CaRe consistently outperforms the evaluated inference-time hallucination-mitigation baselines.
b6acf5f1712e21558d1979a12cfae8df0b944080.title: Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations by Correcting Modality Misrouting in Omnimodal LLMs

b715b2affb8796e9f221a7053aa79e8372ccfdd0.summary: arXiv:2611.17610v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-agent language model evaluations often compare a communicating system with a single greedy pass, which confounds coordination with extra samples and test-time compute. We introduce Parity-Aware Compute Evaluation (PACE): a six-dimensional resource vector, four baseline categories, and a directional rule that credits a gain only against a baseline using at least as much of the declared resources and rules a gain out against any baseline using no more. We audit 9 published studies. Across the 72 deduplicated baseline cells that report both a greedy and a sampled baseline, the sampling gap, by which the sampled baseline lowers the multi-agent difference, averages -0.036 with studies weighted equally (negative in 64 cells), and 53 of the 123 paired contrasts that beat a greedy pass become nonpositive against the sampled baseline. Against sampled or budget-matched baselines the mean difference is -0.042; all eight Category B/C study means are negative and the one Category D study is positive. In a controlled experiment with an open-weight model, debate and mixture-of-agents do not clear the equal-token self-consistency frontier on MMLU-Pro (debate -0.015); on Hidden Profile, split-view debate exceeds a lower-budget pool yet trails content-mismatched placebo and four-choice chance. We release a seven-item checklist, an evaluation card, and command-line utilities.
b715b2affb8796e9f221a7053aa79e8372ccfdd0.title: PACE: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs

b747adfb22b3ef8e8d9c3d96d4c4987a93419e42.summary: arXiv:2611.31160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Designing what an agent should optimize can be as difficult as optimizing the agent itself. Existing language-model-based reward-generation methods typically refine objectives for predefined tasks and couple the decision of what to explore with the synthesis of how to implement it, potentially narrowing the resulting behavioral repertoire. We introduce Habitats, a framework for open-ended evolution of executable agent objectives. Habitats maintains a population of reward-policy pairs and evaluates every policy under every population reward, producing a cross-fitness matrix that exposes self-mastery, transfer, and functional diversity. A population-level Planner uses this information to select parent rewards and issue targeted mutation directives, while a separate Mutator translates those directives into validated reward programs. We evaluate Habitats in a discrete Card Sandbox and three continuous-control environments (Cart-Pole, Hopper, and Cheetah) against Independent Generation and Direct Mutation baselines. Across four environments and three random seeds, Habitats achieves the highest macro-averaged final Specialist Quality and Behavioral Diversity, with final diversity reaching 1.8x that of Direct Mutation and 2.5x that of Independent Generation. Finally, across ten downstream objectives unseen during evolution, frozen Habitats policy libraries achieve higher paired win rates than size-matched Direct Mutation and Independent Generation libraries at 10,000 adaptation episodes, while also surpassing task-specific policies trained from scratch for 20,000 episodes. These results suggest that separating population-level planning from reward synthesis enables the discovery of diverse, learnable, and reusable behaviors.
b747adfb22b3ef8e8d9c3d96d4c4987a93419e42.title: Habitats: A Framework for Open-Ended Evolution of Agent Objectives

b762b224d684edc7536a9fdc12bd7ec65da83e3d.summary: arXiv:2611.28529v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Determining the function of genes across the tree of life is one of the major challenges in biology. Generative AI approaches to this problem generally fall into two categories: language models trained on biological sequences that are able to predict structure and function from signals in those sequences; and generalist language models trained on text, that are able to reason about biological function symbolically. A default operating assumption is that protein language models do not perform well on symbolic tasks, and that generalist language models do not perform well on sequence tasks. However, a recent report showed that frontier generalist models perform surprisingly well on next-residue prediction tasks. We set out to explore whether these capabilities extended to protein annotation. We assigned different frontier generalist models a variety of protein annotation tasks, including predicting the presence and coordinates of Pfam domains, loss of functional catalytic residues, and predicting structure and activity. On all annotation tasks, the frontier models performed well above chance; we did not benchmark them against specialised tools. The models also make characteristic hallucination errors, and they state them as confidently as their correct calls. Though untested against specialised methods, the nascent ability of frontier models to perform protein annotation from sequence alone is intriguing. The ability to reason over sequence, structure, and symbols in a single model allows for a neurosymbolic approach where a combination of sequence, experimental data and knowledge from the literature can be holistically combined to improve on de novo functional annotation of the protein universe. Prompts, test sets, model outputs and code: https://github.com/ai4curation/fable-sequence-to-function. Summary of results: https://ai4curation.io/fable-sequence-to-function/
b762b224d684edc7536a9fdc12bd7ec65da83e3d.title: General-purpose language models are neurosymbolic reasoners able to annotate proteins from sequence

b76b2493494fbb539255bf1367f8b0c21ac81d67.title: An on-device AI agent for Android

b77f0e482deef83ab40359a44422bb86dce4f5c1.summary: arXiv:2611.31475v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatial reasoning agents increasingly rely on external tools, such as 3D reconstruction, segmentation, and geometric computation, to answer questions that a multimodal large language model (MLLM) cannot resolve from pixels alone. Tool access, however, shifts the bottleneck to orchestration: the agent must decide which tools to call, in what order, and how to interpret their outputs, yet a stateless agent repeats the same mistakes across tasks. We ask whether a frozen tool-using agent can improve its orchestration from its own interaction history, without parameter updates. We present SpatialCraft, a self-evolving framework that maintains two forms of external knowledge: Experiences, condition-action tactics distilled by contrasting rollouts of the same task, and Skills, multi-step procedures with explicit activation and termination conditions. Three designs couple the two streams. Experiences can be anchored to a Skill, appearing only while it is active rather than once per task. A Contrastive Utility Score estimates each Experience's effect by randomly withholding it across rollouts of the same task, separating its contribution from task difficulty, and Experiences with consistently positive utility are consolidated into the Skills they support. Across five spatial benchmarks and four backbones, SpatialCraft achieves the best accuracy in all 20 settings, showing that a frozen agent can learn to orchestrate spatial tools from its own experience.
b77f0e482deef83ab40359a44422bb86dce4f5c1.title: SpatialCraft: Evolving Procedural Intelligence from Experience and Skills for Spatial Reasoning Agents

b7b878d9e7fbbcb9e0fec3907c8daf645ec5b8ec.summary: arXiv:2607.03836v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Despite remarkable progress in machine translation, Vision Language Models (VLMs) struggle on historical manuscripts, a domain that stresses core Natural Language Processing (NLP) capabilities: low-resource transliteration, archaic vocabulary, and noisy input signals. We present a systematic framework for evaluating the full image-to-translation pipeline on medieval Latin manuscripts, a setting in which scribal shorthand, ligatures, and parchment degradation expose failure modes that are invisible in clean-text benchmarks. Benchmarking on the CATMuS Latin dataset reveals a specialization gap: domain-specific Optical Character Recognition (OCR) models reduce character error rate by up to 4.3$\times$ compared to general-purpose VLMs, despite operating at orders of magnitude fewer parameters. We introduce the Interpres-Parallel-Corpus (IPC), a novel dataset comprising 1,383 aligned manuscript image lines, transcriptions, and expert translations, to our knowledge the first of its kind for medieval Latin. Our experiments uncover a complexity paradox: the simplest pipeline, a specialized OCR model feeding directly into a VLM, outperforms all multi-component variants. Adding retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or post-OCR correction introduces prompt saturation and error propagation that degrade aggregate translation quality. These findings offer both a new benchmark and practical guidance for deploying translation systems in low-resource historical settings.
b7b878d9e7fbbcb9e0fec3907c8daf645ec5b8ec.title: When Simpler Is Better: Evaluating Translation Pipelines for Medieval Latin Manuscripts

b7bfc5c1ec749b9dff743e14e0de15798c22f0bf.summary: arXiv:2611.28396v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) predict the label of a query row conditioned on a context of labelled rows, without training on them. Drawn from operational data, the context becomes an attack surface. We study targeted in-context poisoning in its simplest form: an attacker with write access to the context's source places exact copies of a target row there with the wrong label. On 30 OpenML datasets for binary classification, one such poison row flips on average 53% (TabICL) and 65% (TabPFN) of the predictions correct without attack, and three poison rows flip almost all. The same copy with the true label flips almost none, and performance on the remaining rows hardly changes. Predictions flip by two routes: in TabICL, the target row's embedding rotates towards the mean of the wrong class; in TabPFN, the poison row pulls genuine rows of the wrong class along. The TFMs thus infer soundly, but from forged evidence. Predictions of trained models flip as well: almost always for a random forest, for CatBoost as often as for the TFMs, hardly for a logistic regression. New with TFMs is not the kind of vulnerability but the timing: the data take effect at the moment of prediction, not through training, and a poison row in a live context can be deleted afterwards. Three established requirements must therefore cover the context: access control for its source, traceability per prediction, which can also deter, and validation at prediction time. A detection mechanism shows how such validation can work.
b7bfc5c1ec749b9dff743e14e0de15798c22f0bf.title: Targeted In-Context Poisoning of Tabular Foundation Models: An Empirical Study

b7fe5b006ced7c0cf00ce24edf55deea35bb94b5.summary: arXiv:2611.31076v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Slay the Spire 2 (STS2) is a single-player deck-building game that requires long-term planning under heavy randomness. We present AlphaDefect, an expert-level AI system for STS2: for each character, one network trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO) makes every decision of a run, in combat and outside it. At the highest difficulty, Ascension 10, on two versions of the game current in November 2026 and on test seeds not played in training, AlphaDefect wins 62-77% of runs across six characters with greedy play and 68-80% with test-time search, after 1.3 to 6.7 billion decisions of training per character; runs uploaded by human players of all levels are won 11-20% of the time at the same difficulty. The networks read the game as entity records that identify each card, relic and enemy through a learned embedding and attributes from the game data, together with consequences of public information computed by the engine. Ablations show how much the agent depends on this encoding: without these identities, the network did not win a single run, and without the computed consequences it won 8.3 points fewer. To our knowledge, AlphaDefect is the strongest publicly reported STS2 agent as of November 2026.
b7fe5b006ced7c0cf00ce24edf55deea35bb94b5.title: AlphaDefect: Expert-Level AI for Slay the Spire 2

b82694bc2191de9e361d6e38a7f80be06f00e5be.summary: arXiv:2611.31264v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often prompted with role- or persona-based instructions, yet persona conditioning has mainly been evaluated through character fidelity or aggregate benchmark accuracy. We study persona conditioning as a task-execution steering signal that changes how models interpret, structure, and sustain responses. Using paired instances derived from real user role-play logs and expanded into simulated multi-turn continuations, we compare with-persona and no-persona conditions while fixing task content, constraints, user simulation, and evaluation criteria. Across eight models, persona conditioning improves expert content depth and procedural fidelity, and these gains survive length control. At the same time, it lowers strict instruction-following accuracy by 17 to 30 points in every model evaluated, and increases unsupported real-world specificity through persona-induced elaboration. These results suggest that persona prompting is not a general-purpose performance improvement technique, but a selective task-execution policy shift with both behavioral gains and reliability risks.
b82694bc2191de9e361d6e38a7f80be06f00e5be.title: How Persona Conditioning Changes Open-Ended Task Execution: A Paired Evaluation of Behavioral Gains and Reliability Costs

b83591b78c97bdce223c35bef1bfb4cd4055b894.summary: arXiv:2609.00070v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) is a foundational technique for structural and phase characterization in materials science, yet automating its analysis and evaluating it end-to-end remains challenging. Doing so requires an agent to interpret diffraction patterns, run refinement software, manage strongly coupled parameters in a physically meaningful order, and assess both numerical fit quality and physical validity. We propose AutoXRD, an LLM agent framework that organizes powder XRD analysis into refinement stages, uses diffraction diagnostics to select actions, and checks the resulting fits against crystallographic and physical criteria. We further introduce XRDBench with two complementary tracks. XRDBench-QA contains 100 tasks assessing scientific reasoning and decision-making, whereas XRDBench-E2E contains 34 end-to-end workflows requiring data interpretation, crystallographic software execution, iterative refinement, evidence preservation, and reporting. Across 1,340 runs of ten recent LLMs, models average only 57.8 out of 100, falling from 61.9 on XRDBench-QA to 53.7 on XRDBench-E2E. At the task level, they perform best on refinement-history assessment and result acceptance, but remain substantially weaker on refinement-action selection, phase quantification, indexing, and Rietveld refinement. Among individual models, GPT-5.6 Sol achieves the highest overall score of 81.1, GPT-5.6 Terra scores highest on XRDBench-E2E (81.0), and GPT-5.6 Luna provides the best score-cost trade-off. Moreover, ablations confirm that all six AutoXRD components consistently improve performance. Finally, execution-trace analysis reveals recurring failures in coupled-parameter control, quantitative reasoning, evidence preservation, and workflow termination, motivating stronger scientific constraints, uncertainty quantification, and more efficient planning.
b83591b78c97bdce223c35bef1bfb4cd4055b894.title: AutoXRD: Autonomous Large Language Model Agents and Comprehensive Evaluation for Powder X-Ray Diffraction Analysis

b839d903db8e86a146c43b2dd5eb882997fff0e4.summary: arXiv:2610.32216v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Effective multimodal reasoning requires a model to reliably utilize visual information while sufficiently exploring diverse reasoning paths. To achieve this goal, prior work combines visual dependency and token entropy to reshape sequence-level advantages, but scaling the contribution of token entropy by visual dependency can leave high-entropy tokens with low visual dependency underweighted, despite their important role in reasoning exploration. To address this limitation, we propose PEAR, an adaptive advantage reshaping method for improving perception and exploration in multimodal reasoning. PEAR retains visual dependency as the base signal and adds an entropy-based exploration gain only at high-entropy positions, with lower visual dependency leading to a larger additional gain. The fused signal is then mapped to positive token-level weights that reshape the sequence-level advantage. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B show that PEAR achieves the highest average performance among evaluated baselines across multimodal reasoning benchmarks, alongside leading results on textual reasoning and general multimodal benchmarks.
b839d903db8e86a146c43b2dd5eb882997fff0e4.title: PEAR: Adaptive Advantage Reshaping for Perception and Exploration in Large Vision-Language Models

b84573f658fe2b7e922b95bb20f27b9e9e597c9c.summary: arXiv:2611.32508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents are advancing the automation of data-driven scientific research. Recent advances in recursive self-improvement (RSI) offer the potential for these agents to continuously improve through experience, but evaluating transfer across scientific tasks requires executable, scientifically verifiable tasks and independent assessment of self-improvement gains. We introduce RecurSciBench, a scalable benchmark for evaluating RSI in data-driven scientific research. Its RecurSciPipe framework automatically constructs scientific modeling and data analysis tasks from raw datasets, with execution-based verification and scientific validity checks. RecurSciBench spans four scientific domains, multiple data modalities, and varied scientific objectives. We evaluate four RSI systems by comparing their initial and evolved states on independent tasks after evolution on source tasks, covering within-type, cross-type, and cross-domain transfer. Experiments show that the benefits of self-improvement vary across agent systems and scientific domains. Positive overall gains can coexist with regressions on individual tasks. Experience can transfer across task types and benefit other domains even without measurable gains in the source domain.
b84573f658fe2b7e922b95bb20f27b9e9e597c9c.title: RecurSciBench: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement in Data-Driven Scientific Research

b85928fb49297ae02c7cd8c33ef9e690eb76e411.summary: Babylon.js is a powerful, beautiful, simple, and open game and rendering engine packed into a friendly JavaScript framework. License: Apache-2.0.
b85928fb49297ae02c7cd8c33ef9e690eb76e411.title: BabylonJS/Babylon.js

b85c9d5d35c5c0485c8bd78c5e79c5370e4184ed.summary: arXiv:2611.25360v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. While many benchmarks assess the quality of LLM- powered agents, few ascertain how good LLMs are at building them. To this end, we introduce AppSci-Bench, where we construct a setting akin to how human Applied Scientists build agents for businesses - through eliciting task requirements from stakeholders, exploring the business's infrastructure, and scientifically improve the target agent by designing experiments and internal benchmarks. AppSci-Bench features seven realistic domains - five new ones (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two domains recast from tau3-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026b)(Airline and Banking) - each with a held-out evaluation suite customized for that task. We evaluate seven frontier models and find AppSci-Bench challenging: the best model, Claude Opus 5.0, only reaches a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across 3 build attempts; other models do significantly worse. Models struggle with eliciting task requirements (only 65% for Opus 5.0), build representative internal evaluations (models saturate their own evaluation 65% of the time but fail to solve the held-out task), presenting challenges for future research. The benchmark code is available here: https://github.com/sanjari-orb/appsci-bench.
b85c9d5d35c5c0485c8bd78c5e79c5370e4184ed.title: AppSci-Bench: Can LLMs Build AI Agents and Make Them Better?

b8635fcc1aa399d3f85700c070b139a4b9c0b903.summary: arXiv:2611.28618v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much interaction experience is needed to distill a capable visual agent? We study learning from few tasks and recorded interaction histories. Our framework selects representative trajectories using skill-context coverage and ordered visual-decision similarity. On-policy distillation (OPD) learns through fresh interaction on selected tasks or fresh student responses at fixed histories. Across Navigation, Sokoban, and spatial mapping, even one online training task supports transfer to other tasks. Four fixed trajectories raise a 4B student's success from 49.17% to 82.08% on standard Navigation and from 60.16% to 85.55% on Sokoban, recovering over 90% of the measured gap to a 27B teacher on these panels. On an independent Navigation panel, replay improves success from 45.83% to 76.67%, retaining 91.36% of the same-task online gain without new interaction during optimization. Training repetitions, matched supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and a 9B extension further support the value of compact experience.
b8635fcc1aa399d3f85700c070b139a4b9c0b903.title: Distilling Visual Agents from Limited Interaction Experience

b881f41b6dfe27118b8abbe82c8c272fa6eea5ca.summary: arXiv:2611.31954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models must process continuous streams of visual observations, and the resulting computational cost limits real-time robotic control. Token pruning reduces this cost, but a fixed semantic scale of perceptual representation can overlook information needed at different stages of manipulation. We show that perceptual semantics can guide effective token selection without relying on internal attention when the selection scale adapts to the scene's evolving semantic structure. Based on this observation, we introduce TauPrune-VLA, a training-free method that controls the scale of the retained perceptual representation through a single perception temperature $\tau$. To adapt this scale as manipulation proceeds, TauPrune-VLA updates $\tau$ online using trends in perceptual semantics, with robot-state changes and action magnitude regulating the adjustment strength. While these semantics evolve over the course of manipulation, they remain relatively stable between consecutive frames. This continuity allows retention indices computed from the current observation to be applied at the next policy invocation, enabling token selection to run asynchronously with inference and reducing pruning overhead. Evaluated across diverse VLA models and simulation benchmarks, TauPrune-VLA achieves up to a $1.86\times$ inference speedup while maintaining near-baseline task success rates. We further validate its effectiveness on two real-world robotic platforms.
b881f41b6dfe27118b8abbe82c8c272fa6eea5ca.title: Perception Is Enough, at the Right Scale: Scale-Adaptive Token Pruning for Vision-Language-Action Models

b8ce2eca5751d54c2278f721837fe1512292e348.summary: arXiv:2605.27358v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) has become the de facto architecture for hundred-billion-parameter language models, yet its advantages at sub-billion scales for on-device deployment remain largely unexplored. To close this gap, we present MobileMoE, a family of on-device MoE language models with sub-billion active parameters (0.3-0.9B active and 1.3-5.3B total) that establish a new Pareto frontier for on-device LLMs. We first formulate an on-device MoE scaling law that jointly optimizes MoE architecture under mobile memory and compute constraints, identifying an on-device sweet spot - moderate sparsity with fine-grained and shared experts - that is simultaneously memory and compute-optimal. Building on the derived architectures, we train MobileMoE with a four-stage recipe covering pre-training, mid-training, instruction fine-tuning, and quantization-aware training, all on open-source datasets. Across 14 benchmarks, MobileMoE matches or exceeds leading on-device dense LLMs with 2-4$\times$ fewer inference FLOPs, and matches or surpasses the state-of-the-art MoE OLMoE-1B-7B with up to 60% fewer parameters. To bridge the last mile to mobile deployment, we provide the first efficient MoE inference on commodity smartphones with comprehensive on-device profiling. At comparable INT4 weight memory, MobileMoE-S delivers $1.8$-$3.8\times$ faster prefill and $2.2$-$3.4\times$ faster decode than the dense baseline MobileLLM-Pro.
b8ce2eca5751d54c2278f721837fe1512292e348.title: MobileMoE: Scaling On-Device Mixture of Experts

b8dfc084ade289aef4b1f224063541d7be71d0ef.summary: arXiv:2611.29274v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reusable skills provide specialized procedures, but large language model (LLM) agents must still determine how to organize and adapt their use. We introduce MetaSkill, a two-layer framework for reusing problem-solving methods across tasks and domains. The method layer selects from 26 curated methods and binds abstract roles to task objects. The execution layer uses the instantiated method to identify intermediate objectives, coordinate native skills, and guide repair or method reselection. On 89 SkillsBench tasks and 995 ToolHop examples, MetaSkill outperforms the evaluated baselines in all six configurations, with accuracy gains of 3.51-13.48% over the strongest baseline. Ablations support explicit method-guided orchestration beyond direct method injection and further gains from method reselection.
b8dfc084ade289aef4b1f224063541d7be71d0ef.title: MetaSkill: Reusable Problem-Solving Methods for Adaptive Skill Orchestration in LLM Agents

b8fa0ec16c152eb9a565a2f1976831981203a62c.summary: arXiv:2601.05465v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Constructing reliable evidence chains across massive corpora is a core challenge in open-domain multi-hop question answering. Single-pass retrieval struggles to locate the bridge passages required for chained reasoning. In multi-step pipelines, early retrieval errors can cascade across hops, and trajectory-level training makes it hard to attribute errors to specific stages. We propose PRISMA, a multi-agent framework with a Plan-Retrieve-Inspect-Solve-Memoize Architecture that reflects expert information seeking behavior. PRISMA uses structured generation as an inter-agent communication schema. Each agent's output constrains its reasoning and defines the input interface for downstream agents. An Inspector audits the evidence chain at each hop and triggers targeted recovery. We adopt a decoupled training strategy with agent-specific rewards. Stage I specializes the Planner and Solver as task experts. Stage II freezes the trained pipeline and trains the Inspector on trajectory-conditioned verification. A recovery-gain analysis quantifies the net contribution of verification. Across all ten benchmarks, PRISMA consistently outperforms all trained baselines and delivers overall performance competitive with larger closed-source API models, supporting efficient real-world deployment. The code is available at https://github.com/prisma-research/PRISMA.
b8fa0ec16c152eb9a565a2f1976831981203a62c.title: PRISMA: A Schema-Coordinated Multi-Agent Framework for Open-Domain Multi-Hop Question Answering

b93753bad1bf19d9262b54ccb9360b63bcaeabda.summary: arXiv:2611.28603v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers capabilities from large language models to smaller students, yet stronger teachers do not always yield better students. Recent studies report diminishing or even negative returns from teacher scaling. We hypothesize that these limitations arise in part from insufficient student capacity to absorb the teacher's knowledge. We therefore investigate loop and recurrent computation as a way to expand the student's effective capacity by modifying its computation graph while keeping the backbone parameter count fixed. Under teacher-forced KD during pretraining, weight-shared looping improves performance but retains teacher-size saturation, whereas cross-token recurrence avoids the observed reversal with larger teachers. In mathematical post-training under both teacher-forced KD and on-policy distillation (OPD), recurrent students scale better with increasing teacher size than looped and vanilla LLMs do. Crucially, we show that a pretrained LLM can be readily fine-tuned into a looped or recurrent architecture jointly with OPD, without repeating pretraining. Our recurrent Qwen model improves with larger teachers and consistently outperforms looped and vanilla LLMs. This suggests a new post-training paradigm that integrates architectural conversion into distillation, avoiding a separate conversion stage while substantially improving student performance and maintaining near-vanilla inference latency.
b93753bad1bf19d9262b54ccb9360b63bcaeabda.title: Bridging Teacher-Student Capability Gaps with Recurrent Computation

b987c549a5c26ef4c345a46556c6b39234960607.summary: arXiv:2611.30397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard neural network training typically applies optimizer-generated update signals to model parameters at every iteration. This work introduces a spatiotemporal view of parameter updating and proposes Event-Driven Parameter Dynamics (EPD), which separates candidate-update generation from their application through an intermediate state with accumulation, event-triggered release, and reset. In a canonical coordinate-wise instantiation, accumulation produces temporal integration, release imposes a spatial budget, and reset separates successive inter-release intervals, while conventional dense updating is recovered as a boundary case. Across four model--optimizer configurations on CIFAR-100, EPD maintains final performance close to conventional training even when only a small fraction of coordinates are released at each step, including the 1\% regime. Matched-control experiments further show that temporal accumulation, state-dependent selection, and post-release reset each contribute to the observed behavior. Together, these results identify parameter-update realization as a controllable dimension of optimization and provide a concrete basis for studying its temporal and spatial organization separately from candidate-update generation.
b987c549a5c26ef4c345a46556c6b39234960607.title: Event-Driven Parameter Dynamics for Spatiotemporal Parameter-Update Application in Deep Learning

b9a1a62df1a40fef5810bf6bc0fbd6e71fe35025.summary: arXiv:2611.32483v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Driving world models anticipate action consequences through representations of how the world evolves. For autonomous driving, these representations must capture both the surrounding scene and the ego vehicle's motion under a candidate plan. We propose CodeWAM, a driving world model that incorporates executable code as part of its world representation. Code represents ego dynamics by expressing how the vehicle state evolves under plan execution, while a learned visual model captures scene-dependent consequences. Executing the code produces a candidate-conditioned motion sequence, which is evaluated relative to the prior plan and recorded motion history. The resulting execution consequences and learned scene outcomes jointly represent the candidate's future, enabling the planner to assess both what a plan may lead to and how the vehicle transitions into that future. The selected plan becomes part of the next decision's execution context, linking successive choices within the model. CodeWAM achieves 93.6 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, 92.1 EPDMS on v2 navtest, and 50.6 EPDMS on NAVHARD. Further experiments demonstrate improved pairwise execution consistency and gains on Hydra-MDP and DrivoR without additional training, supporting executable code as a complementary representation for driving world models.
b9a1a62df1a40fef5810bf6bc0fbd6e71fe35025.title: CodeWAM: A Code World Action Model for End-to-End Autonomous Driving

b9c8ef732897ca34f0d6b11c001985e0682160cd.summary: arXiv:2611.28158v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language model agents are increasingly asked to run ongoing multi-day operations rather than finish isolated single-turn tasks. In daily operations, today's choices reshape later observations and cash constraints because empty shelves hide lost walk-in demand, short-shipped customers quietly shrink future orders weeks later, and emergency buying drains working capital. We introduce SMB Bench, a calibrated 90-day wholesale simulator with 18 causally paired tasks and an 859-run frontier trace dataset, to ask what experience and learning signal make an agent better at noticing, attributing, and acting on the delayed consequences of its own decisions in unseen businesses. Across 16 frontier models, only 3 outperform a fixed buying rule; models often record a relevant diagnosis in their notes without changing later purchases in time, showing that diagnosing a problem, changing behavior, and improving a business are separate achievements. To study how experience improves those failures in an open model (Qwen3.8-27B), we used training-business records to identify operational rules and archived frontier quarters as starting states to continue from rather than transcripts to copy. On an unseen test business under identical evaluation instructions, the trained policy followed customer-protection commitments more consistently and reduced severe-loss quarters, while the additional profit benefit remained uncertain. Carrying those commitments through the quarter exposed the cost of fulfilling them, as early-quarter stocking habits left the buyer relying on emergency supply and a deteriorating supplier. The results separate recognizing a delayed effect, acting on it consistently, and coordinating surrounding decisions so that the response improves profit. SMB Bench connects these observations to a learning method by turning archived decisions and their consequences into reusable training experience.
b9c8ef732897ca34f0d6b11c001985e0682160cd.title: Measuring and Teaching Language Model Agents to Act on Delayed Consequences

b9e66ce76570df77a64deec23d1dca4376aa4ca9.summary: arXiv:2611.31358v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Visual creation demands expressive imagery together with precise control over text, layout, and structure. We introduce Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation, an agentic framework that connects these capabilities through Pixel as Code. Raster images are represented by learned discrete visual tokens, while structured artifacts use explicit programs. A shared generation-and-rendering interface connects these representations to visual feedback across images, vector graphics, webpages, and documents. A Nemotron-native harness coordinates planning and raster candidate selection, with targeted repair for editable structured and hybrid artifacts. To support this interface, we develop Nemotron-Labs-Image-Tokenizer, the autoregressive raster generator Nemotron-Labs-Image-30B-A3B, and the structured-code model family Nemotron-Labs-VisionCode. On approximately 178K images spanning six visual domains, our tokenizer improves reconstruction PSNR from 26.08 to 29.57 dB over Emu3.5 IBQ. It also provides 7.13x faster encoding and 10.93x faster decoding at batch size one on A100. In standalone evaluation, one Nemotron-Labs-VisionCode variant surpasses Kimi K3.1 Pro on the aggregate across Chart2Code, MMSVG, Design2Code, and Image2Struct. At the system level, the Nemotron-native configuration raises GenEval2 Soft-TIFA GM from 31.71 to 52.56 using the same raster generator. With our best setting, Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation achieves performance competitive with GPT Image 2 and Nano Banana Pro across most benchmarks with available comparisons.
b9e66ce76570df77a64deec23d1dca4376aa4ca9.title: Nemotron-Labs-VisualCreation: Pixel as Code for Agentic Visual Creation

ba078383aae93e94e3bb88de52bed6f6f8b28e7b.summary: arXiv:2611.15108v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Proof-assistant kernels with strict propositions---Lean 4, Agda's Prop, and Coq/Rocq's SProp---build proof irrelevance into conversion ($p \equiv q$ for $p, q : P$), equating all derivations of a theorem. While natural for pure mathematics, judgmental proof irrelevance breaks provenance in verified scientific stores, where predicates, refinements, and institutional maps must distinguish independent derivations for consilience and counterfactual retraction; with subsingleton elimination, it also breaks normalization and algorithmic transitivity. We present the type-theoretic and institutional foundations of Eigenius, a kernel for provenance-preserving scientific stores. First, we formulate a dependent kernel with cumulative universes (Prop, Set, $\mathsf{Type}_k$ for $k \ge 1$), impredicative Prop, inductive families with index-forced subsingleton elimination, and intensional identity types: conversion $\equiv$ is untyped orthogonal-CRS joinability, while proof irrelevance is a witnessed axiom ($\mathsf{irrel} : \Pi P:\mathsf{Prop}.\,\Pi p,q:P.\,\mathsf{Id}\,P\,p\,q$). Second, coercion-free subsumption unifies cumulativity, $\Pi$-covariant subtyping, and ontology inclusions; its bidirectional fragments ($\mathcal{K}_0, \mathcal{K}_1$) satisfy subject reduction, match declarative typing, and compile to heuristic-free checkers ($\mathcal{A}_0, \mathcal{A}_1$) sound and complete relative to strong normalization. Third, we link external verifiers via constructive institutions (Adopt, Discharge, Relativize), internalize justification logic with Why-provenance $\mathsf{supp}(j,P)$, and type open-world knowledge graphs via TTR. Finally, we prove consistency in Grothendieck universes and mechanize the metatheory in Lean 4 with zero sorry.
ba078383aae93e94e3bb88de52bed6f6f8b28e7b.title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions: A Proof-Relevant Type Theory for Verified Science

ba706a0fac781c003ca2a537a6976b252be07d5e.summary: arXiv:2611.32639v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the $\pi_{0.5}$. Project page: https://refocus-robotics.github.io.
ba706a0fac781c003ca2a537a6976b252be07d5e.title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning

bab0f4dab0fb36ff76b7dc3a3bff68bf042c836f.summary: arXiv:2611.31251v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language model (LLM) chatbots are increasingly used by patients seeking cancer information, but their safety when users present evidence-misaligned beliefs about treatment remains uncharacterized. We hypothesized that LLMs exhibit validation bias, affirming rather than correcting such beliefs, and evaluated this with a 2x2x2 factorial design crossing conversation format (single-turn vs multi-turn), treatment type (evidence-based vs alternative), and query valence (positive vs negative). Framing was evidence-aligned (supporting evidence-based treatments or questioning alternative therapies) or evidence-misaligned (promoting alternative treatments or questioning evidence-based therapies). We analyzed 1,272 conversations (6,360 interactions) across 14 LLMs from 6 vendors, scored by an LLM judge (GPT-5-mini) validated against human annotation on a 6-dimension safety rubric. The primary outcome was the unsafe response rate, defined as a Weak classification or any critical failure. Evidence-misaligned framing increased unsafe response rates compared with evidence-aligned framing (14.4% vs 5.1%; OR 3.14, 95% CI 2.07-4.78; P < .001), and the association persisted after accounting for clustering by LLM. Among 429 conversations classified as Strong under evidence-aligned framing, 22.6% were downgraded in their paired evidence-misaligned counterpart. Multi-turn conversations had lower unsafe response rates than single-turn conversations (5.2% vs 14.7%; P < .001). Unsafe response rates varied by vendor from 1.8% to 36.8%. LLMs exhibited significant validation bias in oncology, with unsafe responses nearly tripling under evidence-misaligned framing. Evaluations limited to neutral, fact-seeking queries may overestimate real-world safety, and safety testing of medical AI systems should include evidence-misaligned user framing.
bab0f4dab0fb36ff76b7dc3a3bff68bf042c836f.title: Validation Bias in Large Language Model Responses to Cancer Treatment Queries: A Factorial Cross-Sectional Study

bace3098c5fe08b0935b7a58d664ae0b66cec668.summary: arXiv:2611.30766v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating register-transfer level (RTL) code from natural-language specifications, their reliability remains limited on designs with complex control logic and temporal behavior. This stems from a fundamental semantic gap: high-level natural language often leaves implementation-critical details underspecified, forcing LLMs to infer unstated assumptions. This paper presents Layered Formal Guidance, a novel framework that bridges this semantic gap by using formal properties as an intermediate semantic layer between natural-language specifications and RTL generation. Our framework applies formal guidance across three layers: property-driven specification augmentation before generation, property-consistency checking after generation, and counterexample-guided refinement after checking. Experiments on RTLLM benchmarks and various open-source IP designs demonstrate that our framework achieves higher functional correctness and lower sampled output-trace diversity. Furthermore, we show that Layered Formal Guidance can flexibly augment both general-purpose LLMs and domain-specific models to substantially improve their generation reliability.
bace3098c5fe08b0935b7a58d664ae0b66cec668.title: Bridging the Semantic Gap from Natural Language Specifications to RTL with Layered Formal Guidance

bb05917fe6db86ecf0fcf7276f2da4a4d7828e09.summary: arXiv:2611.32496v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As the use of reinforcement learning (RL) becomes more widespread in cyber-physical systems, it becomes increasingly important to design RL agents that are able to adapt to changes in their environments in order to maintain safety and reliability. This paper addresses the question of whether different classes of RL algorithm are more robust against forgetting previously learned behaviours, a critical issue in continual learning, in non-stationary environments. We evaluate the robustness of representative examples of three important classes of RL algorithm in a non-stationary autonomous parking environment. These are Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which is a model-free on-policy algorithm, Soft-Actor-Critic (SAC), which is a model-free off-policy algorithm, and Drama, which is a model-based algorithm. The agents must learn to successfully park in four different scenarios, which are presented successively, with parking spaces oriented at varying angles. We find off-policy algorithms appear to be more robust compared to on-policy algorithms due to their use of replay, while model-based algorithms do not appear to offer any direct advantage over model-free algorithms. These experiments also highlight the additional challenges of finding robust abstractions of the environment, and oversensitivity to hyperparameters.
bb05917fe6db86ecf0fcf7276f2da4a4d7828e09.title: Assessing Robustness to Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Deep Reinforcement Learning for Cyber-Physical Systems
