d70410584b905d172f229e2797f7427e4cbea017.summary: arXiv:2611.28680v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: High-stakes vertical medical tasks, such as postoperative pathological staging and long-term survival prediction, demand multi-step clinical reasoning over heterogeneous evidence under weak supervision and high outcome uncertainty. While we first orchestrate CliAgent, a domain-tailored clinical agent workflow that systematically grounds predictions in multi-modal patient evidence, manually designed medical agents remain constrained by static, brittle rules. Moreover, existing recursive self-improvement (RSI) methods suffer from feedback ambiguity and severe development-set overfitting when evolving agents in high-noise medical domains. Focusing on improving the improver, we propose Semantic PID-RSI, an evidence-guided control-theoretic framework for medical agent self-improvement. Inspired by PID control, our improver evaluates candidate modification batches via three diagnostic roles: P isolates current clinical failure modes, I synthesizes longitudinal evidence from past trials, and D estimates response dynamics and regression risks (D-pre/D-post). Selected plans are compiled into behavior contracts for staged probing and independent adoption judging. Instantiated and validated on challenging oncology tasks (pT/pN staging and survival prognosis), evolving CliAgent with Semantic PID-RSI on a 3B-activated open-weight model achieves substantial gains (up to +6.27 C-index points), outperforming overfitting-prone RSI baselines and approaching the performance of frontier proprietary models (e.g., GPT-6 series) equipped with CliAgent.
d70410584b905d172f229e2797f7427e4cbea017.title: Improving the Improver: Semantic PID Control for Medical Agent Self-Improvement

d70b3aae5bffdb0829087a67de2ef6854238cd74.summary: arXiv:2611.30583v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As the intelligence of an AI agent increases relative to a trusted monitor, so does the risk that the monitor will fail to understand the agent's actions or to evaluate them confidently. We introduce interrogation protocols to a high-stakes AI control setting, and allow the monitor to ask the untrusted agent questions about confusing actions. For interrogation to improve safety, a weaker model must be able to distinguish misleading explanations produced by an attack policy from genuine ones produced by an honest policy. We find that on a held-out subset of BashArena, an interrogation protocol improves safety at a 1% audit budget from 72.6% for an actions-only baseline, which does not use interrogations, to 79.5% (+7.0 pp [+0.9, +20.1], 95% paired bootstrap interval), but most of this uplift can be captured by having a trusted model state a specific concern. More broadly, our work suggests that interrogating agents can improve safety, allowing monitors to catch more attacks at a larger capability gap.
d70b3aae5bffdb0829087a67de2ef6854238cd74.title: Interrogation Protocols for AI Control

d73c205e30e75f334d449b80b72cb066d34c05be.summary: arXiv:2606.11576v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern Vision-Language Models (VLMs) benefit from chain-of-thought prompting and test-time scaling, but these gains often come with prohibitive inference cost due to large visual contexts and long decoding chains. We view this cost through two coupled axes: Visual Context Scaling (VCS), which controls how much visual evidence is passed to the language model, and Visual Reasoning Scaling (VRS), which controls how much inference-time reasoning search is performed. Existing methods typically optimize one axis at a time, leaving the joint allocation of compute across these axes underexplored. We introduce Adaptive Visual Inference Scaling (AVIS), a lightweight policy that adapts both VCS and VRS per query. AVIS realizes VCS through Key Diversity Visual (KDV) pruning, a training-free $O(N)$ key-based rule for removing redundant visual tokens before prefilling, and realizes VRS through adaptive self-consistency, using a learned difficulty predictor to select the number of reasoning rollouts. AVIS is deployment-friendly and compatible with shared-prefill inference, where all rollouts reuse a single prefilling pass and KV cache. Across diverse image and video reasoning benchmarks, AVIS improves the accuracy--compute trade-off relative to VCS-only and VRS-only baselines, and remains effective on top of RL post-trained VLMs while keeping compute and latency low.
d73c205e30e75f334d449b80b72cb066d34c05be.title: AVIS: Adaptive Test-Time Scaling for Vision-Language Models

d73cbc448deeea79aee9567a064c4bff373b1f74.summary: arXiv:2611.30168v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Developing reliable machine translation (MT) systems hinges on our ability to distinguish superior translations from inferior ones. However, existing evaluation paradigms, whether limited to coarse overall rankings or misaligned with human preferences, fail to deliver interpretable, fine-grained feedback in reference-free settings. We present a Fine-Grained Ranking Evaluation method (FiRE) that leverages off-the-shelf large language models to perform criterion-driven pairwise comparison across three complementary dimensions: faithfulness, fluency, and consistency of style, instead of producing a single holistic judgment. To enable rigorous meta-evaluation of evaluation paradigms in the absence of any suitable testbed, we construct the first human-annotated, reference-free benchmark for fine-grained ranking evaluation, achieving substantial inter-annotator agreement. Through meta-evaluation on this benchmark and existing MQM datasets, FiRE demonstrably outperforms regression-based and error-analysis metrics in aligning with human comparative judgments, while providing more informative insights into translation quality. Finally, our examination of LLM evaluator biases (position and self-enhancement) and their handling of tied cases offers guidance for more nuanced MT evaluation. Code and benchmark resources are available at https://github.com/wygao8/FiRE-MT.
d73cbc448deeea79aee9567a064c4bff373b1f74.title: FiRE: Fine-grained Ranking Evaluation for Machine Translation

d740404e27f79d3cdccc2fbfa0497e2b91a65512.summary: arXiv:2611.22033v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous shopping agents that process multimodal product listings (consisting of visual and text data) and recommend purchases on behalf of consumers. Naturally, one might assume that models with more thinking power would make higher-quality purchasing decisions. To test this belief, we ask two questions about such agents: does asking a model to think harder make it choose better products, and does the confidence it reports tell us the likelihood it may be wrong? We benchmark ten frontier models on three product-choice benchmarks built from WebShop, Amazon's SQID and Wayfair's WANDS platforms to see if LLMs with more thinking power actually make better-quality product purchase decisions. Across all three benchmarks, we found that increasing the thinking effort does not increase decision quality in a statistically meaningful way. The same change in thinking effort raises stated confidence at a statistically significant level, so extra thinking buys confidence rather than correctness. We also measure the calibration of these models (how well their reported confidence percentage matches their true correctness percentage) in these tasks and show that most models are not well-calibrated at every effort level. We also find that errors are strongly shared: when one model errs in a task, several others tend to err on that same task. Furthermore, on tasks where several models all err, a large number of them pick the same wrong product.
d740404e27f79d3cdccc2fbfa0497e2b91a65512.title: Thinking Harder Doesn't Lead to Better Choices: Reasoning Effort Increases the Confidence but Not the Correctness of LLM Shopping Agents

d75488516f28ba108442bb37fd98f73131e9052a.summary: arXiv:2611.30399v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Determining action reversibility requires checking whether the effects of an action can be undone. Recent work has extended reversibility to fully observable non-deterministic (FOND) planning. It distinguishes weak reversibility, where reversal may succeed, from strong-cyclic reversibility, where reversal is guaranteed under fairness. These notions are qualitative: they say whether reversal is possible, but not how costly it is. We introduce cost-sensitive reversibility for non-deterministic actions. Given positive action costs, we define weak and strong reversal budgets, $k$-bounded reversibility, and a distinction between finite strong reversal and strong-cyclic reversal with unbounded worst-case cost. We relate the resulting notions in a reversibility lattice, prove cost-aware policy-merging results, and show how to compute restricted weak and strong universal uniform reversal budgets using cost-optimal classical planning and worst-case-optimal FOND search, respectively. We also give an admissible lower-bound test for rejecting $k$-bounded reversibility. These notions support finer-grained safety decisions: a small finite strong budget bounds recovery cost, whereas a small weak budget certifies only a cheap possible recovery path. Actions without an acceptable strong bound may therefore warrant human approval, as in tool-using agent systems.
d75488516f28ba108442bb37fd98f73131e9052a.title: Cost-Sensitive Reversibility of Non-Deterministic Actions

d76f183a671bea4f6f55d02fc339df370125df84.summary: arXiv:2611.25214v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific discovery requires revisiting the hypotheses in light of new evidence and identifying promising directions beyond those already explored. However, research agents often make claims that are not supported by their observations, explore a narrow hypothesis space, and retain beliefs despite recognizing conflicting evidence. These failures motivate the search for an explicit epistemic state that captures both beliefs about existing hypotheses and directions for further exploration. To this end, we propose Epistemic Compass (EpiCompass), a plug-and-play scaffold that maintains this state through an epistemic tree linking hypotheses, evidence, beliefs, and revisions. As an investigation progresses, EpiCompass reassesses the hypotheses explored against accumulated evidence and uses unresolved conflicts and unexplored directions to guide hypothesis generation. It selects candidates by anticipated epistemic gain, accounting for both refinement of existing hypotheses and expansion of the hypothesis space, and verifies the final conclusion against the accumulated evidence. Experimental results across three scientific discovery benchmarks and three LLM backbones demonstrate that EpiCompass consistently outperforms baselines, with further analyses showing reductions in errors of unsupported claims and failures to revise beliefs. Our code is available at https://github.com/tianyi-lab/EpiCompass.
d76f183a671bea4f6f55d02fc339df370125df84.title: Steering Automated Scientific Discovery via Audited Epistemic Exploration

d785cab5c86fe8c23b2c80df1cd19705ee0c0292.summary: arXiv:2611.30588v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the manufacturing domain, equipment maintenance tasks depend on expert knowledge. Their documentation is often stored in heterogeneous formats and sources. The enhancement of LLMs with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is promising for bridging the scattered knowledge, but traditional vector-based RAG shows weaknesses with two characteristics which are common in real maintenance queries: complex causal chains and cross-domain synthesis. To address this, we propose SuSi-RAG, a hybrid Graph RAG solution, that matches a user query and each maintenance record using subgraph similarity. This work shows an in-use system: SuSi-RAG has run on an active Bosch production line for more than eight months, handling 10,664 question-answer interactions and demonstrates upper bound answer accuracy of 96.25% (confirmed error rate 3.75%). In a proof-of-concept, SuSi-RAG improves top-1 retrieval accuracy from 61.5% to 96.2% and expert-rated answer quality from 44.9% to 84.1% against a vector-based baseline. We present an integrated operational feedback loop to update SuSi-RAG.
d785cab5c86fe8c23b2c80df1cd19705ee0c0292.title: SuSi-RAG: A Hybrid Graph RAG for Equipment Maintenance

d7cf2a1bf180aed2e05e286303445085d875acf3.summary: arXiv:2609.34047v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal models increasingly interpret visual environments, but their ability to recognize the same building across photographs, floor plans, elevations, sections, and renderings remains poorly characterized. We introduce ARCH-B, a benchmark of 354 four-choice questions across 11 cross-representational archetypes, constructed from a building-linked corpus of 3.9 million architectural images using visually similar distractors, model-guided difficulty screening, and manual validation. We evaluate 25 multimodal models and collect 5,830 responses from non-expert human participants. Model accuracy ranges from 10.45% to 83.90%, compared with a human baseline of 35.35%. Models perform comparatively well on mixed-representation outlier detection and photograph matching, but remain weaker on floorplan-to-photograph correspondence. Human and model difficulty across archetypes is only weakly correlated (Spearman's (\rho=0.33)). Held-out evaluation confirms that the difficulty identified during screening generalizes beyond the curation models. ARCH-B provides a diagnostic evaluation of visual correspondence and representation transfer across architectural media.
d7cf2a1bf180aed2e05e286303445085d875acf3.title: ARCH-B: Architectural Representation, Comprehension and Hierarchy Benchmark

d7d9c686fcc5ca0020b535ba1a8a7a8731445624.summary: arXiv:2604.13991v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are prone to generating factually incorrect outputs. Recent work has applied conformal prediction to provide uncertainty estimates and statistical guarantees for the factuality of LLM generations. However, existing approaches are typically not prompt-adaptive, limiting their ability to capture input-dependent variability. As a result, they may filter out too few items (leading to over-coverage) or too many (under-coverage) for a given task or prompt. We propose an adaptive conformal prediction approach that extends conformal score transformation methods to LLMs, with applications to long-form generation and multiple-choice question answering. This enables prompt-dependent calibration, retaining marginal coverage guarantees while improving conditional coverage. In addition, the approach naturally supports selective prediction, allowing unreliable claims or answer choices to be filtered out in downstream applications. We evaluate our approach on multiple white-box models across diverse domains and show that it significantly outperforms existing baselines in terms of conditional coverage.
d7d9c686fcc5ca0020b535ba1a8a7a8731445624.title: Adaptive Conformal Prediction for Improving Factuality of Generations by Large Language Models

d824f13e247c85dc462e2ef5915a426dead921fe.summary: arXiv:2611.32032v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agreement among large language models is not physical evidence for mutating production infrastructure. Because generative models share pretraining priors and conform to peer rationales during deliberation, voting ensembles correlate errors instead of providing independent fault tolerance; yet attaching rigid deterministic checks to unconstrained agent outputs paralyzes incident remediation. We present Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums (PIEQ), an execution-bound certification layer that keeps every language model strictly outside the trusted computing base. PIEQ unifies assumption-based truth maintenance, physical provenance isolation, control-theoretic plausible-world safety shielding, and linearizable concurrency governance around three distinct obligations: certifying diagnostic preconditions from disjoint physical failure domains, gating candidate mutations across all unrefuted fault worlds while falling back to read-only diagnostic probes under ambiguity, and binding admission certificates to target execution through snapshot barriers, revision checks, authorization freshness, trusted temporal-precondition policies, and capability-tiered enforcement. Across formal guarantees, automated etcd fault suites, frozen software benchmarks, and live language-model runs, PIEQ achieves zero within-assumption unsafe admissions and zero false-precondition commits, converting occasional agent proof omissions into recoverable false blocks rather than unsafe actions. On a physical PostgreSQL/Patroni cluster, PIEQ gates supervised failovers alongside Patroni and etcd's native split-brain protection and enforces a full Tier E2 contract inside a single serializable PostgreSQL transaction for bounded capacity reservations. All benchmarks are author-labeled, live model snapshots are unpinned, and Tier E2 physical failover promotion as well as multi-host hardware fault isolation remain open work.
d824f13e247c85dc462e2ef5915a426dead921fe.title: Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums: Execution-Bound Evidence Certification and Plausible-World Safety Gating in Agentic Control Planes

d831938b547e28348ca6525fa2f020e38ec01712.summary: SGLang is a high-performance serving framework for large language models and multimodal models. License: Apache-2.0.
d831938b547e28348ca6525fa2f020e38ec01712.title: sgl-project/sglang

d8403f240703608897d280425c2ec2d07f040fb4.summary: I'm between jobs right now, and I'm bad at sitting idle. I could have built yet another portfolio site with a chatbot and a smiling robot avatar, but I wanted to spend the time on something people might actually use. There was a second reason. My feed is full of stories about LLM agents that burn thousands of dollars in tokens overnight. I suspected that most of them say more about the process than about the tools, and I wanted to check that on real work. So over about three weeks, with Claude Code on a $20/month Pro plan as the main tool (plus $100 of promotional credits that were expiring anyway, and some free-tier model sessions for the routine parts), I ported four native libraries to fully managed C#, with no P/Invoke and no native binaries: - Leptonica.Managed - Leptonica 1.87.0, image processing and the base of Tesseract OCR; about 2,700 functions. https://github.com/sensboston/Leptonica.Managed - Stb.Managed - seven of Sean Barrett's stb libraries (image load/save, resize, TrueType, rect_pack, DXT, Perlin). https://github.com/sensboston/Stb.Managed - MetadataSharp - EXIF/MakerNotes, IPTC, XMP and ICC read/write. Not a port: written from the specs, with Exiv2 as the reference. https://github.com/sensboston/MetadataSharp - MdfLibrary.Managed - mdflib, the ASAM MDF format of automotive data loggers, with the same API as its Windows-only C++/CLI wrapper, plus a cross-platform viewer with live CAN capture. https://github.com/sensboston/mdflib.net All four are on NuGet under MIT. I wouldn't call this vibe coding. The model wrote most of the code, but the work went the way any port of this size should go, with or without an LLM. First we discussed the architecture: what maps to what in C#, what stays bit-exact and what may be optimized, what is ported and what is left out. Then came a written plan in stages, each with a measurable exit condition. Before the first line of the port, the native library was built and became the oracle; the tests compare against it, not against the model's opinion of what the output should be. Then the work went in small batches, each merged only when CI was green. The checks are boring on purpose: pixel by pixel against Leptonica's golden files, byte by byte against stb, tag by tag against exiv2 on its own test corpus, file by file against the native MdfLibrary. Parsers are fuzzed. It still isn't bulletproof: the GPU path of Stb.Managed passed every test on ILGPU's CPU accelerator and did not work at all on a real CUDA card. Tests are only as honest as the hardware they run on. One result surprised me: the managed code is faster than C on most operations - about 1.3-2.0x single-threaded for Leptonica (regular Release build of the C library) and 1.5-1.8x for stb (-O3 -march=native). The JIT emits Vector128/256/512 code for the actual CPU, and Leptonica's C code has almost no SIMD. It is not faster everywhere: stb's hand-written SIMD resize still wins on one core, and JPEG on ARM64 is slower. The slow cases are listed in each repo. Total extra cost beyond the subscription: $0. The expensive part was waiting for usage limits to reset; my patience turned out to be the scarcest resource in the project. Happy to answe
d8403f240703608897d280425c2ec2d07f040fb4.title: Four C/C++ libraries ported to pure managed .NET on a $20 plan

d840ae6c58f296efc035b3af04c573b8ac2bcf88.summary: arXiv:2611.31582v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Latent interfaces let agents in a multi-agent system communicate through continuous representations rather than decoded text. Prior work reports performance and efficiency gains, but neither separates latent communication from the agent harness nor examines its internal components, leaving its actual contribution unclear. We propose LatentLens, a framework that decouples the latent interface at two levels: externally from the agent harness, to measure its contribution to overall performance (RQ1), and internally into realignment compatibility, information accessibility, and propagation dynamics, to identify the benefits and limitations of each (RQ2). Across seven benchmarks with Qwen3 models, adding the latent interface to the same harness does not improve and can even substantially degrade accuracy. Internally, latent representations retain some domain information, but incompatible realignment can substantially degrade performance, and repeated latent steps can amplify representation-level failures. Thus, while latent representations may preserve information, they do not necessarily ensure effective communication, which also requires compatible realignment, information accessibility, and stable propagation.
d840ae6c58f296efc035b3af04c573b8ac2bcf88.title: LatentLens: Rethinking Latent Interface in Multi-Agent Systems

d865f15886c97b379f8dd313b5272eacaa810fd1.summary: Your wellbeing buddy in Mac's notch Discussion | Link
d865f15886c97b379f8dd313b5272eacaa810fd1.title: Wellbreak

d88d19b23e89dbcaa33683c30c64d54b7c2c23cc.summary: arXiv:2611.30990v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As incentives to digitize more and more aspects of medical healthcare are gaining traction, additional medical data is becoming available. A major goal is to use this data to gain further insights, support medical staff, and ultimately improve patient care. This demands sophisticated solutions that can handle current and future vast amounts of data, all without disrupting well-established workflows of care takers. Additionally, the solution must fulfill the documentation and risk-management obligations of the Medical Device Regulation (MDR), which governs whether a device may be used in patient care in Europe. In this context, we introduce the AMPEL platform, an open-source solution for creating clinical decision support systems (CDSS) that fulfil the requirements of the MDR. Centered around a message broker (Kafka), it adopts an event-driven, distributed architecture, allowing for scaling and efficient processing of medical data as it gets generated. Relying on platform-specific events to implicitly describe the platform's interfaces makes it both extensible and agnostic to the hospital information system in use. With these events being defined in the Protocol Buffers format, medically evaluated algorithms can be independently implemented in a variety of programming languages and easily linked to the platform, extending its analytic capabilities as desired. The platform features a basic UI and alert functionality that can be used to gain medical staff's attention and present analysis results in a traceable and explainable fashion. We further show in a use case how the platform was used to build LAMPE, a CDSS developed and operated at University of Leipzig Medical Center. It demonstrates how the platform solution can be used in a complex and already established environment, while acknowledging current limitations and outlining planned developments to overcome these.
d88d19b23e89dbcaa33683c30c64d54b7c2c23cc.title: The AMPEL Platform: An Open-Source Project for Developing Hospital-Wide Clinical Decision Support Systems under EU-Regulation

d8c10ac3848a847742125f61a7f341dbdecdb3c2.summary: arXiv:2509.23103v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multiplication-avoiding neural operators are attractive for compute-in-memory (CIM) architectures, but directly replacing conventional convolutions often causes accuracy degradation. We investigate whether this limitation arises from multiplication avoidance itself or from the representation on which the operator acts. In this work, we introduce Hadamard Transform-assisted multiplication-avoiding (HMA) operators that combine Walsh--Hadamard transform features with multiplication-avoiding channel mixing. To identify where conventional multiplication remains necessary, we employ a gated formulation in which conventional and HMA operators compete through learned layer-wise coefficients. ResNet-18 experiments show that intermediate convolutional layers assign greater weight to HMA, whereas the earliest layers and final classifier retain greater contribution from conventional computation. Guided by this observation, we construct a compact hybrid HMA network and train it using knowledge distillation from a conventional teacher. On CIFAR-10, the resulting ResNet-18 student achieves 91.2\% accuracy compared with 90.4\% for the corresponding conventional baseline while reducing parameters by 68.25\%, conventional MACs by 85.71\%, and general multiplications by 85.54\%. Across ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and MobileNetV2 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet, HMA with knowledge distillation matches or improves the conventional models. These results show that Hadamard-domain feature restructuring can improve the accuracy--complexity tradeoff of multiplication-avoiding networks and provide a practical path toward efficient CIM inference.
d8c10ac3848a847742125f61a7f341dbdecdb3c2.title: Rethinking Multiplication in Neural Networks with Hadamard Transform-Assisted Operators

d8c9f93ce7ad0500a8d3ebea771eabbd0a54230c.summary: arXiv:2609.37128v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Skill evolution improves the capabilities of large language models by analyzing trajectories generated under a given skill and modifying the skill accordingly. Existing approaches typically generate a single trajectory per question. However, this provides insufficient optimization signals since it requires inferring effective skill edits from a solitary path. It is difficult to pinpoint which actions caused the failure in a failed trajectory, or to determine which actions in a successful one should be incorporated into the skill. Furthermore, they rely on a local batch of trajectories for analysis, making the optimization direction susceptible to noisy evidence. To address these, we propose SkillCome, a Skill-evolution method based on group Contrast optimization with dual memory. For each question, SkillCome generates trajectories and performs group contrast analysis to precisely identify key behavioral divergences between successful and failed trajectories, offering reliable optimization signals. The dual memory system further accumulates evidence from historical steps to track patterns shared across different groups, leading to more generalized optimization directions. Together, SkillCome builds a systematic optimization process that transforms experience from observed successful trajectories into reusable skills. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks spanning question answering, reasoning, and agentic tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. SkillCome consistently outperforms baselines across five models of varying families and scales, with gains up to +5.69 points. Our code is available at https://github.com/tdlhl/SkillCome.
d8c9f93ce7ad0500a8d3ebea771eabbd0a54230c.title: SkillCome: Group Contrast Skill Optimization with Dual Memory

d9053bc7e92b76f7cbba3566f7bc92968a630328.summary: arXiv:2611.32958v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI agents are beginning to automate data analysis, orchestration, and simulation steering in HPC environments, but they introduce a security problem that existing cluster defenses do not address: the hijacked authorized agent. An adversary can subvert an agent through prompt injection, poisoned shared data, compromised tools, or multi-agent coordination, then exfiltrate sensitive data through legitimate encrypted LLM API traffic. We propose behavioral attestation as a runtime defense for this setting. Our system, AEGIS, compiles task-derived behavioral constraints, monitors agent actions with ebpf-based syscall interception, verifies evidence against constraint profiles, correlates behavior across agents, and triggers slurm-level containment. On the real attestation path, AEGIS detects all four implemented attack classes with sub-second median latency at a 1-second interval and low measured verifier overhead. Controlled experiments show full attack-suite coverage, stronger detection than representative baselines, and no observed false positives on the evaluated benign workflows.
d9053bc7e92b76f7cbba3566f7bc92968a630328.title: Attestation is All You Need: Toward a Zero-Trust Architecture for HPC AI Agents

d90c758e4fbfc07747a42eb493ef6988a9eb6acb.summary: arXiv:2509.20509v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Policy gradient methods usually rely on entropy regularization to prevent premature convergence. However, maximizing entropy indiscriminately pushes the policy towards a uniform distribution, often overriding the reward signal if not optimally tuned. We propose replacing the standard entropy term with a self-regulating complexity term, defined as the product of Shannon entropy and disequilibrium, which quantifies the distance from the uniform distribution. Unlike pure entropy, which favors maximal disorder, this complexity measure is zero for both fully deterministic and perfectly uniform distributions, i.e., it is strictly positive for systems that exhibit a meaningful interplay between order and randomness. These properties ensure the policy maintains beneficial stochasticity while reducing regularization pressure when the policy is highly uncertain, allowing learning to focus on reward optimization. We introduce Complexity-Regularized Proximal Policy Optimization (CR-PPO), a modification of PPO that leverages this dynamic. We empirically demonstrate that CR-PPO is significantly more robust to hyperparameter selection than entropy-regularized PPO, achieving consistent performance across orders of magnitude of regularization coefficients and remaining harmless when regularization is unnecessary, thereby reducing the need for expensive hyperparameter tuning.
d90c758e4fbfc07747a42eb493ef6988a9eb6acb.title: Complexity-Regularized Proximal Policy Optimization

d974fcea131d3abb3f7476f4b0476e28afd3dd9c.summary: Lastbook 1.1.17 packages a downloadable offline library, maps, video and optional local AI for desktops, with a deliberately narrow network design.
d974fcea131d3abb3f7476f4b0476e28afd3dd9c.title: Lastbook 1.1.17 Packages Offline Knowledge, Maps and AI

d9837e4d2e5c2c8fd701fb64fea62d313f5d7671.summary: arXiv:2611.25950v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate surface modeling of multi-transparent interfaces to achieve accurate light transmission. The interplay of errors in geometric structure, light paths, and observation results during the reconstruction of transparent media with a high number of layers makes this a challenging problem. Some existing techniques address the reconstruction of transparent scenes by reducing the number of layers or simplifying light paths; however, this limits their direct applicability to high-order transparent scenes. We propose GaussTrans, a compact framework for light transport in high-order transparent scenes, consisting of three components: Gaussian-Field Hybrid Surfaces, Transport-Coupled Refinement, and Primitive-Guided Implicit Intersection. Gaussian-Field Hybrid Surfaces use a hybrid approach combining Gauss surfaces and fields to reconstruct different interfaces. Transport-Coupled Refinement reduces coupling errors by evaluating the entire light path. Primitive-Guided Implicit Intersection combines primitive support regions to reduce errors in the intersection of interfaces and rays. In experiments on datasets such as RefRef, GaussTrans achieves significantly higher accuracy with relatively low spatial storage requirements.
d9837e4d2e5c2c8fd701fb64fea62d313f5d7671.title: GaussTrans: A Gaussian Interface Framework for Multi-Layer Refractive Transport

d98644b0835452721e49d6cd890985004ff5edce.summary: arXiv:2611.31089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM quantization reduces storage but often degrades predictive fidelity at low bit rates. We propose a training-free, CDF-free, Gaussian-CLT-motivated progressive residual-sign quantization framework that uses randomized orthogonal mixing to promote Gaussian-like residual distributions and improve sign based reconstruction of Transformer weights. Each stage independently normalizes residuals and analytically calibrates reconstruction, progressively recovering quantization errors. The framework enables flexible storage-fidelity trade-offs without learned codebooks, empirical CDFs, or trellis optimization. We evaluate GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B across attention and MLP projections. At five residual stages, joint quantization preserves near-baseline predictive fidelity, achieving perplexities of 32.16 and 12.73, compared with full-precision values of 29.89 and 11.07, respectively. Ablations further demonstrate that orthogonal mixing substantially improves reconstruction over identity-based sign coding, while activation-aware scaling improves output fidelity and reduced-precision statistics lower storage overhead with negligible perplexity degradation. Comparisons with conventional quantizers establish the method's progressive fidelity recovery and characterize its storage-quality and runtime trade-offs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of orthogonally mixed residual-sign coding for flexible, training-free Transformer weight compression.
d98644b0835452721e49d6cd890985004ff5edce.title: Orthogonally Mixed Sign Coding with Progressive Residual Refinement for Transformer Weight Compression

d98b10fe34a79cf811fed85a9469ab599171f87c.summary: ### Key Features and Enhancements - **Rubin Support (Preview)** - Added preview support for NVIDIA Rubin (SM107), validated on Vera Rubin. - Added DeepSeek-V4 and Kimi K3 support on Vera Rubin. - **Model Support** - Added DeepSeek-V4 support on Blackwell and Rubin (preview). - Added Kimi K3 support on Blackwell and Rubin (preview), including multimodal and multi-node serving. Attention data parallelism (DEP16) requires GB300-class GPU memory. - Added Qwen3.5 support on Hopper, Blackwell and Rubin (preview), including MTP and NVFP4 on Blackwell, and Qwen3.6 and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next support on Blackwell. - Added MiniMax-M3 support on Blackwell and Rubin (preview). - Added GLM-5, GLM-5.2, Kimi-K2.5 and Step-3.7-Flash support on Blackwell. - Added Nemotron Nano Omni support on Hopper and Blackwell. - Added Gemma 4 support on Blackwell, including multimodal. - Added Laguna support on Hopper and Blackwell. - Added prefix caching for Mamba hybrid models, such as Qwen3.5 and Nemotron Super V3. - **Features** - **Performance:** - Optimized DeepSeek-V4, DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3.5, Gemma 4, MiniMax-M3 and Kimi K3 with model-specific kernel fusions. - Added locality domain (uGPU) localization for NVFP4 MoE on Rubin, which keeps memory traffic local to each GPU die. d9f62c0c1e67d27dc814e8c6a53c9be36677f73b.summary: arXiv:2611.28548v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Action Quality Assessment (AQA) aims to evaluate the quality of human actions, yet existing methods are predominantly developed and evaluated on individual datasets with different task formulations and assessment criteria. We introduce X-AQA, the first unified training and evaluation framework for general-purpose AQA with multimodal large language models (MLLMs). We construct X-AQA-40K, a training corpus comprising 40,163 samples from 22 data sources across four domains: competitive sports, fitness exercises, rehabilitation, and general skills. We convert heterogeneous annotations into a unified question-answering format, incorporating dataset-specific annotation guidelines and official scoring rules when available. Using this corpus, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B to develop a single MLLM capable of handling diverse AQA tasks. We further establish X-AQA-Bench, which evaluates both in-distribution (ID) performance on datasets represented during training and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization on four held-out datasets. The resulting model outperforms all evaluated open-source MLLMs on X-AQA-Bench and achieves competitive performance relative to proprietary MLLMs. Ablation studies further demonstrate that multi-domain joint training and explicitly providing assessment criteria in prompts both improve OOD generalization. X-AQA establishes a unified foundation for advancing general-purpose AQA across diverse real-world domains. Data and models are released at \hyperlink{https://huggingface.co/collections/Kelly0510/x-aqa}{here}.
d9f62c0c1e67d27dc814e8c6a53c9be36677f73b.title: X-AQA: Unifying Action Quality Assessment with Multimodal Large Language Models and Multi-Domain Learning

da00803918c5dd70f5aba4fe092ddbc6047fe517.summary: arXiv:2611.28418v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Design search often uses cheap learned predictions to choose which candidates deserve expensive tests, but these tests can fail, especially on the unusual designs that optimization favors. We introduce WingBench, a multifidelity benchmark in which optimizers and AI agents design transonic wings with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) inside the search. They can query a learned aerodynamic surrogate and spend a fixed budget of sequential CFD evaluations, each returning a score or a failure type. WingBench grades the design each method recommends, reporting separately whether it receives a valid score and how good that score is. Using WingBench, we contribute a study of five baseline optimizers and a comparison of three AI agent methods, which produced 6,629 CFD evaluation records. Feedback helps baseline optimizers deliver valid designs when it changes their later proposals, but the differential-evolution variant does so with lower aerodynamic quality. An open-ended research agent finds designs of similar quality to the strongest baselines over 32 CFD queries, with different prior information and unmatched total computation. In early search, our reflection and planning implementations do not consistently improve on it. We release the data, code, agent prompts, and analysis scripts for reproducibility.
da00803918c5dd70f5aba4fe092ddbc6047fe517.title: WingBench: Benchmarking How AI Agents Search for Better Designs

da1b02b0911907c2996d370c662177923443e5f2.summary: arXiv:2611.33098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents built on frontier language models are expensive. At every step, the frontier model re-reads its entire context and executes every subtask regardless of its difficulty. This paper explores the simple thesis that much of this cost can be removed by delegating easy subtasks to a small language model, or SLM, that runs on hardware one already owns. To test it, we build Delegent, a simple and effective agent harness built on Claude Code, in which the frontier model stays in charge of every task but hands focused subtasks, such as investigating code, running tests, and searching a corpus, to SLM subagents. Existing approaches such as cascades and model routers usually choose which model executes the entire task, whereas in Delegent, the frontier model always leads the execution and delegates easy subtasks to the SLM. No router or model is trained, so either model can be swapped freely. With the help of a 27B FP8 SLM, Delegent reduces the frontier cost of long-horizon coding by 67% and of agentic search by 59%, with no loss in task performance, and even a 2B SLM that fits on a laptop reduces the coding cost by 66%. The savings grow with the legwork that the frontier model would otherwise do itself, and a short instruction, which leaves the main coding tasks to the frontier model, accounts for most of the saving and keeps the 2B SLM from losing tasks. Code: https://github.com/castorini/delegent
da1b02b0911907c2996d370c662177923443e5f2.title: Delegent: A Multi-Agent Harness That Reduces Cost without Sacrificing Performance

da5b69d14b71cc52a1c4aef4275102febae37085.summary: arXiv:2611.32940v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Metacognition includes knowing one's own strengths and weaknesses across kinds of tasks, not only judging whether a single answer is correct. We test whether vision-language models (VLMs) know in advance which kinds of visual tasks and image conditions are hard for them, across a wide range of open and proprietary models. Because some tasks are hard for every model, we separate what a model knows about this shared difficulty from what it knows about itself. We find that VLMs know little in advance about their visual weaknesses. They misjudge their overall accuracy and do not even know which kinds of tasks are hard for every model, and most misjudge how degraded images affect them. We further train VLMs to predict their own accuracy, which teaches them their own level of accuracy on kinds unseen in training but not which kinds are hard for them. However, information about these weaknesses appears once a model starts solving. On a few unlabeled questions of a kind, the probability a model assigns to its own answers follows weaknesses particular to the model, across kinds of tasks and image conditions. VLMs thus hold information about their own weaknesses that their stated predictions do not yet reflect. By separating what is particular to a model from what holds for every model, our evaluation offers a test for methods that aim to teach VLMs their own weaknesses, and the answer probability offers them a signal to start from.
da5b69d14b71cc52a1c4aef4275102febae37085.title: Do Vision-Language Models Know Their Own Visual Weaknesses? Probing Capability-Level Metacognition

daca13ec6c8e315c11361c729ed3dcbb3e533145.summary: arXiv:2611.31789v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coupled surge-pitch motions drive unsteady vortex interactions and dynamic wake meandering behind floating offshore wind turbines, complicating three-dimensional wake reconstruction from limited measurements and transfer across turbine scales. Large-eddy simulations coupled with an actuator line model generate fixed and surge-pitch wakes at motion-based Strouhal numbers $St=fD/U_\infty$ of 0.2-0.6 (where $f$, $D$, and $U_\infty$ are the motion frequency, rotor diameter, and inflow velocity) for the National Renewable Energy Laboratory 5 MW ($D=126$ m) and International Energy Agency 22 MW ($D=284$ m) turbines. A physics-informed Fourier neural operator framework combines four-dimensional spectral convolutions with incompressible continuity and rotor-forced momentum-residual regularization to reconstruct three-dimensional unsteady wakes from two observation planes. Trained on the 5 MW fixed and $St=0.2$-$0.5$ cases, the framework recovers near-wake double-peak deficits, motion-driven wake expansion, and coherent vortices through $St=0.6$ (mean wake-center and half-width errors within 1.3% and 1.0% of $D$), while 10% planar sampling preserves near-dense accuracy (relative $L_2$ error 0.0689 versus 0.0684). Applying transfer learning from the 5 MW to the 22 MW turbine lowers the three-dimensional streamwise-velocity error at $St=0.6$ by 36% relative to zero-shot inference (0.1066 to 0.0682), halves scratch-training error with one fixed case (0.0835 versus 0.1693), and restores wake-center tracking and motion-locked harmonics ($St$-$3St$). Large-scale motion-induced dynamics transfer cleanly across turbine scales, whereas fine-scale vortex breakdown remains damped. The framework shows potential for three-dimensional wake reconstruction and downstream-inflow assessment in floating wind farms.
daca13ec6c8e315c11361c729ed3dcbb3e533145.title: Three-Dimensional Wake Reconstruction and Cross-Scale Transfer for Floating Offshore Wind Turbines via Physics-Informed Fourier Neural Operators

db28ec8fb0b0c895e0bbc122e30411f66fda3c21.summary: arXiv:2611.31101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speaking early turns a prediction into an irreversible public commitment. We introduce SayWhen, a test-time controller that selects a task-directed act shared across typed continuation plans and controls its release as speech. A persistent veto blocks playback when intervening transcripts invalidate the candidate. We define regret-free early speech (RFES) to measure supported pre-endpoint releases without scored incompatibility. On a 72-prefix branching diagnostic, the generated-plan frontier attains 6.0% RFES with zero observed mean regret, versus 8.2% RFES and 0.068 regret for Matched Top-One. Measured planner latency constrains this path; a deterministic retail schema attains 31.7% RFES, compared with 32.0% for the complete policy. In a separate 30-task $\tau$-Voice simulation, schema-derived candidates with cached text-to-speech (TTS) audio attain 21/30 task-level RFES. Eligible audio begins 1.51 seconds before the user-audio endpoint among the 22 tasks with early speech, or 1.11 seconds over all 30 tasks with zero for tasks without eligible early speech. Semantic veto and endpoint waiting each pass 16/30 tasks. Together, the studies demonstrate a controlled coverage-compatibility trade-off and schema-based pre-endpoint operation, making the supported public commitment an explicit unit of voice-agent control.
db28ec8fb0b0c895e0bbc122e30411f66fda3c21.title: SayWhen: Set-Valued Semantic Commitment for Low-Regret Early Speech

db2ee3dc2fb5c2359882abbdd8dd3cbe8af2af03.summary: arXiv:2611.29592v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As medical VLMs are increasingly evaluated for clinical decision-support scenarios, knowing when to trust their predictions is critical. Closed-ended medical VQA has become a common benchmark format because it enables automated scoring. Yet, systematic investigation into whether this format changes the reliability problem remains scarce. We identify a failure mode that we call stable wrongness: models can produce incorrect yes/no answers that remain confident and repeatable even when patient-specific visual evidence is removed or mismatched. This failure violates the premise behind sampling-stability uncertainty methods, including recent hallucination-aware calibration (HAC) variants: disagreement is informative only when errors are unstable. When shortcut-driven errors are themselves stable, sampling agreement can remain deceptively high. Motivated by this limitation, we introduce Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity (CAS), which shifts reliability estimation from answer stability to evidence sensitivity. CAS uses cross-modal counterfactual interventions, such as text-only, black, and corrupted images, to audit whether a committed yes/no answer remains supported when visual evidence is invalidated. Across 7 VLMs and 3 benchmarks, CAS outperforms the best HAC-family scores across all evaluated settings, achieving a macro-averaged AUROC gain of +0.150 for error detection. Mechanistic analysis further shows that CAS recovers hidden errors in the HAC-confident region and that its strongest standalone signal is counterfactual decision-boundary shift rather than hard prediction stability. Our findings suggest that closed-ended evaluation should test visual dependence, not only answer stability, in safety-critical medical contexts.
db2ee3dc2fb5c2359882abbdd8dd3cbe8af2af03.title: Rethinking Closed-Ended Medical VLM Evaluation: From Stable Wrongness to Counterfactual Answer Sensitivity

db41eb363ead51de6112da62da10fe6d6e7069f1.summary: arXiv:2611.26557v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reliable multimodal decision models must preserve semantic decisions across presentation changes, ignore irrelevant additions, and distinguish supporting from conflicting text, yet existing studies examine decision-interface biases and multimodal behavior separately without matched backbone comparisons. We introduce \textbf{MM-SystemOneBias}, evaluating 8 decision models and 5 backbones on 5,323 original instances across 9 datasets, 11 task scenarios, and 6 interventions: option order, option label, external judgment, image--text description, irrelevant information, and rating scale. Decision models remain sensitive across interventions: incorrect external judgments introduce errors in 20.14\% of originally correct responses on average, conflicting descriptions redirect decisions even when rejected in isolation, and answer probabilities on unchanged decisions show mean absolute shifts of 2.92\% to 8.97\%. Relative to backbones, decision models improve presentation, rating-scale, and irrelevant-information stability, yet face a trade-off on added text: they lose less accuracy to misleading cues while gaining less from correct judgments and often losing accuracy under consistent descriptions. These findings highlight visual grounding and probability robustness as key priorities.The code and dataset is available at https://github.com/ALIENS32/MM-SystemOneBias
db41eb363ead51de6112da62da10fe6d6e7069f1.title: MM-SystemOneBias: Evaluating Bias in Multimodal Jev-Style System One Decision Models

db497e0065c9257cbf0df13012716a708680c1af.summary: arXiv:2611.29978v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Biomedical target-ranking platforms combine genetics, literature, experimental evidence, tractability, and clinical precedent because each is useful for target discovery. A single integrated score, however, can be awkward to reuse for a narrower question such as which genes have direct evidence for disease risk or etiology. We examine this issue in Open Targets associations for Alzheimer disease (AD) and Parkinson disease (PD). Genetics-linked evidence and protein-oriented evidence are scored in separate channels and combined only at the end. In AD, the Open Targets overall top 20 contains 7 curated genetics-supported genes and 10 symptomatic pharmacology controls; the default late fusion contains 15 curated genes and no symptomatic controls. In PD, late fusion retains 13 curated genes and removes the 5 symptomatic controls present in the platform top 20. A genetics-only ranking reaches similar curated recall (14 genes in AD, 13 in PD), so most of the gain over the platform score comes from emphasizing genetic evidence; the protein channel mainly raises the number of tractable targets in the shortlist (from 9 to 12 in AD and from 8 to 10 in PD) without readmitting symptomatic controls. These results are stable across fusion weights from 0.35 to 0.75, perturbed protein-channel weights, and rule thresholds. An optional post-ranking rule further lowers high-clinical/low-genetic targets such as ACHE and GRIN1 without changing top-20 curated recall. The procedure is deterministic and uses public Open Targets fields. Because the component scores remain available, individual rank changes can be inspected and the ranking can be reproduced from the same data snapshot.
db497e0065c9257cbf0df13012716a708680c1af.title: Separating Genetic and Protein Evidence in Open Targets: An Auditable Re-ranking Study

db7fc5f2ac6a56fe62289438e1ac9e5d5f44fca2.summary: arXiv:2608.07954v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models can answer knowledge-intensive questions more reliably when they are grounded with knowledge graphs, but systems such as Think-on-Graph and Reasoning-on-Graph repeatedly query the same graph neighborhoods across different questions. In this work, we study this repeated retrieval in Knowledge Graph Question Answering~(KGQA) workloads and propose KGCache, an in-memory cache for one-hop knowledge graph neighborhoods. KGCache is designed to be compatible with both iterative traversal (ToG) and one shot planning (RoG) KGQA paradigms. KGCache is placed between the KGQA engine and the backend serving the KG, so repeated entity requests can be served from cache instead of issuing new KG queries. We evaluate KGCache on WebQSP and CWQ using LRU, LFU, and a trace-aware Oracle policy. Our analysis shows that both datasets contain substantial entity reuse among starting entities and entities reached during traversal. We also explore semantic caching for similar queries, which shows additional hit-rate gains on WebQSP and needs further accuracy testing on CWQ. Entity caching accelerates KG retrieval by up to $1.91\times$, while semantic-context caching achieves up to $1.08\times$ full-system speedup in the evaluated configurations, with each hit being up to $17.98\times$ faster. End-to-end gains are bounded by the share of runtime spent on KG retrieval, so caching is most beneficial when KG access is slow, e.g., with remote or large-scale KG backends.
db7fc5f2ac6a56fe62289438e1ac9e5d5f44fca2.title: KGCache: Amortized Subgraph Retrieval for KG Reasoning with LLMs

db908200bbeb38c14e243221a084808950f2b30e.summary: arXiv:2611.29150v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold.
db908200bbeb38c14e243221a084808950f2b30e.title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images

dbfe077e3286b1e9bd8e35b98cc57d0694ce904b.summary: arXiv:2611.31800v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents commonly use the full interaction history as a proxy for state, retaining all past observations and actions regardless of whether they remain relevant. We instead ask what information an agent actually needs to carry forward. We define agent state as a compact abstraction of interaction history that preserves the competence of a fixed reference agent, with the minimal such abstraction as the ideal. Because matching the reference agent's behavior is unnecessarily restrictive and difficult for black-box policies, we define sufficiency through task performance rather than behavior matching. We represent state abstractions as deterministic recursive programs and search over them using an LLM-guided genetic algorithm. Across ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, the learned abstractions preserve near-reference task success while reducing mean policy input by up to 71% and 57%, respectively. The resulting programs are directly inspectable, providing an explicit account of what information is retained, updated, and discarded during interaction.
dbfe077e3286b1e9bd8e35b98cc57d0694ce904b.title: Learning Compact State Abstractions for LLM Agents

dc07177c96f503ee0f810f591d79c9ebd15b8b75.title: Show HN: Apfel – The free AI already on your Mac

dc4b3f786946cabc32261a55c2a7d0c1afaa5d07.summary: arXiv:2611.00807v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI data analysis today is three fragmented worlds: LLMs understand semantics but cannot compute; BI aggregates precisely but is stateless; ML processes large-scale data on a stateful kernel but lacks semantics. This paper proposes a combination mechanism, named Multi-engine Joint State Data Analysis, that fills a still-open gap - the multi-engine joint context: the data context is embedded into LLM conversational analysis, where the LLM serves only as the semantic, reasoning, and orchestration layer (not computation) and connects four engines through the 1M context window - Python and R ML kernels, SQL over relational databases, Cypher over graph databases - yielding two multiplications, "semantics and precise computation" and "relational and graph", under enterprise-grade governance. The novelty is a four-dimensional coordinate system: horizontal (engine kinds), vertical (state flow - the watershed), spatial (business generalization), temporal (iterative convergence); a deterministic grounding method (one-shot injection of schema.json + notes.md, M+S) carries the spatial and temporal dimensions. Empirically, all four dimensions are substantiated: horizontally, four engines are quantified - SQL, Cypher (96.5% on CypherBench movie), ML in Python and R (TabReD weather); vertically, state flows across engines and grounding is reused across kernels; spatially, SQL generalizes across three business databases - AdventureWorks 91.3%, financial 95.3%, formula_1 94.6% (average), about 20-23 points above single-shot SOTA 74.45%; temporally, accuracy converges monotonically as notes accumulate. The core invariant - the separation of semantics from computation plus a cross-data-domain persistent context - does not expire as LLMs and agents evolve or engine forms change.
dc4b3f786946cabc32261a55c2a7d0c1afaa5d07.title: AI Data Analysis: A New Approach - Multi-engine Joint State Data Analysis

dc94cbee6463b9767ec8692cd9cc578ffcc6dc19.summary: arXiv:2611.31559v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based user simulation can support interface design, accessibility research, and interactive-agent evaluation, but standard computer-use agents are optimized for task completion rather than reproducing how people perceive, reason, and act. We introduce COGENT (COGnitive agENT), a modular cognitive architecture for simulating user interaction with desktop interfaces. COGENT draws on established cognitive theories, such as Norman's action cycle and ACT-R, to enable explainable, intervenable, and modular user simulation by decomposing the simulation process into cognitive modules with explicit representations of perception, memory, user state, intentions, and action selection. We begin by presenting six intervenability demonstrations, each tracing how a single edit to memory, a user attribute, or a processing module propagates through the cognitive pipeline to produce a behavioral change. We evaluate COGENT's behavioral and attributional fidelity across three benchmarks -- AgentNetBench, A11y-CUA, and SENSE-42 -- finding that it achieves statistically significant fidelity gains over computer-use baselines in reproducing recorded human behavior and recovers the relational structure among human self-reported psychological states. Together, these demos and evaluations demonstrate COGENT's utility toward more faithful, explainable, intervenable, and modular LLM-based cognitive simulations.
dc94cbee6463b9767ec8692cd9cc578ffcc6dc19.title: COGENT: A Modular Cognitive Architecture for Agentic User Simulation

dcdcbc3e1921aa99a79930f64fc78d52a545f063.summary: arXiv:2604.28123v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The standard post-training recipe for large multimodal models (LMMs) applies supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on curated demonstrations followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). However, SFT introduces distributional drift that neither preserves the model's original capabilities nor faithfully matches the supervision distribution. This problem is further amplified in multimodal reasoning, where perception errors and reasoning failures follow distinct drift patterns that compound during subsequent RL. We introduce PRISM, a three-stage pipeline that mitigates this drift by inserting an explicit distribution-alignment stage between SFT and RLVR. Building on the principle of on-policy distillation (OPD), PRISM casts alignment as a black-box, response-level adversarial game between the policy and a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) discriminator with dedicated perception and reasoning experts, providing disentangled corrective signals that steer the policy toward the supervision distribution without requiring access to teacher logits. While 1.26M public demonstrations suffice for broad SFT initialization, distribution alignment demands higher-fidelity supervision; we therefore curate 113K additional demonstrations from Gemini 3 Flash, featuring dense visual grounding and step-by-step reasoning on the hardest unsolved problems. Experiments on Qwen3-VL show that PRISM consistently improves downstream RLVR performance across multiple RL algorithms (GRPO, DAPO, GSPO) and diverse multimodal benchmarks, improving average accuracy by +4.4 and +6.0 points over the SFT-to-RLVR baseline on 4B and 8B, respectively. Our code, data, and model checkpoints are publicly available at https://github.com/XIAO4579/PRISM.
dcdcbc3e1921aa99a79930f64fc78d52a545f063.title: Beyond SFT-to-RL: Pre-alignment via Black-Box On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal RL

dce80da00d64b5b23f0411d8173839ef7cfbcfd4.summary: arXiv:2611.31801v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Brainprint authentication enables continuous identity verification, but EEG data are privacy-sensitive. Existing feature-level encrypted authentication (FLEA) schemes protect extracted features under a trusted-client assumption. We show theoretically and empirically that a compromised client with access to plaintext query features and continuous authentication scores can exactly recover a registered template after finitely many interactions. To address this risk, we propose TopoCryptoEEG, a homomorphic-encryption-based framework that encrypts preprocessed EEG data at the client and performs feature extraction, template matching, score computation, and threshold centering on ciphertexts at the server. This extends protection from extracted features to preprocessed EEG data and removes the client-side plaintext-feature interface exploited by the attack. For efficient encrypted authentication, we develop Multi-Window Topology-Aware Encoding (MWTE) and a Topographic Branch Model with Linear Fusion (TopoFuse-MLP) to preserve EEG spatial information while limiting multiplicative depth. Query-Patch Coordinate Packing (QPCP) and Lane-Preserving BSGS Evaluation (LP-BSGS) further reduce ciphertext operations. Experiments on HGD and BCICIV-2a show high authentication accuracy, with homomorphic computation taking 1-2 s on CPUs and about 14 ms on GPUs. TopoCryptoEEG achieves over 18x average speedup over the EER (IMWUT 2025) baseline, supporting practical privacy-preserving brainprint authentication.
dce80da00d64b5b23f0411d8173839ef7cfbcfd4.title: TopoCryptoEEG: End-to-End Encrypted Framework for Brainprint Authentication

dcea5824ab9b5cf963b354d2f0c091e6ac07184a.summary: arXiv:2611.30685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-term time series forecasting supports decisions in energy, transportation, weather and finance, where forecasts are produced continuously and often on constrained hardware. Recent work has moved in two directions. One scales Transformers and pre-trained foundation models to millions or hundreds of millions of parameters. The other shows that models with only hundreds to tens of thousands of parameters remain competitive on the standard benchmarks. Existing surveys organize forecasting models by backbone and treat efficiency as a side topic, so the reasons these small models work, and the way their sizes are reported, remain unexamined. This survey focuses on lightweight long-term forecasting. It provides a taxonomy of about thirty-five models in six families, with a common notation and an architecture diagram for each core model. It offers a structured-linear view in which the smallest models are linear maps restricted by frequency truncation or period folding, and it tests each restriction in closed form on eight benchmarks. It complements the literature review with an audit of sixteen official code repositories, which reproduces published parameter counts and reveals reporting gaps of up to 289 times. Finally, it gives practical guidance on model selection and reporting, and summarizes open problems.
dcea5824ab9b5cf963b354d2f0c091e6ac07184a.title: How Many Parameters Does Forecasting Need? A Survey and Code-Level Audit of Lightweight Long-Term Time Series Forecasting

dd14642e69efc2ae32c87256d990bf725907b08b.summary: arXiv:2611.15246v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling Problem (FJSP) is a fundamental and challenging optimization problem in smart manufacturing. Although recent deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches can learn effective scheduling policies through interaction with the environment, their performance often degrades as problem scale and processing-time uncertainty increase. In this paper, we propose DredRL, a dual representation enhanced diffusion-policy reinforcement learning scheduler. DredRL first constructs enhanced dual representations of operations and machines through self- and cross-attention mechanisms to capture both intra-entity and inter-entity dependencies. A diffusion model is further employed as the policy network, generating scheduling decisions through iterative denoising conditioned on the encoded state to enhance policy expressiveness and robustness. Extensive experiments on synthetic, public, large-scale, and stochastic FJSP benchmarks demonstrate that DredRL outperforms state-of-the-art learning-based schedulers across most configurations. Compared with SOTA learning-based methods, DredRL reduces makespan by up to 5.44% on synthetic instances. It also achieves the best learning-based performance on three of four public benchmarks and outperforms the stochasticity-aware algorithms on stochastic benchmarks. These results demonstrate that combining enhanced dual representations with diffusion-based policies provides an effective and robust approach for large scale scalable FJSP scheduling in complicated environment.
dd14642e69efc2ae32c87256d990bf725907b08b.title: Dual Representation Enhanced Diffusion Policy for Flexible Job Shop Scheduling

ddafca5340bf384eeeeafb1b5745aee8fe2c4677.summary: arXiv:2611.29859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) has re-emerged as a One Health concern since 2024, and the public is increasingly consulting large-language-model (LLM) chatbots for health information during outbreaks. Before a chatbot's accuracy can be meaningfully assessed, its consistency must first be understood, so that any single response can be trusted as a fair representative of the model's behavior. We characterized the semantic repeatability and reproducibility of GPT-5 (OpenAI) and Gemini 3 Flash (Google) on 15 H5N1 One Health questions sourced from social media discourse by adopting and extending a centroid-based evaluation framework. Each question was submitted 30 times and reformulated using five Chain-of-Thought (CoT) variants with 30 runs each, yielding 5,400 responses. Pairwise cosine similarity was computed on MPNet embeddings, with sensitivity analyses across three additional transformers. Statistical inference combined standard nonparametric tests (paired Wilcoxon and Friedman with Holm--Bonferroni correction) with inter-embedding agreement statistics (ICC(2,k) and Cronbach's $\alpha$) introduced here as a methodological addition. Both models produced high mean consistency (0.93--0.97, rescaled to {[}0, 1{]}). GPT-5 showed reproducibility significantly higher than repeatability (W = 3.0, p = 0.0003), whereas for Gemini 3 Flash the two metrics were statistically indistinguishable (W = 42.0, p = 0.33). Differential Diagnosis ranked among the top two CoT framings for consistency in both models. The tested chatbots behave as semantically stable sources on H5N1 One Health questions, and the developed consistency evaluation framework is portable to other domains.
ddafca5340bf384eeeeafb1b5745aee8fe2c4677.title: Semantic repeatability and reproducibility of GPT-5 and Gemini 3 Flash on H5N1 One Health questions

dec57d02201bb22e542727ba473d5af57cd8a724.summary: arXiv:2604.16241v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models perform well on broad knowledge benchmarks, yet their animal-domain competence remains poorly characterized under a consistent protocol. We introduce BAGEL (\textbf{B}enchmarking \textbf{A}nimal knowled\textbf{G}e \textbf{E}xpertise in \textbf{L}anguage models), a 6,822-question multiple-choice benchmark drawn from Wikipedia, Global Biotic Interactions (GloBI), and bioRxiv. It spans encyclopedic species knowledge, ecological interaction inference, and interpretation of animal-focused preprints. Questions are generated automatically and screened by GPT-5.5 using a rubric calibrated on 150 expert-reviewed items; this process is not exhaustive human adjudication. We evaluate 14 models without external retrieval, using model parameters and question-local evidence. Accuracy varies sharply by source and question type: frontier models that excel on Wikipedia and bioRxiv remain comparatively weak on GloBI participant identification, where pooled errors reveal ecological role confusion. A 100-item post-release bioRxiv probe provides preliminary evidence that GPT-5.4's literature performance is not entirely due to verbatim recall, without ruling out broader training exposure. Proprietary checkpoints lead the best open-weight systems overall, but aggregate scores incompletely characterize animal-domain competence.
dec57d02201bb22e542727ba473d5af57cd8a724.title: BAGEL: Benchmarking Animal Knowledge Expertise in Language Models
