fcc875a984952c941a2ed5a0faa19341aaec3cdd.summary: arXiv:2609.32782v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Respiratory support can shape the short-term physiological trajectory of critically ill patients, but patients receiving the same intervention may follow different physiological trajectories. Clinical patient dynamics models typically predict future states from recent physiology and recorded interventions, while physiological change is mainly represented through the predicted future state. We propose a response-aware patient dynamics model that explicitly represents physiological change during autoregressive state updating. The model decomposes predicted physiological change into state-dependent baseline dynamics and respiratory-support-associated deviations, with room air providing a reference for the decomposition. We provide a formal analysis of this reference-anchored formulation. A response pathway encodes the predicted physiological change and uses it to update the latent patient state across the forecast horizon. Across ICU cohorts from two independent institutions, the proposed model achieves comparable overall trajectory prediction to patient dynamics baselines, with more consistent improvements when physiological states are changing.
fcc875a984952c941a2ed5a0faa19341aaec3cdd.title: Learning response-aware patient dynamics for respiratory support

fcd0cc82bcff7b79aecc53e3921179a3a5d7d94d.summary: arXiv:2611.29936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has demonstrated strong performance in improving large language model (LLM) reasoning, yet its credit-assignment signal remains coarse. Outcome verifiers provide scalable supervision by judging whether a completed response is correct, but they do not directly indicate which intermediate reasoning tokens contribute to success or failure. As a result, policy optimization can be inefficient, especially when training base models directly from sparse outcome feedback. In this paper, we introduce SAEPO, a Sparse AutoEncoder-guided token-level credit assignment method for outcome-supervised Policy Optimization. Rather than treating correctness only as a rollout-level (sequence-level) signal, SAEPO uses a pretrained sparse autoencoder (SAE) to build token-level semantic representations within reasoning trajectories; it scores each token based on the SAE concepts (e.g., penalizing wrong "final-answer" tokens but rewarding correct "reasoning-process" tokens), learned in an unsupervised manner, to achieve fine-grained credit assignment. SAEPO is a plug-in advantage-shaping module compatible with various policy optimization algorithms. We instantiate SAEPO with both GRPO and GSPO, covering token-ratio and sequence-ratio policy-gradient objectives, and evaluate SAEPO across three LLM backbones on six math and two code benchmarks. Empirical results show that SAEPO improves both the math and code benchmark averages over the matched baselines, with gains of up to 6.63% and 5.57%, respectively. On Qwen3-1.7B-Base, training curves also show faster early accuracy growth. Feature and token-level analyses suggest that the SAE-derived signal favors question-relevant concepts and reasoning tokens.
fcd0cc82bcff7b79aecc53e3921179a3a5d7d94d.title: SAEPO: Sparse-Autoencoder-Guided Credit Assignment for Policy Optimization

fcedeedb711f66c2f1b4e15089b524312a61c152.summary: arXiv:2611.29105v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ensemble Logic (EL) is a family of modal logics over metric monoids whose modal parameters are terms with quantified variables. We study its member over the Euclidian space, called Spatial Ensemble Logic (SEL), for biomedical images. Geometric element ensembles (GELs) represent atomic propositions by finite lists of effectively presented semi-algebraic sets, principally closed balls. Translation, dilation and erosion preserve individual balls up to emptiness in any dimension. Translation and dilation act element-wise, but element-wise erosion gives only an inner bound. For $k\geq 2$, finite unions of balls are closed under neither intersection nor erosion. We therefore separate record representation from the evaluation domain. Our main result is a satisfaction-preserving translation over GELs into the first-order theory of real closed fields. It yields computable semi-algebraic satisfaction sets, decidable model checking and finite real algebraic evidence. For a fixed formula and dimension, model checking has polynomial data complexity under stated rationality and bounded-degree assumptions. Combined complexity is PSPACE-hard and in EXPSPACE. On the line, rational interval data admit linear-arithmetic evaluation with rational evidence, under rationality assumptions on the norm, query and evaluation point. For $k\geq 2$, rational balls can force irrational witnesses. Lower and upper annotation bounds propagate through formulas. Synthesis of a ball ensemble is decidable within a prescribed budget of balls and undecidable without one. In a vascular use case, medial ball ensembles decide calibre and stenosis queries at stored centers by comparing stored numbers. We also examine how far evaluation can proceed element-wise when the union forming a support is deferred to the point of evaluation.
fcedeedb711f66c2f1b4e15089b524312a61c152.title: Spatial Ensemble Logic for Biomedical Imaging: Geometric Element Ensembles in Euclidean Space

fcf814c6ca45b55863e5c67ab4178ab7c237236f.summary: arXiv:2611.30042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interactive world models generate virtual environments autoregressively from player actions and visual history. However, visual history alone cannot reliably capture the evolving states of independently acting non-player characters (NPCs) in real games, particularly when they are outside the camera view. Recent multi-agent world models address this challenge through joint multi-view generation or persistent shared state, but often rely on external observations, like maps or scene geometry, or predefined state transitions. We present SWAM, a State-aware World Action Model that separates agent-state evolution from autoregressive visual generation in interactive 3D environments. A lightweight state model propagates character dynamics from actions without consuming generated frames, combining motion priors with learned scene-dependent corrections. The predicted states then guide an autoregressive diffusion transformer alongside visual history through a novel conditioning scheme. Rather than requiring an explicit scene geometry map or visibility tests, the conditioning indicates where characters may appear, allowing the diffusion model to learn their appearance and occlusion. This design enables NPCs to evolve independently of visual generation while maintaining consistent observations across visibility changes, interactions, and respawns. Evaluations in a custom Godot-based first-person shooter game demonstrate improvements in visual fidelity, NPC consistency, and long-horizon stability over existing approaches.
fcf814c6ca45b55863e5c67ab4178ab7c237236f.title: SWAM: State-aware World Action Model for Multi-Agent 3D Environments

fd03d4991635b72a1b136d95eb533617b4fa51e0.summary: arXiv:2610.36673v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: What is the intrinsic reason of emergence of macroscopic order parameter out of microscopic systems? In this article, we apply to physics the collective predictive coding (CPC), the theory of language/symbol emergence. As our language emerges out of our human communications, physical macroscopic order parameter emerges out of communications among atoms --- each atom is regarded as an agent who predicts each other's behavior through inference. We present three examples of classical spin systems: two-dimensional ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, a two-dimensional spin model with competing stripe orders, and the fully connected Sherrington--Kirkpatrick spin-glass model. In all of these examples, proper macroscopic order parameters including the replica overlap emerge automatically through communication informatics of CPC, only from observed spin configurations. We call the learned macroscopic coordinate the collective predictive order. Furthermore, for the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, the equilibrium distribution of the collective predictive order yields an emergent potential with the symmetry and thermal evolution characteristic of a Landau potential. Notably, the emergence of the collective predictive order does not refer to any structure of microscopic Hamiltonians/Lagrangians. Thus our ``Atom-as-an-Agent" (AaaA) principle offers a completely data-driven method for the emergence of macroscopic order, that is, machine learning physics.
fd03d4991635b72a1b136d95eb533617b4fa51e0.title: Atom as an Agent: Emergent Order by Collective Predictive Coding

fd0735c627b88d561cd76b39d163f4681f04d44f.summary: arXiv:2611.28173v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agents can agree because they relied on the same flawed evidence. We use an exact model of nine binary votes to examine when a verifier should intervene. In the main comparison, workers err 20 percent of the time under ordinary conditions, shared failures occur in 10 percent of cases, and the verifier errs 2 percent of the time in either state. When worker error during a shared failure is 80 percent, checking close votes yields 7.93 percent verdict error, compared with 9.06 percent for random checks at the same expected check rate. The ordering reverses at 90 percent worker error during failure. At the matched check rate for that regime, checking close votes yields 9.98 percent error, random checks yield 9.41 percent, and ranking checks by their expected error reduction yields 6.73 percent. The model also shows that passing branch vote counts preserves the flat majority and reduces the number of messages the root receives. A design guide and a documentation audit of four Python frameworks translate these findings into implementation choices.
fd0735c627b88d561cd76b39d163f4681f04d44f.title: Selective Verification in Multi-Agent Orchestration with Large Language Models

fd4934840eb90078ed5763614c0f95e14304434a.summary: arXiv:2611.28692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Should your AI twin go meet people on your behalf? We built LLM twins of 710 real people from their other conversations in the CANDOR corpus, sent them to meet each other in 5,680 simulated first conversations, and checked every rehearsal against what the real people said after meeting for real (355 held-out, participant-disjoint pairs, against baselines that include each person's rating history). The rehearsals work: a twin's conversation predicts real liking ($\rho$=0.277), carries information that questionnaires and rating history do not have (partial $\rho$=0.16 [0.05, 0.26]), and recovers most of what the same reader gets from the real conversation (0.321). Swap controls show that this signal travels through the conversation, not through the persona card. What, then, does a twin need to judge like you? Not your voice: making twins talk more like their owners, with person-specific activation steering and a LoRA trained on their own speech, did not help in a pre-specified test and lowered accuracy in an exploratory second round (-0.183 [-0.294, -0.066]). Nor simply your stated ratings: a persona-prompted twin that holds the conversation does not yet carry its owner's judgment, and when told its owner's past ratings it anchors on them instead of weighing them. Learning helps: a small appraisal head trained on other real conversations, which combines the twin's post-call answers with its owner's rating history, lifts rehearsal-based prediction above the history baseline out of fold (+0.059 [0.001, 0.115], against +0.022 without the twin's answers; pre-specified primary contrast +0.056 [-0.001, 0.111]). We propose an attribution protocol for twin-based social simulation and identify learned appraisal as the component twins need next.
fd4934840eb90078ed5763614c0f95e14304434a.title: Can Your AI Twin Meet People for You? It Can Hold a Conversation. But What Does It Need to Judge Like You?

fd56d4b2e51d0164708371c9e8e9d7ab7721f3bc.summary: arXiv:2611.23700v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Emergency care requires auditable decisions, but a language-model agent just outputs text. We introduce Decision2Care, a decision agent that generates a probability for every option at each step. It diagnosed 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases with 86.5% accuracy in a median of 2.2 s; language-model agents reached 86.1 to 91.7% but took more than 90 s. Its drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than documented first-day care and with about half as many records, it predicted death as well as three ICU clinicians. In the four cases where it was confident but wrong, we traced each decision to one imaging report. Our study suggests that an agent's work-up can be reviewed like a clinician's, motivating prospective trials.
fd56d4b2e51d0164708371c9e8e9d7ab7721f3bc.title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents

fd9f856d5ae1368e3fc277c15152ce3a232ef0f2.summary: arXiv:2611.28067v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the compression of the 48 feed-forward network (FFN) matrices of the Vision Transformer ViT-L/16 to 2--8 bits with four schemes: a per-token grid, a fixed Gaussian Lloyd--Max table, a table fitted to the matrix, and a random-sign Hadamard rotation followed by the fixed table. We evaluate on 50,000 images. At 4 bits the top-1 accuracy of the four schemes lies within 0.8 points of the float32 model, while the agreement with its predictions ranges from 98.4\% to 94.4\%. We use the angular error between the compressed and the float32 residual stream, followed through the blocks, as a portable measure that ranks the schemes as the final classification does and shows where the ranking is built: with rotation the angle grows close to the square root of the number of blocks, the signature of independently accumulating errors, while the other schemes are amplified in the later blocks. The same measure shows that a scheme that is better on one block in isolation can be worse in the whole network. To address this inconsistency we introduce an angular measure of the spectrum of the output of a block, which in isolation orders the schemes as the whole network does where they diverge most. We support these observations with real samples and with statistically generated ones. The scope is one model, the FFN weights only, and float evaluation of compressed weights; no speed-up is claimed. The error measures and the sample generation, however, can be applied to other models and precisions.
fd9f856d5ae1368e3fc277c15152ce3a232ef0f2.title: Following the Error Through a Compressed Network:An Angular Measure for FFN Weight Compression in ViT-L/16

fda8aa33d5a3b5d2a0e901ffc0b3e1f8399d588c.summary: arXiv:2605.07719v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Long-context LLM serving increasingly relies on CPU-resident context KV cache, driven by KV offloading and disaggregated prefill--decode execution. Although block-sparse attention reduces KV access, existing designs remain inefficient: GPU-centralized execution fetches selected KV blocks from CPU memory at each decoding step, making it PCIe-bound, while CPU--GPU partitioned execution places CPU-side sparse attention on the critical path, leaving substantial GPU time idle. This paper presents Mosaic, a CPU--GPU coordinated block-sparse attention system for efficient long-context decoding with CPU-resident context KV. Mosaic builds on three key insights: output-contribution-aware KV budgeting, head-specific and granularity-aware sparse configuration, and cross-device coordinated scheduling for sparse tasks over CPU-resident KV. Guided by these insights, Mosaic integrates a lightweight head-property predictor, a granularity--budget selector, and a priority-based scheduler to automatically configure and coordinate sparse attention, preserving output quality while improving efficiency on heterogeneous architectures. Across 2 models, 3 benchmarks, and 40 tasks, Mosaic preserves near-FULL quality while achieving a better overall quality--efficiency tradeoff than the evaluated baselines. Compared with the best-quality fixed Quest configuration, Mosaic improves TPOT by up to 3.7$\times$. We further validate Mosaic across four hardware configurations and in a large-model multi-GPU deployment.
fda8aa33d5a3b5d2a0e901ffc0b3e1f8399d588c.title: Mosaic: Efficient CPU--GPU Coordinated Block-Sparse Attention for Long-Context Decoding

fe09f9511c5abb25c97a030556bed6a35509d46c.summary: arXiv:2610.33667v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Resolving a repository-level issue typically requires a software-engineering (SWE) agent to localize the faulty code, reproduce the failure, and patch the code. Reinforcement learning trains such agents from a single test result on the final patch, while on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) adds token-level supervision from a teacher with privileged evidence, exposing the full reference patch at every step. Neither provides stage-specific guidance for localization or reproduction. We propose SWE-Ladder, which turns the verified repair of each training instance into stage-specific evidence: the changed files and lines for localization, the fail-to-pass tests for reproduction, and the diff for patching. A rule-based router assigns each step of an end-to-end rollout to a stage based on its tool call, a frozen teacher sees only the matching evidence, and the stages are distilled in repair order while GRPO optimizes the full trajectory. With Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on SWE-bench Verified under the R2E-Gym scaffold, SWE-Ladder improves pass@1 from 9.6% to 16.4%, compared with 10.4% for GRPO and 12.4% for OPSD with the full patch. Under the OpenHands scaffold, it improves pass@1 from 13.0% to 17.6%. Reversing the stage order under R2E-Gym reduces pass@1 to 11.4%.
fe09f9511c5abb25c97a030556bed6a35509d46c.title: SWE-Ladder: Learning to Localize, Reproduce, and Patch via Progressive Privileged Self-Distillation

fe3874ad5b779bb4e3bd1f65931afe9f5f77a190.summary: arXiv:2611.29440v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Designing simple inventory policies becomes increasingly difficult as operational features and system configurations expand. We develop an Agentic Inventory-Policy Discovery System based on explicitly defined simple operational formula (SOF) policy and template classes. Large language models (LLMs) revise symbolic structures, while a numerical engine fits parameters separately for each instance and evaluates the induced policies. Multicriteria parent selection, state-specific operational diagnostics, and reusable symbolic motifs guide structural evolution. A three-stage progression develops shared templates across instances and configurations with varying state dimensions. Experiments on 15,600 instances spanning 50 demand distributions cover lead times, perishability, their combination, and lead times with limited customer patience. The discovered templates improve aggregate empirical performance over evaluated SOF benchmarks and are competitive with policies requiring more elaborate online computations. For a lost-sales system with a three-period lead time, we develop an average-cost decomposition and prove that, under specified demand and cost conditions, a capped dual-shortfall specialization of a discovered policy strictly outperforms every policy in the considered capped base-stock benchmark class. This analysis links the performance advantage to the discovered replenishment mechanism. Together, these results highlight the potential of agentic discovery to generate simple inventory policies with strong empirical performance and identify operational mechanisms amenable to rigorous theoretical analysis.
fe3874ad5b779bb4e3bd1f65931afe9f5f77a190.title: Agentic Discovery of Simple Symbolic Inventory Policies

fe6727bf216bf151e819b376189d17d92cd91b18.summary: arXiv:2611.28745v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal large language models can state the rules of a video game, but do they apply them when they only see the game? We introduce RuleCraft, 1,240 image questions over 155 Minecraft rules with outcomes verified in the game engine, each asked in text, on the image with the game named, and on the bare image. Six widely used models know the rules and recognize the game, yet answer the bare image by real-world physics: naming the game raises their accuracy on rules where the game departs from reality by 8.2-19.8 points on a main set and by 33.8-52.7 on a hard stress-test set. Their errors pick the real-world outcome, the gap is largest where the game leaves a scene unchanged, and reasoning traces state the game's rule, then answer by reality. On the main set, naming the game mostly swaps the real-world default for the game's. The pattern holds with reasoning, recurs in two more games, and persists on questions the models themselves take to be about the game; one neutral sentence asking for the rules of the world shown recovers much of the gap. Evaluations that name the game measure knowledge of its rules, not world selection.
fe6727bf216bf151e819b376189d17d92cd91b18.title: Multimodal LLMs Know the Game but Assume the Real World

fe74e64c4724fb57177ea0252428fa9d44cf8078.summary: People often find me through my writing on AI and tech. This creates an interesting pattern. Nearly every week, vendors reach out asking me to write about their products. While I appreciate their interest and love learning about new tools, I reserve my writing for topics that I have personal experience with. One conversation last week really stuck with me. A founder confided, “We can write the best content in the world, but we don’t have any distribution.” This hit home because I used to think the same way. Let me share what works for reaching developers. Companies and individuals alike often skip the basics when trying to grow their audience. These are proven approaches I’ve seen succeed, both in my work and in others’ efforts to grow their audience in the AI space. 1. Build on Great Work Here’s something surprising: few people take the time to thoughtfully engage with others’ work in our field. But when you do, amazing things happen naturally. For example, here are some recent posts I’ve enjoyed that present opportunities to engage with others: Shreya Shankar’s DocETL Eugene Yan’s work on AlignEval Ben Claive’s work on rerankers Jeremy Howard’s work on llms.txt In the above examples, you could share how their ideas connect with what you’ve built. You could add additional case studies and real-world insights. If you deeply engage with someone’s work and add your insights, they often share your content with their audience. Not because you asked, but because you’ve added something meaningful to their work. Swyx has written a great post on how to do this effectively. The key is authenticity. Don’t do this just for marketing—do it because you’re genuinely interested in learning from others and building on their ideas. It’s not hard to find things to be excited about. I’m amazed by how few people take this approach. It’s both effective and fun. 2. Show Up Consistently I see too many folks blogging or posting once every few months and wondering why they’re not getting traction. Want to know what actually works? Look at Jason Liu . He grew his following from 500 to 30,000 followers by posting ~ 30 times every day for a year. You don’t have to post that often (I certainly don’t!), but consistency matters more than perfection. Finally, don’t just post into the void. Engage with others. When someone comments on your post, reply thoughtfully. When you see conversations where you can add value, provide helpful information. Finally, don’t be discouraged if you don’t see results immediately. Here’s some advice from my friend (and prolific writer), Eugene Yan : In the beginning, when most people start writing, the output’s gonna suck. Harsh, but true—my first 100 posts or so were crap. But with practice, people can get better. But they have to be deliberate in wanting to practice and get better with each piece, and not just write for the sake of publishing something and tweeting about it. The Sam Parr course (see below) is a great example of deliberate practice on copywriting. 3. Get Better at Copywriting This changed everything for me. I took Sam Parr’s copywriting course just 30 minutes a day for a week. Now I keep my favorite writing samples in a Claude
fe74e64c4724fb57177ea0252428fa9d44cf8078.title: Building an Audience Through Technical Writing: Strategies and Mistakes

ff39323c74c2dd8ae4425853675844b650417a53.summary: arXiv:2603.11045v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Inverse problems for stiff parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs), such as the inverse heat conduction problem (IHCP), are severely ill-posed: the forward map rapidly damps high-frequency interior structure before it reaches the boundary. Soft-constrained physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), which embed the PDE as a residual penalty, decouple the diffusivity from the surface data in their standard two-network inverse formulation, and the evaluated variants fit boundary measurements while leaving the interior field essentially untouched. We propose Neural Field Thermal Tomography (NeFTY), a hard-constrained neural field framework for label-free three-dimensional inverse heat conduction. NeFTY represents the unknown diffusivity as a continuous coordinate-based neural network, and at every optimization step passes the candidate field through a differentiable implicit-Euler heat solver with harmonic-mean interface flux, so that the simulated temperature satisfies the discretized heat equation up to the solver tolerance. Adjoint gradients propagate the surface reconstruction error back to the network weights at solver-level memory cost, making test-time inversion tractable on a single GPU. Across synthetic 3D benchmarks, NeFTY outperforms soft-constrained PINN variants, a voxel-grid baseline, and classical L-BFGS voxel inversion through the same solver on label-free volumetric recovery, and it transfers to real thermography data, surpassing classical signal-processing baselines in both defect segmentation and depth estimation. Additional details at https://cab-lab-princeton.github.io/nefty/
ff39323c74c2dd8ae4425853675844b650417a53.title: Neural Field Thermal Tomography: A Differentiable Physics Framework for Non-Destructive Evaluation

ff861f12da551be7d42b87abdc72606686a40fdd.summary: arXiv:2608.27953v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Counterfactual reasoning requires models to reason beyond the observed world and explain how altered conditions propagate through downstream consequences. Existing benchmarks largely target bounded settings with fixed variables or single gold outcomes, overlooking open-domain scenarios requiring causal-process evaluation. To this end, we present $\textbf{WhatIfBench}$, a diagnostic benchmark for open-domain, open-form, long-horizon counterfactual causal reasoning, containing 220 what-if questions across STEM, HSS, and Hybrid scenarios. To evaluate free-form responses, we further propose $\textbf{PRISM}$, which first converts each natural-language explanation into a Response-Derived Semantic Causal Graph of events, states, and mechanisms. On top of this graph, PRISM then jointly applies a Process Metric assessing graph-level causal validity and a Rubric Metric assessing answer-level explanatory adequacy. Evaluating six frontier LLMs with this framework, we find that WhatIfBench remains far from saturated: even the strongest model reaches only a 64.62% final score. Further analysis reveals persistent causal gaps, premise drift, and topology fragmentation, suggesting that fluent counterfactual narratives often mask fragile causal processes. The benchmark, code, and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/zju-gt/WhatIfBench.
ff861f12da551be7d42b87abdc72606686a40fdd.title: The Illusion of What If: Evaluating the Breakdown of Counterfactual Reasoning in LLMs

ff8eeb389da7fc7ef150a77a8369c012aaf1e1d3.summary: arXiv:2611.28013v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: With the public awareness of artificial intelligence (AI) applications such as large language models (LLMs) and generative text-to-video models reaching unprecedented levels, there is an increasing need to reconcile the perspectives held by informed practitioners, who research and develop these technologies, with the interests and opinions of the general public, who constitute the majority of people impacted by technological developments. In this work, we survey practitioners (i.e., academics and industry professionals) alongside members of the general public on perspectives relating to pertinent areas of artificial intelligence, including perceived benefit and risk, the ability for models to achieve consciousness and output art, and the use of copyright protected material for model training. Alongside comparisons of diverse perspectives on these topics, we additionally contextualise the findings with a discussion of relevant literature that supports and refutes the myriad observed stances.
ff8eeb389da7fc7ef150a77a8369c012aaf1e1d3.title: Do as I Say, Not as You Do: Assessing Public Versus Practitioner Perspectives on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Language Technologies

ffc7f10ffb6eb11f1d39fd52791fcf45a92c7509.summary: arXiv:2611.29003v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conversational diagnosis prediction requires accurate, early, and stable predictions from ongoing clinical dialogue, yet dialogue-level labels do not specify when to commit. We propose a two-phase framework for learning deferral and diagnosis decisions. First, iterative commitment-boundary estimation constructs Defer/diagnosis supervision without annotated commitment times. Second, Defer-aware supervised fine-tuning initializes a policy, refined through reinforcement learning with trajectory-level rewards for timeliness, first-commit accuracy, and post-commit stability. On EMSDialog and MediTOD, DoC commits early, achieving the highest first-commit accuracy among post-trained methods (76.7%/51.2%) and the lowest post-commit error overall (16.4%/48.3%).
ffc7f10ffb6eb11f1d39fd52791fcf45a92c7509.title: DoC: Learning to Defer or Commit for Timely, Accurate, and Stable Conversational Diagnosis Prediction

ffd6e7d494f4787947f72860c675ac3a50e2333c.summary: arXiv:2603.02531v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Beyond classifier-free guidance, attention-space guidance extrapolates between a strong and a weak attention map within a single forward pass. However, two questions that govern its behavior remain unexamined: along which direction the extrapolation should proceed, and for how many sampling steps it should be applied. The first governs sample quality, and the second governs cost. Interestingly, viewing attention as sparse Hopfield retrieval answers both questions. At every sampling step, the informative direction is the component of the residual parallel to the sparse retrieval output. The guidance acts on the prompt in proportion to the attention mass that image queries assign to text tokens; and since the prompt shapes the image only in the early part of sampling, guidance matters only while the prompt is still being read. Building on this analysis, we propose Retrieval-Gated Attention Guidance (ReGA), which extrapolates only along this parallel component and applies the update only over the early steps holding half of the total prompt-attention mass. Extensive measurements inside the attention layers of UNet and MM-DiT backbones confirm both theoretical predictions. Across various backbone models, in multi-step and few-step regimes, ReGA consistently improves text alignment and human-preference scores over existing attention-space guidance methods, while adding as little as 2% inference time on MM-DiT backbones.
ffd6e7d494f4787947f72860c675ac3a50e2333c.title: Guidance Ends When Reading Ends: Retrieval-Gated Attention Guidance for Diffusion Models through a Hopfield Lens
